- **The Keyboard Shortcuts window** (Help › Keyboard Shortcuts, ⌥⌘/) lists every key the app
  answers, and nothing in it is written by hand. Keyboard gives the host its keys
  (`registrar.keyboardHelp { $0.keyboardHelpRows }`): a row for each thing they do, named as the
  tool's label, the command's title or the shortcut's own title says, keys under one name in one
  row (⌘↓, ↩ and ⌤ open the selection), the four arrows held alike written as one ("⇧←↑→↓"). A key
  no shortcut has is said beside the code that reads it, with the core's `registrar.keyHint` (no
  import of Keyboard): `registrar.keyHint("⌥ Drag", "Drag a Copy", while: .pointer)` in Selection,
  `registrar.keyHint("@", "Mention a Shape", while: .text)` in Mentions; Keyboard says the core's
  (⇧ keeps a drag to one axis, ⌘ makes a scroll zoom). The window (CanvasUI's
  `KeyboardShortcutsWindow`, opened by the app's delegate as Settings is) reads those rows and the
  menu bar as it opens: Tools, then each menu with its items' keys and the keys registered for the
  command an item runs, then Canvas (the registered keys no item carries), Pointer and Editing Text,
  each key once. So a key a plugin registers, a menu item a plugin's command gets, or a hint a
  plugin says is listed with no change to the window; CompositionTests'
  `keyboardShortcutsShippedTests` hold every shipped shortcut and menu key to being listed once, the
  restacking keys under Arrange, and Lock's ⇧L and Create Frame's ⇧⌘F under Canvas, since no menu bar
  item runs their commands.
- **The Shape menu** (between Edit and Arrange) is the selected shapes' context menu in the menu
  bar, so what it offers (Lock, Create Frame, Turn into …, Is a ▸, Color ▸) is reachable without a
  right-click, and what is a command has a key. It's [generated](#context-menus): an item of a context
  menu can run a command (`MenuItem(command: .createFrame, in: FramesMenuGroup.self)`),
  which gives it the command's title and shows its first key, and the plugin that makes context
  menus (ContextMenus) answers the core's point for the selection's menu (`registrar.menuForSelection`),
  told which commands to leave out: every one a menu bar item already runs, so Cut, Copy, Paste,
  Duplicate, Delete, Select All, Group, Ungroup and the restacking items are in Edit and Arrange and
  not in Shape, and a submenu left with nothing goes. The menu fills itself each time it opens,
  from the key window's board, and empties as it closes, so it holds nothing at rest (the Keyboard
  Shortcuts window drops it) and its keys are shown, not live. Its items dim as their commands do,
  and reach the window they were made for.
- **Arrange's restacking** (`]`, ⌥], ⌥[, `[`) are Reordering's own commands, placed after Group and
  Ungroup by their declarations (`menu: "Arrange"`, orders 100 to 130) and `.whenIdle`, so dimmed as
  their rule says and while text has the keyboard.
- **Keys that type stay out of text.** The menu bar never takes a key held without ⌘ from
  text: ⇧1, `]` and `[`, ⌥] (a quote on a US layout), ⌃ keys (emacs bindings). Elsewhere the item that
  names the key takes it (a digit by its number-row key), and leaves it while it's dimmed (AppKit's
  own menus take a dimmed item's key and beep). A ⇧⌘ letter goes to the item that names ⇧, and to
  none where only the letter without ⇧ is named: ⇧⌘F isn't Find's ⌘F.
- **Only on the canvas.** A key reaches the shortcuts while the canvas has the keyboard: typed in a
  note or a panel field, it's text, and a control in the panel that has the keyboard answers its own
  keys. What they do is still the same registered thing: Delete in the table of contents' list runs
  the `.delete` command, as Delete on the canvas and Edit › Delete do, and Escape anywhere in the
  panel gives the keyboard back to the canvas. The menu bar's other key equivalents (⌘S, the View
  menu's zoom) belong to their items and work wherever the keyboard is; with text or a panel's
  control focused, ⌘Z is the menu's, whose Undo is the text's own there and the board's elsewhere.
- **A key no shortcut takes** goes on to AppKit's key bindings, as any view's would. The standard
  actions they send that have a key of their own come back to the shortcuts as that key:
  `deleteBackward:` as ⌫, `deleteForward:` as ⌦, `insertNewline:` as ↩ and `cancelOperation:` as ⎋.
  So ⌃H (an emacs binding for `deleteBackward:`) does what Delete does, and so does a user's own
  key binding for it, or accessibility's cancel. The moves they send (an arrow key with nothing to
  nudge, `moveLeft:`; Page Down, `scrollPageDown:`) and what they'd type (`insertText:`) stop at
  the canvas, which does nothing with them, so a stray key doesn't beep. The canvas answers no other action, which goes on
  up the responder chain.
- **Tooltips.** `registry.help(for: tool)` is a tool's label and its key, "Note (N)", and
  `registry.help("Next", forCommand: .findNext)` a button's that runs a command,
  "Next (⌘G)" (Find's panel); a command with no key, the table of contents' way up
  (`.goUpBoard`), is its title alone. The toolbar (CanvasUI) can't see
  Keyboard, so Keyboard gives the tips to [the host's slot for them](#host-slots)
  (`registrar.toolTips`), which the toolbar reads (`registry.toolTip(for:)`). Its picker (`ToolPicker`) is an
  AppKit segmented control, since SwiftUI's segmented `Picker` dims none of its segments: one a
  tool, selected as the tool is current, and dimmed while the editor doesn't take the tool
  (`editor.isToolEnabled`, observed, so it follows a board shown, or a lock that lands above it).
  A click on a segment the editor refuses leaves the selection on the current tool.
- **The core's part** is one hook, like the secondary click's: at most one plugin claims key strokes
  (`registrar.keyStrokes { editor, stroke in ... }`, returning whether it took the key). `CanvasView`
  hands every key it gets to the editor (`editor.keyDown`, host API), as a `KeyStroke`: its
  characters as the keyboard's layout types them with no modifier but ⇧, the modifiers held, and
  whether it's a repeat. Without a claim, no key does anything on the canvas. Keyboard gathers each
  editor's shortcuts by chord once, in a service (`KeyboardState`), since the registry is frozen.
  The plugin that claims key strokes claims their releases too (`registrar.keyReleases { editor,
  stroke in ... }`): `CanvasView.keyUp` hands the editor each key let go (`editor.keyUp`), and
  `editor.keysReleased()` every key at once, as the canvas loses the keyboard, its window stops
  being key or a menu begins tracking (`NSMenu.didBeginTrackingNotification`: its loop takes the
  keys), where no release would reach it; a key let go with ⌘ held, which NSApplication never hands
  the key window, reaches the canvas that has the keyboard through a local event monitor. Keyboard
  runs a shortcut held down
  (`registrar.shortcut(chord, "Title", whileHeld:released:)`) once as it goes down, takes its
  repeats, and runs its release as it comes up: Space's, which holds the core's hand
  (`editor.isHandHeld`: a press pans as the Hand's does, whatever the tool, which stays the tool,
  since `setTool` would reset an arrow's targeting; the open hand, the closed one while it pans, and
  no hover meanwhile; held during another press, a drag, it waits for that one: the drag keeps its
  cursor, and at its release the tool hears the pointer leave and the open hand shows). The middle
  button pans the same way, through its own host entry point (`editor.panPointerDown`, from
  `CanvasView.otherMouseDown`), editing going on; released over a view the canvas hosts (the note
  being edited), the pointer leaves the canvas there, as a left press's release does. One press at a
  time: a left press during the middle button's pan ends the pan and is the press from then on.

## TextEditing

TextEditing ([`Sources/TextEditing`](../Sources/TextEditing)) is the text under every editable text
in the app, and the one list shown at a caret. It's a core module that depends on no other
module of the project, so it knows no canvas, registry, plugin or panel, and a plugin that types
into text imports it without importing the inspector: Arrows for an arrow's label, StickyNotes for its editor on the canvas, DetailPanel for its text boxes, Mentions for its text view
and its picker, SlashCommands for its list at a slash. It holds `EditingTextView`, how the app
checks the spelling of what's typed (`Spelling`), the caret list (`CaretList` and
`CaretListWindow`), `CaretListSubstitutions`, `StringDrawingLayout` ([where string drawing puts
text](#where-string-drawing-puts-text)) and the metrics they draw by (`TextEditingStyle`,
internal). TextEditingTests hold the list and its window, and the spelling settings, on TestKit
and CanvasTesting alone. What a list ranks typed text with isn't here but in [FuzzyMatching](#fuzzymatching).

### The text view

`EditingTextView` is an open `NSTextView` with what a host needs and SwiftUI's `TextEditor` doesn't
give, which a plugin subclasses for text of its own: Mentions' `MentionTextView` is one (a note's
editor on the canvas and the panel's `MentionTextArea`'s), and so
is every view the panel's boxes adopt `DetailTextContent` on ([Text of a plugin's own:
`DetailTextBox`](#text-of-a-plugins-own-detailtextbox)). So is an arrow's label's: it's mention
text, typed into a `MentionTextView` with the arrow as its owner.

- **What it adds does nothing until it's set**, so the same class with none of it set is a plain
  text view (a note's editor on the canvas is a `MentionTextView` with only `onCommit` set, which
  ends editing, and `commitsOnLeaving` off):
  `onCommit` (⌘↩, the keyboard leaving, and the view leaving its window with the keyboard, a turn
  later; without it ⌘↩ goes on as any key does), `commitsOnReturn` (with `onCommit`, Return
  commits and ⇧↩ is a new line), `commitsOnLeaving` (on unless set: off, only ⌘↩ commits, for
  text a host ends itself: a note's on the canvas, which ends with editing), `commitsWhileReadOnly` (⌘↩ commits
  read-only text too, for a commit that only ends editing: a type note's words while the
  model writes them), `onLeave` (the keyboard left, whatever for, after any commit), `onExit` (Escape: a host's hand-back to the canvas, the panel's) and
  `placeholder`.
- **Keys the view holds.** A view that shows a list at its caret ([below](#a-list-at-the-caret):
  Mentions' `@` picker and slash commands' list, a code editor's completions) keeps its window and says so, `override var
  caretListWindow: CaretListWindow? { pickerWindow }`, and `EditingTextView` does the rest, for
  every such list alike. While one's open, the view `holdsKeys`: the list's commands
  (`CaretList.perform`) go to it before the delegate's turn, a pick and a close through the
  window's `pickHighlighted()` and `closeList()`, which run its owner's; Return and Escape are never
  `onCommit`'s or `onExit`'s, and ⌘↩, where the text commits, closes the list and commits, as it
  does with none. ⌘. comes as no key: the window sends `cancelOperation:` up the responder chain
  from the view, which closes an open list; with none, the view doesn't answer it
  (`responds(to:)`), and it goes on up as though the view weren't there. The keyboard leaving the
  view, the view leaving its window and its being made read-only close the list too. What's left
  to the subclass is when a list opens, what it lists, and what a pick puts in. A subclass that
  holds keys for something else says so, `override var holdsKeys`. A view that `offersCompletions`
  (a code editor with completions, while it can be written) has ⌥⎋ for its own too, list or not:
  AppKit's `complete:`. Tests read where a list is placed and what it lists through
  `caretListWindow`.
- **A key first.** `onKeyDown` is asked of each key before the text has it (not while a list holds
  the keys, nor while text is being composed): true keeps it. A note's editor reads ⇧↩ and Tab with
  it, so a key is the host's without a subclass, and an open `@` or `/` list still has Tab.
- **Enabled or dimmed.** `showEnabled(_:)` shows the text as its host does: enabled, or dimmed
  (read-only, or something else writing it). By default the text's color, the label's or the
  secondary label's, set only when it changes; a view that colors its text itself says how
  (`MentionTextView` fades whole, text and pills, by its `alphaValue`). A host dims it through
  this and never by SwiftUI, so read-only text is still selected and copied, and the view still
  hears clicks.
- **The placeholder** is drawn dimmed where the text starts while there's none, in the view's
  font, else `TextEditingStyle.placeholderFont` (the system's, 11 pt).
- **Spelling.** `spelling = .app` checks the words typed as the app does (`Spelling.app`, Edit ›
  Spelling and Grammar), the same in every text that's words: a note's editor, an arrow's label's, a title's field, the panel's boxes of words (`DetailTextArea`,
  `MentionTextArea`). Check Spelling While Typing is on until it's turned off, Check Grammar With
  Spelling off until it's turned on, and Correct Spelling Automatically as System Settings has it
  until it's turned either way, the three kept in the user defaults. A text's own toggles for them
  (the menu bar's items, which go to the text with the keyboard, and the same ones in its context
  menu) change the settings, and every text that follows them changes at once. The words it's told
  to ignore come back to the settings as the keyboard leaves it, and every text that follows them
  ignores them from then on, until the app quits: an editor on the canvas is made for one editing,
  and AppKit keeps a view's ignored words in a spell document of its own, which goes with it. Without settings (`nil`), the view checks
  as AppKit has a text view check, marking no words as they're typed, for text that isn't words:
  code, a query, a name typed to pick a shape. A test gives a view settings of its own, over a
  defaults suite of its own (`Spelling(defaults:)`), never the app's.
- **Highlights.** `highlights` is a list of `TextHighlight`s (a range of the text and a fill), drawn
  with the background, so the text is over them, as rounded rects the height of a mention's pill in
  the text's font, reaching 2 points past the text at both ends, one for each line a range wraps
  over (`frames(of:)` says where, in the view's coordinates; TextKit 2 only, as `caretFrame` is).
  It's how an owner marks text that means something to it, with nothing for a host to forward: the
  view redraws when they change, and lets go of them when it's made read-only. Pass a fill that
  follows the surface the text is on, the text's own color at a low alpha, as a pill's does.
- **TextKit 2.** AppKit gives a text view whose class overrides `draw(_:)` TextKit 1, so
  `EditingTextView` draws its placeholder in `drawBackground(in:)`, and a subclass that needs TextKit
  2 (pills are attachments, laid out as the canvas lays them out) keeps it. On TextKit 2 it also
  puts the selection where a press began editing (`placeSelection(at:selectingWord:)`) and says
  where the caret is (`caretFrame`), as the editors on the canvas use them ([Editing:
  `MentionTextView`](#editing-mentiontextview)).

### A list at the caret

What a view shows over its text at its caret is the app's one caret list, whatever the text
(Mentions' `@` picker, slash commands' list and a code editor's completions are built on it). Its model, `CaretList`, is
headless: rows (`CaretListRow`: a header, an item, or the one row an empty list shows), the
highlight (the first item as rows are set; ↑ ↓ wrap, a page of `rowsShown` stops at the ends), and
`perform(_:)`, which says what a text view
command does to it (↑ ↓ ⌃P ⌃N and Page Up and Down move, Return and Tab pick, but aren't taken
with nothing highlighted, Escape, ⌥⎋ and F5 close; every other command is the text's). An item
(`CaretListItem`) is what its row shows, one line: a title with its matched characters in
semibold (in the item's `font`, if it has one), a symbol in its tint before it, a
`trailingSymbol` after it (a read-only shape's lock), a `detail` at the trailing end (its
`detailMatched` characters in semibold too, as a title's, and its `detailDimmed` ones fainter: Jump To's path), and what
VoiceOver says, the title and detail unless it says otherwise (matched characters aren't said), and `separated`, a line one point
thick across the top of its row (the words row under the shapes a pill's list offers), and a `chip`, a color: the row's symbol and title are then drawn in a capsule of that color, white on it (`TextEditingStyle`'s chip constants: 20 points, less 4 in a row it doesn't fit, 12-point text, matched characters semibold), and its highlight is the accent at 15% behind the capsule instead of the accent with white text (a type's color, in `/is-a`'s list); a row without one is drawn as ever. Its size is its owner's
(`CaretListMetrics`: width, row height, rows shown, the offset below the anchor), its look
`TextEditingStyle`'s. `CaretListWindow(list, accessibilityLabel:over:anchor:pick:close:post:)` shows
it: a borderless child of the text's window that never takes the keyboard (not deferred, so a
click's events name it, shown or not; a board's window, which ends a run of panel writes on a
click in another window, leaves clicks in its children alone), under the anchor
range's `firstRect` (its rows' text under the anchor's start; above the line where there's no
room below; on screen), following every view the text is in as it moves or scales, and asking
its owner to `close` once the anchor leaves the text's visible rect or the window stops being
key. A list that isn't at the text's caret takes a rect of its own instead:
`CaretListWindow(list, accessibilityLabel:over:anchorRect:pick:close:post:)`, a closure giving a rect
in screen coordinates (asked each time the window is placed; nil leaves it where it is), which the
window sits centered under at its metrics' width, below it or above it where there's no room, on
screen; the text view is then only its parent window's and what it follows, and the anchor can't
leave it (Jump To's palette, whose field is an `EditingTextView` and whose list is under the
capsule); VoiceOver hears it change and go through `post`, which an owner may route (Mentions counts
what its picker says). The owner decides the rest: when it opens and closes, what the query is,
what it lists (`setRows`), and what a pick inserts (`pick` gets the row's index); it calls
`listDidChange()` after each change and `dismiss()` as it closes. Every list ranks typed text
alike, with [`FuzzyMatcher`](#fuzzymatching), not TextEditing's: a list's owner imports FuzzyMatching
for it.

A list over text its own substitutions would rewrite (an `@query`, a `/name`) takes them as it opens
and turns them off while it's open: `CaretListSubstitutions(of: view)` holds the view's spelling
correction, text replacement, smart quotes and smart dashes, `CaretListSubstitutions.off` is all
four off, and `apply(to:)` sets a view's, so its owner puts them back as they were when the list
closes.

### Where string drawing puts text

The canvas draws text with string drawing (`NSAttributedString.draw(with:options:
.usesLineFragmentOrigin)`: a note's, an arrow's label), which says nothing of where it put each
character. `StringDrawingLayout(string, width:minimumLineHeight:)` does: an offscreen
`NSLayoutManager` with the 10.2 typesetter, which breaks lines and sets glyphs across them as string
drawing does (an alignment the paragraph names included), its lines stacked down the box as string
drawing stacks them, each at least `minimumLineHeight` (`lines`, `lines(fitting:)` for a box's
height). `lineRects(of:height:)` is where each range (UTF-16) is drawn: a rect a line it's on, as
wide as a selection of it would be (`enumerateEnclosingRects`: `boundingRect(forGlyphRange:)`
misplaces part of a centered line with that typesetter), as tall as the line, none past the box. It
lays out once, as it's made, so one kept per text and width makes a range's rects a lookup: what
[Find](#find)'s highlights are drawn from (Mentions keeps one with each built text, with its pills'
stand-ins in it, an arrow's label's too: it's mention text).

## FuzzyMatching

FuzzyMatching ([`Sources/FuzzyMatching`](../Sources/FuzzyMatching)) matches what's typed against
text: three matchers on one folding, a heap for the best few of what they match, and the "did you
mean" a language's refusal offers (`Suggestions`), a core module that depends on no other module of the
project (it knows no canvas, registry or plugin, and not TextEditing), pure and nonisolated, so any
thread runs it and its values are `Sendable`. FuzzyMatchingTests hold it on TestKit alone.

- **`FuzzyMatcher`** ranks a query against labels, as every list that ranks typed text does
  (Mentions' `@` picker, slash commands' list, a code editor's completions, and Jump To), so they
  agree. A `Query` is the typed text folded once (lowercased, without diacritics, each run of
  whitespace one space) and a `Label` a label folded once (each scalar marked where it starts a
  word, with the `Character` it came from); a label takes its best tier (`FuzzyRanking`): exact 1000,
  prefix 800, each word of the query a prefix of a word of the label in order 600, substring 400, a
  subsequence at most 300 (fzf's scoring: word starts, runs and the first character count, gaps
  cost), and, for a query of 4 characters or more that matched nothing above, one typo 100 (a
  Damerau edit of a word's prefix). `match(_:in:)` gives a `FuzzyMatch`: the score and the label's
  matched characters, as ranges of `Character` offsets, for a list to set in semibold.
  `matches(_:in:)` matches a list of labels, and `rank` is the two passes a list over many labels
  makes (every tier but the typo's over the labels it gives by index, nil for one it leaves out,
  then the typo's over the rest only when fewer than 8 matched), which Mentions' catalog makes
  over its keys, kept back to back in one buffer (`appendKeys`).
- **`TextSearch`** is Find's matcher: a query, a phrase of words, searched for in texts. A text is
  folded once (`FoldedText`) the way a label is, but a Unicode scalar at a time (a decomposed `e`
  and acute accent folds to `e`, as `é` does; whitespace is a space; `ß` is `ss`), into UTF-16
  units, with a table back to the original's units kept only if folding changed any scalar's length
  (ASCII, the usual text, folds in one pass over its bytes and keeps nothing). `hits(in:)` gives
  `TextHit`s, each a range of the original's UTF-16 units (a text view's, `NSString`'s) and whether
  it's `isExact`, in text order, at most `TextSearch.hitCap` (100): first every place the query's
  text is, mid-word too, one after another and never overlapping (as a browser's: "aa" in "aaaa" is two; whitespace runs equal to one
  another, so a phrase finds its words across a line break); then, from a word's start, the places
  it would be but for typos, each word of four letters or more with one edit (a letter changed,
  added, left out, or two swapped), the first letter of every word right, shorter words exact, the
  last word allowed to be a prefix of the text's word (typing mid-word keeps its hits), the end
  chosen as the matcher's typo tier does (no edit, then nearest the query's length) and never over
  a space of the text. A fuzzy hit that overlaps an exact one is dropped, so a hit is never twice.
  The query is made once per keystroke (`TextSearch(_:)`) and each text once; `hits(in:isCancelled:)`
  allocates only its hits and the ranges it finds on the way, and asks `isCancelled` every 64K units of a text (what it's found
  so far comes back, for the caller that cancelled to drop), so a keystroke can replace a search
  inside one long text, not only between texts.
- **`BoundedHeap`** keeps the best `capacity` of what's inserted, in a heap with the worst on top (the
  caller's `isWorse` says which), so an insert costs a logarithm of the capacity and `sorted()` gives
  the best first: Mentions' `@` picker and Jump To's list both keep their few rows' worth of matches
  in one, instead of sorting every match.
- **`PathMatcher`** is Jump To's: a query for a shape by the containers on the way to it, as VS Code's
  file switcher takes a path. A path is segments from the outermost container to the shape's own
  title, the leaf. The query splits on whitespace into pieces, which go into the segments in order,
  a group of neighbors to a segment (several pieces in one segment are one `FuzzyMatcher` query of
  the words joined), segments may be skipped, and the last group goes in the leaf. A group in a
  container may score only the exact, prefix, word-prefix, substring and typo tiers, never a bare
  subsequence (a container is named, the leaf is looked for); the leaf's, any tier. The score is
  `PathRanking.leafWeight` (2) × the leaf group's tier score, plus the containers' groups' scores,
  less `PathRanking.skipPenalty` (25) for each segment skipped, which is one that holds no group
  once a piece has gone into an earlier one (what's above the first group is unmentioned, not
  skipped). A query is at most `PathRanking.maximumPieces` (8) pieces, the words after the last
  part of it.
  `match(path:)` takes a path as strings and gives the score and, per segment, the matched
  characters (`Character` offsets, and `PathMatcher.utf16Ranges(_:in:)` converts them to UTF-16
  offsets), and how many segments it skipped. A caller that ranks thousands of shapes in a tree
  doesn't: it keeps a `PathMatcher.Row` per container, the best score for each count of pieces placed
  so far along the chain from the root through that container, found from the parent's row
  (`advance(_:through:)`, nil for an untitled container, a skip; it costs a match of every group of
  the pieces that fit, at most 28 at eight pieces, once per container, not per shape beneath it), and a leaf's score is
  `leafScore(after:label:)` from its parent container's row, which costs one match of each group of
  its label, a few for a few pieces. A one-piece query has no path in it: that's `FuzzyMatcher` over
  the leaves.
- **`Suggestions`** is the "did you mean" a refusal offers for a word a language doesn't have (a
  title, a kind, an attribute, a word of `canvas draw`'s or `canvas query`'s), DrawScript's, Draw's
  and Queries': `closest(to:among:limit:)` gives the few most like it, best first (the same but for
  case, spacing and × written as x; then one inside the other; then sharing a word; then a few
  letters off, a swapped pair one edit), and `isNearMiss` whether one title is a slip of another.
  It folds on its own (lowercased, whitespace one space, × as x), not as the matchers do, and counts
  edits only where they decide something, so a board's titles cost their folding.

## Palette

Palette ([`Sources/Palette`](../Sources/Palette)) is the color math: a core module that depends
on no other module of the project (it knows no canvas, registry, plugin, kind or named color), pure,
nonisolated and `Sendable` but for the few lines that make AppKit's colors. A module that makes a
color that follows the appearance, or checks that one reads, imports it. PaletteTests hold it on
TestKit alone.

- **`RGB`** is a color as its sRGB components, 0 to 1, with no alpha: `RGB(hex: 0x4465E9)`,
  `RGB(hexString: "#4465E9")` (or `#46E`, in either case; nil for anything else), `hexString` (six
  digits, in capitals), `over(_:alpha:)` (what a faint fill of it looks like on a ground),
  `luminance` and `contrast(with:)` (WCAG's, 1 to 21), which every floor below is in.
- **`OKLCH`** is the same color as how light it is, how colorful and which hue (Oklab in polar
  form). A color's variations are made there: moving `lightness` alone keeps what the eye calls the
  same color, where moving sRGB's components, or HSL's lightness, turns its hue. `OKLCH(rgb)` and
  `.rgb` convert, and `.rgb` of a color too colorful for sRGB is the most colorful one of the same
  lightness and hue, so lightening a color only pales it where it must and never turns it.
- **`Tone`** is a color in the light appearance and in the dark (`tone[dark: isDark]`).
- **`Swatch`** is the looks one color is drawn in. A color is a starting point: what draws it draws
  one of seven roles worked out from it, each a `Tone`, so the same color suits a line, a surface,
  text and a sheet of paper, on either canvas. `Swatch(color)` makes them the same way for every
  color:

  | Role | What draws it | How it comes from the color |
  |---|---|---|
  | `solid` | A line or a symbol on the canvas, and a fill that holds text | The color itself where it reads on the canvas at 3:1 (`lineContrast`), else the nearest lighter or darker color of its hue that does |
  | `onSolid` | Text on `solid` | White, or black where white is under 4.5:1 (`textContrast`); one of the two always reads |
  | `wash` | A faint surface on the canvas | `solid` at 14% over the canvas (`washStrength`) |
  | `surface` | A large surface that holds shapes (a region, a card) | `solid` at 5% (`surfaceStrength`) over a ground raised off the canvas as a panel is (`raised`: white, and a lighter gray in the dark) |
  | `ink` | Text in the color, on the canvas, on `wash` or on `surface` | `solid`, made lighter or darker until it reads on all three at 4.5:1 |
  | `paper` | A sheet of paper (a note) | The hue as a light pastel (`paperLightness`, at most `paperChroma`), the same in both appearances |
  | `paperInk` | Text on `paper` | A note's ink |

  Each floor is met by construction: `Swatch.reading(_:against:atLeast:)` finds the lightness
  nearest the color's that reads against the grounds it's handed, darker on light grounds and
  lighter on dark ones, 2% over the floor so the color still meets it rounded to 8 bits. Paper is
  one sheet whatever the appearance, since paper stays paper in the dark, and as light whatever the
  color, so the inks drawn on a note read on every one. The canvas the roles are made for is
  `Swatch.canvas` unless another is handed in.
- **AppKit.** `NSAppearance.isDark` is the one test for a dark appearance (vibrant and
  high-contrast dark ones are dark); `NSColor(light:dark:)` a color of two `RGB`s that follows the
  appearance it's drawn in, resolved as it's drawn (read its `cgColor` in the drawing, never ahead
  of it); `NSColor(rgb)` and `NSColor(tone)`; and `rgb.cgColor`, for a drawing that knows which
  appearance it's in. A dynamic color whose two values aren't opaque sRGB (a white at an alpha, a
  system color) is still `NSColor(name: nil) { $0.isDark ? … : … }`.

tldraw's colors are the model: each of its named colors has fourteen hand-picked values in a light
and a dark palette (`solid`, `semi`, `noteFill`, `frameFill` and the rest). The roles here are the
same idea with one difference: they are computed from the one color, so a color someone picked gets
the treatment a named one does.

## Host slots

A board's window puts things around its canvas that are plugins': the path of crumbs over its top,
a palette, the inspector beside it, the window's subtitle, the panes of the Settings window, the
toolbar's tips, the keys its menu items show. And the app takes three more things from them: the rows of its Keyboard Shortcuts
window, what its Copy as Image draws, and the commands its command server runs. A plugin can't import the window (CanvasUI) or the
app, and neither can import a plugin (the app and CanvasUI may use only the core and the app's
own modules). So what passes between them is declared beneath both, in the core,
[`Sources/Canvas/Plugins/HostSlots.swift`](../Sources/Canvas/Plugins/HostSlots.swift): ten
extension points a plugin contributes to and the host reads. The menu bar's commands are no slot:
they're the [commands](#commands) plugins declare with a `menu:`, which the window reads as
`registry.menuBarCommands`. The core imports SwiftUI for them,
since its slots hold views, and the wire (CanvasRPC), for the types the commands are said in; it
knows no plugin and no window.

Every point is the core's (`owner` is `.core`), so it's always installed: a plugin contributes from
its own `register`, with no plugin value of its own for it, and a list without the plugin is a
host without its piece. Nothing joins a plugin to the host: the list of what ships only names
plugins ([What ships](#what-ships)).

| Slot | A plugin says | The host reads | Shipped |
|---|---|---|---|
| Views over the canvas (`HostOverlays`, a list in plugin order, a later one over an earlier) | `registrar.hostOverlay(alignment:coveredTop:) { editor, onExit in … }` | `registry.hostOverlays`, `registry.hostCoveredTop(on:)` | Boards' path (`.top`, covering its pill's height off the root), Jump To's palette |
| The inspector (`HostInspectors`, at most one) | `registrar.hostInspector(isRequested:onDismiss:) { editor, onExit in … }` | `registry.hostInspector` | the detail panel |
| The window's subtitle (`WindowSubtitles`, at most one) | `registrar.windowSubtitle { editor in … }` | `registry.windowSubtitle(for:)` | Boards: the board shown's name, none on the root |
| Settings panes (`SettingsPanes`, in plugin order, a title once) | `registrar.settingsPane("Anthropic") { … }` | `registry.settingsPanes` | the Anthropic key's, when the model is Anthropic's |
| Tool tips (`ToolTips`, at most one) | `registrar.toolTips { tool, registry in … }` | `registry.toolTip(for:)`, the tool's label without one | Keyboard: "Note (N)" |
| The key a menu item shows for a command (`MenuKeys`, at most one) | `registrar.menuKeys { command, registry in … }`: a `MenuKey`, a menu's key equivalent and modifiers | `registry.menuKey(of:)`, read by the menu bar's items and a context menu's that run a command; none without one | Keyboard: the first key that runs the command (Delete as Backspace's character) |
| The Keyboard Shortcuts window's rows (`KeyboardHelp`, at most one) and key hints (`KeyHints`, any number) | `registrar.keyboardHelp { registry in … }`; `registrar.keyHint("⌥ Drag", "Drag a Copy", while: .pointer)` | `registry.keyboardHelp`: the one list's rows, then the hints, each row once | Keyboard: every key it registers; the hints of each plugin that reads a key no shortcut has |
| What Copy as Image draws (`ImageSources`, at most one) | `registrar.imageSource(isAvailable:) { editor in … }`: whether there is anything to draw, and the shapes of the board shown a picture of the selection (or the board, with nothing selected) shows | `registry.imageSource` | Clipboard: the shapes a copy would take (`editor.imageShapes()`) |
| The commands (`HostCommands`, at most one) | `registrar.hostCommands(specs:run:)`, both handed the built registry | `registry.hostCommands`: the specs, and how to run one by name | Automation: every plugin's command |

A view a plugin gives is made for a window's canvas: it's handed that board's editor and `onExit`,
which gives the keyboard back to the canvas (`CanvasFocus.take`), and follows the editor by itself.
A view over the canvas is over the whole of it at its `alignment`, and takes clicks only where it
draws. Not a `CanvasOverlay`, which the canvas draws into itself, in the world: these are the
window's views.

The window's side is CanvasUI's, and knows no plugin:

- **`BoardChrome(editor:showsInspector:onExit:)`**, a view modifier the app applies to its canvas
  (`CanvasRepresentable`, after its frame and toolbar): each registered view over the canvas, in
  plugin order, then the registered inspector in an `.inspector`, with the toolbar button that
  shows and hides it (Inspector; its tooltip "Show Inspector" or "Hide Inspector", as View › Show
  Inspector is titled). A registry with no inspector gets none.
- **The inspector follows what wants it.** An inspector may say it's wanted whether or not the
  person has it shown (`isRequested`, read in a view's body, so on observable state), and what
  hiding it meanwhile does (`onDismiss`). The window keeps the rule, for whatever is wanted: wanted
  while hidden, it's shown; no longer wanted, it's hidden again if that's what showed it, and left
  as the person had it otherwise; hidden by the person while wanted, what wanted it is dismissed
  and the keyboard goes back to the canvas. The detail panel is wanted while [a takeover](#the-overview-and-takeovers)
  is active and dismissing escapes it, so ⌘F shows a hidden inspector, closing Find hides it again,
  and hiding the inspector closes Find, though the window has never heard of Find.
- **What the canvas covers.** A view over the canvas says how far down it reaches on a board
  (`coveredTop`: the path's pill, about 35 points inside a subboard). The window tells each board's
  editor the most any says (`BoardDocument` sets `editor.coveredTop` from
  `registry.hostCoveredTop(on:)`), so a fit leaves it clear. A headless editor is told nothing, and
  covers nothing.
- **The subtitle** is read observed by `BoardWindowController`, so it follows a switch of board or
  a rename.
- **`SettingsWindow(registry:)`** hosts the panes, one under another in plugin order, each made
  afresh as the window opens; a pane says what it is itself, so none is headed.
- **`ToolPicker(editor:)`** reads each tool's tip, and shows the tool lock on the selected segment.
- **Edit › Copy as Image** (⇧⌘C) is the window controller's own item (`copyAsImage:`): dimmed while
  `registry.imageSource` has nothing to draw, else it draws the shapes the slot gives from the board's
  own file with `BoardPicture(file:registry:board:showing:)`, so they're drawn as the canvas draws them
  (the file's colors, types and what mentions name are all there to read; only those shapes drawn) (2×, the window's appearance, at most 2048 points a side, 32 of margin) and puts the
  PNG on the pasteboard `BoardConfiguration.imagePasteboard` names: the system's in the app, a test's
  own in tests.
- **View › Focus Inspector** (⌥⌘I) is the controller's too (`focusInspector:`): it shows the inspector
  if it's hidden, then gives the keyboard to the inspector's list or table if it shows one, else its
  first text field, else its first control, top to bottom (the views outside the canvas that accept
  first responder), trying again for a few turns while a view just shown has none; a window with
  no inspector dims it.
- **`CommandServer.Commands(registry:)`** is the commands the server runs beyond its own
  ([The command line](#the-command-line)): none where the list has no command line.

The app's own side is one line: it starts its command server on
`CommandServer.Commands(registry:)`.

Tests: CanvasTests' `hostSlotsTests` hold the points with contributors of their own (order, the
most covered, one inspector, one subtitle, a pane's title once, a tip's default, what Copy as Image
draws, the commands read off the built registry and none without a contributor); CanvasUITests' `chromeTests` the chrome over a real canvas in an
unshown window (each view where it says, the inspector's rule with a fixture that's wanted while a
model says) and `toolPickerTests` the tips; each plugin's own tests what it gives; and
CompositionTests the shipped six (ShippedTests) and the window's behavior with Find
(`findShippedTests`).

## The detail panel

The detail panel is the inspector beside the canvas, after Keynote's: it shows the selected shape
and edits its properties. It's a horizontal ([`Sources/DetailPanel`](../Sources/DetailPanel)) like
any other. It declares two extension points, kinds and other plugins contribute to them, and the
core has never heard of it. Its text boxes are built on [TextEditing](#textediting)'s text view and
caret list.

### Anatomy and conventions

```
┌─ inspector column: 248 to 340 pt, 260 ideal ────────┐
│ ‹ {}  Customer                                      │ header: back, symbol, title (here a
│       2 fields                                      │   field: the card is renamed there)
│ ⟦ Schema ⟧  Issues                                  │ tab strip, hidden with one tab
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ ⌄ JSON                                              │ a titled section collapses; its rows
│   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │   are stock SwiftUI and the panel's
│   │ { "title": "Customer",                      │   │   primitives, here code, monospaced,
│   │   "required": ["email"],                    │   │   as tall as its lines
│   │   "properties": { "name": {}, "phone": {} } │   │
│   │ }                                           │   │
│   └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│   ⚠ “email” is required, but isn’t a property.      │ a status line of the section's own
│                        (scrolls)                    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ (footer)                                            │ footer: status lines, on every tab,
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   hidden when empty (none ship today)
```

The panel owns all of the chrome, and plugins fill it in:

| The panel decides | Plugins provide |
|---|---|
| The header's frame, and its back button (Selection's `.goBack`, Go › Back, called and keyed as the command is, shown while its rule says there's a step back) | The header: a `DetailHeader` (title, subtitle, symbol), or a view built on `DetailHeaderLabel` (Titles' `TitleHeader`) |
| The tab strip, the tab order, and the tab remembered per kind | Which tab each section goes in |
| Section chrome: the header, chevron, insets, dividers, collapsing, and remembered collapse | Section titles, ids and order |
| Scrolling, the footer, and the empty states | The rows in a section, and status lines: the footer's, or a tab's (the Issues tab above, while the card has any) |
| Fonts, control size, the label column and checkbox toggles, all through the environment | |
| Focus: what gives the keyboard back to the canvas | |

With nothing selected the panel shows its overview, a view the host may give it (the app's is [the
table of contents](#the-table-of-contents)), else "No Selection". With several, it shows "N Shapes"
over the kinds selected, then the overview (details are per shape: editing several at once isn't
built). A shape with no sections to show (an arrow, a note without issues, in a list without [Neighbors](#neighbors)'
Connections tab, which every shape has) gets its header, then "No Options". Without `DetailPanelPlugin` installed, the panel says "No Details". A
read-only shape (a [locked](#locking) one, one in a locked frame, at any depth, or one on a locked
subboard's board) shows its whole panel, but nothing in it edits the shape: the panel disables its sections' content, and its header
(a title field), and leaves going back, the tabs and collapsing as they were. A section whose
controls change nothing of the shape says so, `DetailSection(…) { … }.enabledWhileReadOnly()`, and
keeps them working (References' Go to Original: going to a locked reference's shape changes nothing); whatever they
write is refused there all the same. Whether the shape can change is asked where the panel's root
reads the shape's record, on every commit (`editor.isReadOnly(id)`: the rules of the shape and
of the containers it's in, and whether its board can change, O(its depth)), and handed to the shape's
panel as a value, so the shape's panel never reads the document, and draws again when that changes
though the shape's record doesn't: its frame locked or unlocked, or the subboard its board belongs
to, in a commit on another board.

Sections are stock SwiftUI plus a few primitives, and get the look by following these conventions:

- **Rows.** A labeled control is `LabeledContent("Status") { control }`; the panel lines every label
  up in one 72 pt column and hides the control's own label (its placeholder stays). A read-only
  value is `LabeledContent("Fields", value: ...)`. A toggle stands alone, drawn as a checkbox
  with its label after it; in a row, it's a bare box, beside what it governs (a due date's
  checkbox, beside the date). A text box in a row lines its label up with its first line of text, not its top edge.
- **Primitives.** A number is a `DetailNumberField`, and a pair of them (Width and Height) goes in
  `DetailFields`. Multiline text is a `DetailTextArea` (with a `placeholder:` shown while it's
  empty, and an `onCommit:` for text that's acted on once it's done: then Return commits, ⇧↩ is a
  new line, and the keyboard leaving commits too, a turn later if the text view left its window
  with the keyboard, so capture a service in `onCommit` weakly: the board may have gone; `asTyped: true`
  for a value rather than words: the panel's font, and nothing changed as it is keyed, no spelling check or
  correction, quotes, dashes or replacement), code a
  `DetailCodeEditor` (monospaced, typed exactly as keyed: smart quotes and dashes, text
  replacement, autocorrect, spelling, automatic completion, inline predictions, math results and
  Writing Tools off; lines never wrap, so a line's indentation says where it is and line N of an error is
  the Nth on screen, and a long one scrolls sideways; as tall as its lines, from
  `DetailStyle.codeEditorHeight` (a text area's height, so a short text sits in a short box with
  what's said about it close under it) to what the panel shows, less room for its section's title; Tab
  two spaces, Return a new line as indented as the last, one step more after `{` or `[`; ⌘↩ and the
  keyboard leaving call its `onCommit`; `isEditable: false` makes it read-only; `coloring:` colors
  its runs and `completions:` completes it, below), a list a
  `DetailList` (empty, it says No Items), a color `DetailSwatches` (named presets, the chosen one
  marked, then the color well; it spans the row, so it goes in a section of its own, not in a
  `LabeledContent`). `.detailUpdating(isUpdating)` marks a text box something else is writing just
  now (a model): read-only, and so dimmed; nothing is drawn over its text. What's writing it says
  so in words where the person is: a status line of a section's own, a `DetailStatusLine`, drawn
  as the footer's (only its symbol takes the tone; its text can be selected and copied, and a line
  whose selected text has the keyboard as it goes hands the keyboard back to the canvas, as a
  field that goes does), with a spinner in the symbol's place, as wide,
  while `isBusy`, and link buttons under it
  (`DetailStatusAction("Retry") { … }`). Put it where it can't be collapsed away from the person. Text that isn't a string (mentions
  of shapes) goes in a box as a text area's, over a text view of the plugin's own
  ([`DetailTextBox`](#text-of-a-plugins-own-detailtextbox)): Mentions' `MentionTextArea` is one.
  `DetailNumberText` formats and parses numbers with units ("240 pt"), in the user's locale ("2,5 h" in German), as the number field does. A
  `DetailCommandButton(command: .goToOriginal, systemImage: "arrow.up.forward.square")`
  runs a [command](#commands) a plugin declared (`editor.perform`), titled as the command is
  (`registry.title(of:)`, unless `title:` says otherwise), its tooltip the title and the command's key
  ("Next (⌘G)", Keyboard's `registry.help(_:forCommand:)`; none for a command with no key), and dimmed while it can't run
  (`editor.canPerform`): the panel's counterpart of a menu item, borderless like the panel's other
  buttons. It finds the editor in the environment the panel sets, so a section still never sees it.
- **Code's colors and completions.** A `DetailCodeEditor`'s language is its plugin's; the panel
  colors it and completes it. `coloring: { text in … }` names the text's runs (`DetailCodeSpan`:
  a name, a string, a number, a keyword, or what doesn't belong, red and underlined), asked for
  the whole text at every keystroke, so a scan, not a parse. `completions: { text, caret in … }`
  (a `DetailCodeCompleting`, the caret in UTF-16) says what can be typed at the caret, or nil: a
  `DetailCodeCompletions`, the `range` a pick replaces (it holds the caret), what's typed so far
  (`query`), and every candidate, as offered and unfiltered, each a `DetailCodeCompletion` (its
  `label`, a `detail`, the `insert` that replaces the range, the `selection` within it a pick
  leaves, the caret or what's to be typed over, `reopens` where that has completions of its own,
  and `isRelevant`). ⌃Space opens the list (so does AppKit's `complete:`, ⌥⎋ and F5, since macOS
  may keep ⌃Space for switching input sources) while the text can be written, where something's
  offered: nothing opens elsewhere, and nothing beeps. It's the app's one caret list (Mentions' `@`
  picker's too: [TextEditing](#a-list-at-the-caret)), under what's typed, each row the label
  in the code's font, what's typed matched in its semibold, then the detail, which takes what the label leaves (cut short with "…" past that),
  VoiceOver saying both; no header, no footer. While it's open ↑ ↓ (⌃P ⌃N) and Page Up and Down
  move through it, Return, Enter and Tab pick, Escape, ⌘., ⌃Space, ⌥⎋ and F5 close it (the panel
  stays; a second Escape leaves it), ⌘↩ closes it and commits, as ever (the list's key is Return,
  never ⌘↩), and every other key is the text's. After each keystroke and
  move of the caret it asks again and ranks what's offered by what's typed, with
  `FuzzyMatcher`'s tiers (nothing typed: as offered; else the best tier first, then what
  `isRelevant`, then as offered; what doesn't match is left out), and closes once nothing's left,
  the caret leaves the place it opened for (the range starts elsewhere), the text is shown from
  outside or can't be written (`detailUpdating`, a locked shape), the keyboard or the window goes,
  the window stops being key, or what's typed scrolls out of view. A pick replaces the range with
  its `insert`, one step of the text's undo that the box writes as typing (so it joins the field's
  run of writes, and in a board's window a click in the list, a child window, doesn't end it), and
  one that `reopens` opens the list again at once. `onCompleting: { isOpen in … }` hears the list
  open and close (a pick that opens it again, not at all: it's still open), for what waits on the
  person's choosing: text a pick leaves waiting for a value may already be whole (`"type": ""` is
  JSON), so a type's sync holds its idle wait meanwhile. Without `completions`, F5 does
  nothing and ⌥⎋ leaves the panel as Escape does: code gets no dictionary words. A type's JSON is the
  shipped one ([Completing the JSON](#completing-the-json)).
- **Sections.** A tab's first section may be untitled; use it for the main properties. Every
  titled section collapses. Titles are one or two nouns in Title Case.
- **No styling of your own.** No fonts, sizes, padding or backgrounds.
- **Writes** go only through the section's `ShapeBinding`. Sections never see the editor; one that
  shows a plugin's own state about its shape reads that plugin's service, `$x.service(S.self)` (a
  type's sync), from a view of its own, so observing it redraws only that view.

### Tabs are types; any plugin adds one

A tab is a type conforming to `DetailTab`. Any module may declare one, and there's no registration
call: a tab shows for a shape when a shown section that applies to the shape names it.

```swift
public enum TypeSchemaTab {}
extension TypeSchemaTab: DetailTab {
    public static var title: String { "Schema" }
    public static var order: Order<Self> { .after(NeighborsTab.self) }
}
```

Being a type, a tab can't be misspelled, and sharing one means importing the module that declares
it. Its `order` says where it goes among a shape's tabs, beside the others rather than by a number
([Order](#order-where-things-go-among-each-other)); one that says nothing goes where it first
appears, a kind's own contributions first, then the rest in plugin order. As shipped:

| Tab | Its order | So |
|---|---|---|
| A kind's own (a subboard's Description, a reference's Reference) | `.first` | first, before the tab a feature's opt-in brings from the kind's own `register` |
| Types' Types, Neighbors' Connections (`NeighborsTab`, on every shape and always) | none | in plugin order, after a kind's own |
| Types' Schema (`TypeSchemaTab`, on every type) | `.after(NeighborsTab.self)` | right after Connections: a type's panel opens on what is connected to it |
| `StyleTab`: appearance, shared by every kind | `.last` | last, as a shared tab trails in Keynote |
| A tab of the shape's state that comes and goes with it (Validation's `IssuesTab`) | `.after(StyleTab.self)` | after Style, so the others keep their places |

Use the shared `StyleTab` rather than a near-duplicate. Two tab types with one title
would show as two identical tabs, so they're a registry error (`invalid`, below), whether sections
or status lines name them.

### Contributing: two points and their sugar

| Point | Kind | Holds |
|---|---|---|
| `ShapeDetails` | keyed | A header and sections, one contribution per `details` call. Each section claims (target, tab, id), and a header claims its target, so two plugins adding a Color section to a kind's Style tab, or two headers for one kind, are a `conflict`. A kind's own section and a scoped one (an every-box one, say) may share an id; both show. |
| `DetailStatuses` | list | Status lines, the shape's state rather than its settings, as a `DetailStatusContribution`: where they go (the footer, or a tab) and `@MainActor (AnyShapeRecord, DetailContext) -> [DetailStatus]`. |

Plugins write the sugar, not the points:

| Sugar | For |
|---|---|
| `x.details(header:) { sections }` | This kind's header and sections, inside `registrar.shape { x in ... }`. The header is a view made from the shape's binding ([the header](#the-header)). |
| `registrar.details(P.self, header:) { sections }` | Another plugin's kind, typed as its own. |
| `registrar.detailsForEveryBox { sections }` | Every shape with a frame (the kinds with the `.box` capability), editing the frame. Arrows have none, so they don't get these. |
| `scope.details { sections }`, in `registrar.forShapes(holding: P.self)`, `forShapes(adopting:)` or `forEveryShape` | The shapes of the kinds the scope reaches, over the whole record (`DetailSection<AnyShapeRecord>`); its writes change the record, in a step named for the section. For what a feature shows about the kinds that opted into it that no property or box says (Colors' row, on the kinds that hold a color), or, in `forEveryShape`, what every shape has (Neighbors' Connections does). A section that shows only in some state says so with `shownWhile`. |
| `x.details(of: P.self) { sections }`, `registrar.details(of: P.self) { sections }` | An [added property](#added-properties), editing its value: on this kind's shapes that have one, or on every shape that has one (the kinds that hold it: scoped `.holding(P)`). |
| `scope.detailStatus { shape, context in ... }` | Footer lines for the shapes of the kinds the scope reaches. Return `[]` when there's nothing to say. |
| `scope.detailStatus(in: SomeTab.self) { shape, context in ... }` | Lines in a tab for those shapes. The tab shows while the shape has lines there, above its sections if it has any. Validation's Issues tab is one, in `forEveryShape`. |

Both points take [scopes](#scopes): a section or a line for the shapes of other kinds says which, and
one for every kind with no scope is refused (`invalid`).

`details` always takes its trailing builder, so a header alone is `details(header: ...) {}`. A
section is a `DetailSection` naming its tab, with an optional title, an `id` (the title by
default, or "main"), an optional `when` that hides it (and a tab it leaves empty) for some values,
and its content. `when` runs on every render, so keep it cheap. The panel contributes no sections
of its own ([`DetailPanelPlugin`](../Sources/DetailPanel/DetailPanelPlugin.swift) registers only
its state, `registrar.service { DetailPanelState(editor: $0) }`): every section is some plugin's.
Sections for every box, in a Frame tab of their own (DetailPanelTests' `FramesPlugin`):

```swift
registrar.detailsForEveryBox {
    DetailSection("Size", in: FrameTab.self) { $frame in
        DetailFields {
            DetailNumberField("Width", value: $frame.size.width, unit: "pt", in: 1...100_000)
            DetailNumberField("Height", value: $frame.size.height, unit: "pt", in: 1...100_000)
        }
    }
    DetailSection("Position", in: FrameTab.self) { $frame in ... }
}
```

Four pieces for a section's rows. `DetailCheckbox("Title", isOn: $x)` is a label-hidden `Toggle`
beside a `Text` that toggles on a click (4 points apart), for a `LabeledContent` row's content, so
the row reads "Label [] Title" on macOS 14 and 15 alike (a bare `Toggle` in a row puts its title in
the label column on 14). `DetailShapeRow(symbol:tint:name:detail:lines:dimmed:)` is a row for a shape
in a list: the kind's symbol (in `tint`, else secondary) in the status icon's column, the name on
one line in the panel's text size, an optional trailing `detail` at 10 points secondary, up to two
`lines` of 10 point secondary under the name, and `dimmed` for a row that can't be gone to, which
dims the whole row, secondary text too. It uses the panel's own row metrics, which stay internal;
wrap it in a `Button` to make it one. `DetailGroupHeader(_:count:tint:isCollapsed:toggle:)` heads a list
of such rows inside a section and folds it: a disclosure triangle, a dot in `tint` when the list has a
color of its own, the title and the count if given, all one borderless button as tall as a section's
header; the caller keeps whether the list is folded and leaves its rows out while it is.
`DetailSearchField("Search", text: $text)` searches such a list: a magnifying glass, the text typed as
keyed (nothing corrected), and a button that clears it once there's text, as tall as a list row;
Escape, as anywhere in the panel, gives the keyboard back to the canvas. All four are in
`ListRows.swift`, and DetailPanelTests' `listRowTests` hold them.

`when` reads only the value. A section of the shape's state that a service knows (whether its types
give it a field) says when it shows with `shownWhile`, over the record and a `DetailContext`, as
Types' Fields does. A scope picks kinds, never shapes, so a section for only some of a scope's
shapes says which the same way:

```swift
registrar.forShapes(holding: IsAProperty.self) { typeable in
    typeable.details {
        DetailSection(TypesStyle.fieldsTitle, in: TypesTab.self, id: "fields") { $record in FieldsList(record: $record) }
            .enabledWhileReadOnly()
            .shownWhile { shape, context in
                shape[TypeSchemaProperty.self] == nil && context.service(FieldBook.self)?.givesFieldsOrValues(shape) == true
            }
    }
}
```

It's asked on every commit, whatever the commit changed (a drag of another shape), as status
lines are, so it must cost O(1): read a service's cached state. Only the sections that have one
are asked (found once per kind), so a kind without any costs nothing. A section it hides takes its
tab with it when the tab has nothing else to show, and the shape's panel is built again only when
what it hides changes; a view in the section that shows more of that state observes it itself,
since the section is built again only when its shape changes.

How it resolves, per shape:

| What | Order |
|---|---|
| Sections in a tab | The kind's own (from its vertical, a horizontal it opts into, or another plugin that imports it), in plugin order and builder order; then those whose scope reaches the kind (every-box sections, those over an added property on every shape that has it, a scope's `details`), in plugin order. |
| Tabs | By `order`, then first appearance over the same sequence, then status lines'. A tab with no shown section (by `when` and `shownWhile`) and no status line is dropped. |
| Status lines, the footer's and each tab's | The kind's, then those whose scope reaches it, each in plugin order. |
| Header | The kind's own; else the kind's label and symbol (`registry.label(of:)`: what the kind declares, else its placing tool's, else its id). A header without a symbol takes the kind's. |

`DetailPanelState` (`editor.detailPanel`) gathers each kind's contributions once, since the
registry is frozen, and resolves the selected shape's layout (running `when` and the headers) as
it's shown. It also remembers, per editor and in memory, the tab last chosen for each kind and the
collapsed sections. A collapsed every-box section collapses for every kind; a kind's own, for
that kind only.

### The header

A kind's header is a view it makes from its shape's binding, as a section's content is:

```swift
gadget.details(header: { $gadget in DetailHeader(gadget.name, subtitle: gadget.mode.rawValue) }) { ... }
```

- **`DetailHeader`** is the stock header: a symbol, then a title on one line over a subtitle, as the
  panel lays them out. A kind without a header of its own gets one with its label
  (`registry.label(of:)`).
- **A header of the kind's own** builds on `DetailHeaderLabel(subtitle:systemImage:) { title }`,
  that layout with any view as its title, so it looks like every other header.
  `DetailHeaderField(text, placeholder:)` is the title as a field, for a header that renames its
  shape in place: borderless, in the header's font, writing as you type (as the panel's text
  fields do), with the kind's name as its placeholder by default, its spelling checked as the
  app's is (an AppKit field drawn as SwiftUI's plain one is, whose field editor is an
  `EditingTextView` of its own: SwiftUI's fields can't be told to check spelling). Return, like
  Escape anywhere in the panel, gives the keyboard back to the canvas. `isEditable: false` shows
  the title as text in its place, at full strength, for a title that can't be written just now;
  `disabled` dims the field, for a while something else writes it.
- **A header without a symbol** shows its kind's: the panel hands a header view its kind's name
  and symbol through the environment, as the table of contents hands a row its symbol.
- **Headless**, `layout.header` is the header when it's a `DetailHeader` (with its kind's symbol
  if it has none), and `layout.header(as: TitleHeader.self)` reads back a header of another type,
  as the table of contents reads rows back as `ContentsLabel`s.

### Renaming in the header: TitleHeader

Titles publishes the header for a kind whose shapes are renamed in the panel, so no kind writes
its own ([TitleHeader.swift](../Sources/Titles/TitleHeader.swift)). The kind puts it in its slot:

```swift
note.details(header: { $note in TitleHeader($note) }) {}
sub.details(header: { $sub in TitleHeader($sub, placeholder: "Untitled Subboard", systemImage: "rectangle.stack") }) {}
```

It's a `DetailHeaderLabel` whose title is a `DetailHeaderField`. Each keystroke renames the shape
(one transaction), so its pill and its row in the table of contents follow as you type. Given the
shape, it renames the title Titles keeps (`$note[TitleProperty.self]`, which the kind must opt
into with `note.title()`: a debug build stops at one that doesn't): clearing the field, or leaving
only spaces in it, sets nil, since Titles keeps no blank title; anything else is kept as typed, and
one past 80 characters is kept, and warned about. A title derived from what the kind keeps is
renamed where it comes from, given that binding instead: a `String?`, or a `String` blank while
untitled (`TitleHeader($card.text)`). While there's no title it shows its placeholder,
dimmed: the kind's name ("Note"), unless the kind gives one ("Untitled Subboard").
`isEnabled: false` dims it while something else writes the title (a model naming a type);
`isRenamable: false` shows it as text, at full strength, while it can't be written at all. A derived title that can't ever be renamed (a kind's that
nothing names) isn't; a kind with one keeps a `DetailHeader`, if it has a header at all.

Opting into titles doesn't place it: the header is the kind's, which may want its own subtitle,
placeholder or symbol, or no rename in the panel at all.

### A horizontal's opt-in: Boards

The pattern the registrar is built for: a horizontal exposes a way for individual shapes to opt into
a feature, and what the feature brings comes with it, on exactly the kinds that opt in. Opting in
is one line on the kind.

[Boards](#boards) makes the shapes of any kind that owns boards open onto them. It owns its point
(`BoardKinds`: what a kind's boards are called while their owners have no title, and their
symbol), the menu group (`BoardsMenuGroup`), and going in and out of boards; its sugar contributes
to its own point, to Selection's opening and to the menu's, from the same `ShapeRegistrar`, fully
typed ([OpensBoard.swift](../Sources/Boards/OpensBoard.swift)):

```swift
/// The extension point: which kinds' shapes open onto their boards, and what a board is called
/// before its owner is named. At most one per kind.
public enum BoardKinds {}
extension BoardKinds: KeyedExtensionPoint {
    public typealias Contribution = BoardKind                  // a placeholder and a symbol
    public static var owner: PluginID { .boards }
    public static var scope: PointScope { .kinds }             // a kind's boards open one kind at a time: no scope, no every kind
    public static func uniqueKeys(of _: BoardKind, for target: ShapeTarget) -> [AnyHashable] { [target] }
}

extension ShapeRegistrar where Definition: BoardOwning {
    /// Opening this kind's shapes shows their boards: a double-click, Return, ⌘↓, and Open first in
    /// their context menu, which runs what ⌘↓ does.
    public mutating func opensBoard(placeholder: String, systemImage: String) {
        contribute(BoardKind(placeholder: placeholder, systemImage: systemImage), to: BoardKinds.self)
        opens("Open") { shape, editor in editor.showBoard(BoardID(owner: shape.id)) }
        contextMenu { MenuItem(command: .openSelection, title: "Open", in: BoardsMenuGroup.self) }
    }
}
```

- **Opting in.** Subboards writes `sub.opensBoard(placeholder: "Untitled Subboard", systemImage:
  "rectangle.stack")`, and another plugin's kind opts in with `registrar.opensBoard(P.self, placeholder:systemImage:)`. The
  kind declares nothing. Its definition must be `BoardOwning`, which the sugar's `where` holds it
  to, and `BoardKinds.check` holds the form for another plugin's kind to, since that form can't say so in its types.
- **The graph.** Subboards imports Boards and never ContextMenus or Selection, yet its shapes open
  and have Open in their menu. The requirement shows up at startup instead: a list with Subboards
  but without `BoardsPlugin`, `SelectionPlugin` or `ContextMenusPlugin` is
  `ownerNotInstalled`, naming the missing one.
- **No tab.** Opening changes nothing of the shape and has nothing to show or hold, and the canvas,
  the menu and ⌘↓ (Go › Open Selection) open it alike, so the panel has nothing of it: a subboard's is
  its header, then the tabs every shape has.

Another feature in this pattern has the same parts: a keyed point for whatever it needs per kind
(Boards' placeholder and symbol); a menu group, if it has actions; when its shapes hold something,
an added property declared by the horizontal, with sections and items over its value
(`details(of:)`, `contextMenu(of:)`; [added properties](#added-properties)), in a tab of its own
if there is something to show there (Types' Types tab: [what a shape is](#types-shapes-that-hold-a-schema));
sugar that contributes them all from the kind's registrar; and whatever consumes it (a lookup on
`Registry`, an adornment).

### A tab of status lines: Validation's Issues tab

Status lines are a shape's state, not its settings: at the foot of the panel, on every tab, or in
a tab of their own, which shows only while the shape has lines there.
[`ValidationDetailsPlugin`](../Sources/Validation/IssuesTab.swift) lists each shape's
validation issues in an Issues tab. Validation, which owns what an issue is, imports DetailPanel
for it, the only edge between them, and the plugin is a value of its own, so a list can leave the
panel out:

```swift
import Canvas
import DetailPanel

public struct ValidationDetailsPlugin: ListedPlugin {
    public init() {}
    public var id: PluginID { "validation-details" }

    public func register(into registrar: inout PluginRegistrar) {
        // Every shape is checked (its schema, at least), so any may have issues.
        registrar.forEveryShape { every in
            every.detailStatus(in: IssuesTab.self) { shape, context in
                (context.service(ValidationEngine.self)?.result(for: shape.id)?.worstFirst ?? [])
                    .map { DetailStatus($0.message, tone: DetailStatus.Tone($0.severity)) }
            }
        }
    }
}

/// A shape's validation issues. It comes and goes with them, so it trails every other tab, Style too.
public enum IssuesTab {}
extension IssuesTab: DetailTab {
    public static var title: String { "Issues" }
    public static var order: Order<Self> { .after(StyleTab.self) }
}
```

Issues come worst first (errors, then warnings, each in the rules' order), each line its
severity's symbol, red or orange, then its message. The tab is after Style, which is last, so
after every other, and the other tabs keep their places as it comes and goes, though not their width: the
strip shares its width among its tabs, and a kind with one tab (a reference's Connections) gains a
strip with it. Any tab whose lines warn or err draws its worst tone's symbol before its title in
the strip (`layout.alert(in:)`: the triangle or the octagon, in its color; no count), so from
another tab it reads as a tab of problems, as the canvas's outline does. The tab is remembered per kind, as any is: once someone chooses Issues, the next
shape of that kind with issues opens on it, and one without opens on its first tab. A tab's lines
lead it, above any sections another plugin puts there. A status contributor reads services through
`DetailContext`, read-only. Status lines are re-read on every document change, so read a cached
service, as this one reads validation's engine. Without Validation installed there's no engine,
no lines, and no tab. So a note whose title runs past 80 characters has an Issues tab that says
"Title is 90 characters long, and should be at most 80.", and StickyNotes didn't change.

### The full showcase: a type's Schema tab

[Types](#types-shapes-that-hold-a-schema) gives every shape that holds a schema (a note made a type) a Schema tab, where its
schema is written (what it holds in words is the note's own text). `registerTypePanel` (in
[TypePanel.swift](../Sources/Types/IsA/TypePanel.swift)) is one `details(of:)` call, over the added
property every type holds:

```swift
registrar.details(of: TypeSchemaProperty.self) {
    DetailSection("JSON", in: TypeSchemaTab.self) { $schema in TypeSchemaCode(schema: $schema) }
}
```

The section is a view of its own, declaring `@ShapeBinding var schema: SchemaText`, so it can show
what the plugin's service keeps about the shape (`$schema.service(TypeSync<TypeSchemaProperty>.self)`,
the sync's status) and redraw alone when that changes:

```swift
struct TypeSchemaCode: View {
    @ShapeBinding var schema: SchemaText

    var body: some View {
        let sync = $schema.service(TypeSync<TypeSchemaProperty>.self), id = $schema.shapeID
        let status = sync?.status(of: id) ?? .idle
        SchemaCodeEditor(text: $schema.text, for: id, isUpdating: status == .updating(.schema), types: ..., onCommit: { [weak sync] in sync?.commit(id) })
        // the type's Validation issues, a DetailStatusLine each
        TypeSyncLine(status: status, sync: sync, id: id)
    }
}
```

The JSON is a `SchemaCodeEditor` (a `DetailCodeEditor`, colored and completed as a JSON Schema)
over `$schema.text`, its writes one run of undo, with the type's Validation issues under it, a
`DetailStatusLine` each, and the sync's status. The header is the note's: renaming the note renames
the type, whose name is its title.

Plugins fill one type note's panel:

| Part | Holds | From |
|---|---|---|
| Header | the note's title, renamed in place | StickyNotes, with Titles' `TitleHeader` |
| Schema | the JSON, its issues and the sync's status under it | Types' `TypeDetailsPlugin` |
| Issues | the type's issues, worst first ("A schema must be a JSON object."), while it has any | Validation's `ValidationDetailsPlugin` |

### Reading and writing: `ShapeBinding`

A section's content closure gets a `ShapeBinding`. Take it as a `$` parameter, as with
`ForEach($items) { $item in }`:

- **`note.text` reads the snapshot** the panel drew with. Nothing in a section reads
  `editor.document`, so a section isn't rebuilt when other shapes change.
- **`$note.text` is a `Binding`.** Each set writes that one key path into the *live* shape, in its
  own `editor.transact`. A move made after the snapshot survives a rename, two writes in one action
  both land, and setting the value the shape already has commits nothing. After a write, the
  binding reads what it made of the shape, before the panel draws again, as SwiftUI expects of a
  binding: a text field that takes Return (or Escape) straight after a keystroke would otherwise
  put the text from before back.
- **Writes go to the shape the binding was made for**, never to whatever is selected by the time
  they happen. A write to a shape that's gone does nothing.
- **Read-modify-write goes in `update`**: `$badges.update { $0.append("New") }` (DetailPanelTests'
  `Badges`, a list of strings) applies the change to the live value, in one transaction.
- **Bind the narrowest key path.** A collection's binding (`$badges[dynamicMember: \.self]`, and the
  row bindings `ForEach` derives from it) writes the whole collection, rebuilt from what the binding read (the
  snapshot, or its last write). Use `update` for list operations.
- **`$note.shape` is the whole shape** the snapshot came from, a `ShapeRecord<StickyNote>`: its
  props and its [added properties](#added-properties)' values, for what a section or a header shows
  from both (`$note.shape[TitleProperty.self]`, `$note.shape.id`). It only reads; writes go
  through the binding.
- **`$note[TitleProperty.self]` binds an added property** of the shape, a `Binding<String?>`: nil
  while the shape has none, each write one transaction on the live shape, nil removing it (for a
  property whose default is nil). It reads back its last write, as the key paths' bindings do.
  `TitleHeader($note)` renames through it.
- **Three kinds of binding, three write paths.** A kind's own sections get its props, typed, only
  from contributing for the kind: from its own plugin, a horizontal it opts into, or another plugin that imports it.
  Every-box sections get a `ShapeBinding<CGRect>`, the frame, whatever the kind. Sections over an
  added property get its value (`ShapeBinding<P.Value>`), on the shapes that have one. Any
  of them binds an added property of its shape by its type (`$x[P.self]`), through the whole
  record: nil, and writes dropped, on a kind that doesn't opt into it (`$x.holds(P.self)` says
  whether it does). The added properties' bindings one `$x` makes read back the last write through
  any of them, until the panel redraws.
- **Other forms.** A plain parameter works too (`badges.wrappedValue` is the snapshot), and a
  larger section can be a View declaring `@ShapeBinding var note: StickyNote`, passed `$note`.
- **Undo steps.** A write is named for its section, "Change" and the section's title ("Undo Change
  JSON"); in the header, or a section without a title, "Change" and the kind's name ("Undo
  Change Schema", its label). Writes to one field of one shape, one after
  another, are one step, however many keystrokes (a field typed into, a slider or a color
  dragged): a run under the key `[shape, key path]` (for the frame's too), or `[shape, property
  key]` for an added property's binding and `$x[P.self]`, until anything else happens: a write to
  another field, any other change, an action, or the host sealing the run as the user clicks or
  types somewhere else (`editor.undoHistory.seal()`, which the board's window calls). Each `update`
  is a step of its own. A field whose writes go through a method of the
  value, because they change more than the field says, runs as the field does with
  `update(\.field) { ... }`: a write through a method of the field's value is one step
  of the field's run, as a write to the field is.

Tests and tools reach the same bindings with `editor.shapeBinding(id, as: StickyNote.self)`,
`editor.frameBinding(id)` and `editor.propertyBinding(id, TitleProperty.self)`.

Two compiler rules come with this:

- **Keep the sugar's closure types unannotated.** Annotated `@MainActor`, Swift 6.3 compiles a
  `$`-parameter body as nonisolated, and every view initializer in it fails.
- **Never name `Transaction` in a file that imports SwiftUI.** SwiftUI has its own `Transaction`,
  and its `Canvas` view shadows the core module, so `Canvas.Transaction` doesn't resolve either.
  Let closure inference type `$0`.

When each control commits:

| Control | Commits |
|---|---|
| Text fields, `DetailTextArea`, `DetailCodeEditor`, a `DetailTextBox` (`MentionTextArea`), `DetailHeaderField` | On every keystroke, so the canvas follows as you type. With `onCommit:`, a text area or a box also says when it's done (Return, ⌘↩, the keyboard leaving), and a code editor too (⌘↩, the keyboard leaving) |
| Pickers, toggles, steppers, dates, swatches, the color well, list add, remove, move and edit | On change |
| `DetailNumberField` | A draft: on Return, Tab, leaving the field, or the field going away, in one transaction, clamped to its range. Escape drops the draft. Stepping writes at once. A draft lands on its own shape even if the selection moves first. |

### Text of a plugin's own: `DetailTextBox`

`DetailTextArea` and `DetailCodeEditor` edit a string. Text a plugin keeps in a form of its own
(mention text, which holds pills) edits in a `DetailTextBox`: the same box, laid out, bordered and
scrolling as a text area is, over a text view the plugin makes. Mentions' `MentionTextArea` is one
([In the panel](#in-the-panel-mentiontextarea)):

```swift
public var body: some View {
    let text = shape.wrappedValue[keyPath: field]
    DetailTextBox(shape[dynamicMember: field], height: height, placeholder: placeholder, onCommit: onCommit) {
        let view = MentionTextView<Scope>(frame: .zero, text: text, style: MentionStyle.panelText,
                                          owner: shape.shapeID, mentions: shape.service(MentionState.self))
        view.spelling = .app
        return view
    }
}
```

- **The view** is a subclass of [`EditingTextView`](#the-text-view) (an open `NSTextView`, TextEditing's)
  that adopts `DetailTextContent`: its `value`, of a type of its own (`ScopedMentionText`), and `show(_:)`.
  Adopt it on the subclass: `EditingTextView` adopting it would fix every subclass's `Value`. The
  panel's own boxes (`DetailCodeEditor` and `DetailTextArea`) are the same, over an internal
  `PlainTextView` whose value is a string, on TextKit 1 as they always were: a text area's words
  are checked as the app checks spelling (`spelling = .app`), a code editor's code never. A view
  of words sets it too, as `MentionTextArea`'s does.
- **What it adds** is [`EditingTextView`'s](#the-text-view), which does nothing until it's set, so
  the same class outside the panel is a plain text view (a note's editor on the canvas is a
  `MentionTextView` with only `onCommit` set, which ends editing, and `commitsOnLeaving` off). The
  box sets `onCommit`, `commitsOnReturn`, `onExit` (Escape: the panel's hand-back to the canvas) and
  `placeholder` from its arguments.
