- **The binding.** The box writes `value` to the binding after every change the view reports, so a
  field's run of writes is one undo step, as a text area's is. It calls `show(_:)` only when the
  binding changed from outside (an undo of the board, another plugin's write), never for a change
  it wrote, so a keystroke typed before the panel draws again is never lost. `show` changes the
  storage alone (the caret stays where it was, as far as the new text reaches) and never calls
  `didChangeText`, since the box may call it while the board applies an undo step, when nothing
  may commit; then the box drops what typing registered with its undo. In a board's window, Edit
  › Undo is the text's own while it has the keyboard ([Undo](#undo)).
- **Keys the view holds.** A view that shows a list at its caret holds keys while it's open
  ([a list at the caret](#a-list-at-the-caret): Mentions' `@` picker, a code editor's
  completions), and the panel's root, which hears Escape before the view with the keyboard does
  and leaves the panel, lets Escape through only to an `EditingTextView` holding keys: with the
  list open, Escape closes it, and a second leaves the panel. ⌘. comes as no key, the window
  sending `cancelOperation:` up the responder chain; a view with no list open doesn't answer it, so
  the panel's root hears it (`onExitCommand`) and leaves the panel as for Escape. A view that
  `offersCompletions` has ⌥⎋ for its own too, list or not: the panel lets Escape with ⌥ through to
  it, for AppKit's `complete:`, and leaves on it anywhere else.
- **Enabled or dimmed.** A read-only shape, or `detailUpdating` (any `disabled` around the box),
  makes the view read-only, and the box asks `showEnabled(_:)` on every update
  ([a view dims itself](#the-text-view)). The box is dimmed by its view alone, and SwiftUI sees it
  enabled, since SwiftUI takes every click over a disabled representable: so read-only text can
  still be selected and copied, and its view still hears clicks (a pill's double-click follows it).
- **The scroll view** is built by hand around the view `make` returns: `scrollableTextView()` would
  make the class with `init(frame:)`, and a plugin's view may need more to be made.
- **The font** is `DetailStyle.textFont`, the panel's text (11 pt), which a plugin's style takes
  (`MentionStyle.panelText`).

### Focus and hosting

- **Typing in the panel never triggers a shortcut.** Keyboard answers only keys typed on the
  canvas, so "n" typed into a title is text, and Delete and Return in a panel field never delete or
  edit the selected shape.
- **The keyboard goes back to the canvas** on a click on the canvas; on Escape in the panel, which
  drops any number draft first (but for a text view that holds keys: Escape with the `@` picker
  or a code editor's completions open closes the list); and on its own when the panel removes the control that had the
  keyboard (switching tabs, collapsing its section, a `when` hiding it, or a new selection), or is
  hidden with it (View › Hide Inspector, which hides the panel without removing it).
  Otherwise the keyboard would land on the window, and shortcuts would stop. Collapsing an
  unrelated section leaves the field focused.
- **A number being typed lands on its shape** before another board is shown: the panel hears
  `boardWillChange` and commits the draft, as Return would, while its shape is still there to
  write to. (Escape still drops it.)
- **Inside the panel**, Tab moves between text fields (a `DetailTextArea` takes Tab as text, a
  `DetailCodeEditor` as two spaces), and Return commits a number and keeps the field; in the header's title field (`DetailHeaderField`),
  Return is done renaming, and gives the keyboard back to the canvas. Checkboxes don't take the
  keyboard (the macOS default without Full Keyboard Access); a pop-up, segmented control or stepper
  that has it keeps
  shortcuts from the canvas until Escape.
- **Zoom** (⌘=, ⌘-, ⌘0, and ⇧1 and ⇧2 except in text, where they type) works whatever has the
  keyboard: the board's window controller answers the View menu's zoom items with the core's
  zoom commands and Selection's Zoom to Selection. So does Go › Back
  (⌘[).

The panel can't give the keyboard to the canvas itself (it can't import CanvasUI), so the host
passes `onExit`. `CanvasFocus` (CanvasUI) is the handle: `CanvasRepresentable(editor:focus:)` fills
it, and `take()` makes the canvas its window's first responder.

The window places the panel, and knows nothing of it: the panel's plugin gives it as the window's
inspector, [the host's slot for one](#host-slots), and says when it's wanted whether or not the
person has it shown (while a takeover is active, below) and what hiding it meanwhile does (escapes
that takeover):

```swift
registrar.hostInspector(isRequested: { $0.registry.activeDetailTakeover(in: $0) != nil },
                        onDismiss: { $0.registry.activeDetailTakeover(in: $0)?.onEscape($0) }) { editor, onExit in
    DetailPanelView(editor: editor, onExit: onExit)
}
```

and [the app](../Sources/InfiniteCanvas/InfiniteCanvasApp.swift) applies CanvasUI's `BoardChrome` to
its canvas, which puts the registered inspector in an `.inspector` (resizing, collapsing in narrow
windows, and View › Show Inspector, ⌃⌘I) with its toolbar button, and the views plugins gave over
the canvas (the path, [Jump To's](#jump-to) palette):

```swift
CanvasRepresentable(editor: editor, focus: canvasFocus)
    .modifier(BoardChrome(editor: editor, showsInspector: $showsDetails, onExit: canvasFocus.take))
```

### The overview and takeovers

Two points say what the panel shows besides a shape's details. It reads both from the editor's
registry, and never learns what either view is.

- **The overview** (`DetailOverviews`, at most one: a second is a conflict) shows where the panel
  has no one shape to show: in place of "No Selection", and under the header of several
  (data-canvas's details panel takes an `emptyView` and a `multiSelectView` the same way). A plugin
  gives it with `registrar.detailOverview { editor, onExit in … }`, and its view follows the
  editor by itself. The table of contents gives its list (`ContentsOverviewPlugin`, below).
- **A takeover** (`DetailTakeovers`, a list in plugin order: the first that's active shows) is
  `registrar.detailTakeover(isActive:onEscape:) { editor, onExit in … }`: `isActive` (read in the
  panel's body, so on observable state: the panel redraws when it flips), `onEscape` and the view.
  While it's active the panel shows the view in place of everything else, the overview and every
  selection branch, in the panel's own environment, frame and width. Escape and ⌘. in the panel
  call its `onEscape`, then `onExit` (a text view holding keys still hears Escape first).
  [Find](#find) gives its panel, active while Find is open, `onEscape` closing it
  (`FindPanelPlugin`).

Each view is handed the panel's editor and its `onExit`, and is made as the panel is. Both points
are the panel's, so each contributor is a plugin value of its own after `DetailPanelPlugin`: a
list without the panel leaves it out, and one with the contributor and no panel is refused.

### Performance

The document changes on every drag event, so the panel does little per change. It re-reads the
selected shape, whether it can change (the containers it's in, O(its depth)), its status lines and
what `shownWhile` hides, and rebuilds the shape's panel only if any of them changed (`panelsDrawn`,
debug builds, counts it); dragging another shape costs one comparison (`./build.sh bench` holds the
layout of a subboard 100 notes mention, its Connections tab showing, to 1 ms after a drag event
of another note and after a mentioner's rename). A section is rebuilt only when its own shape changes.
Only the current tab is built, a collapsed section's content isn't, and each kind's contributions
are gathered once.
For your part: sections read only their binding, `when`, `shownWhile` and status lines stay cheap,
and anything heavy goes in a service, kept per shape and redone for the shapes each commit's change
set names (`documentDidChange`), as `ValidationEngine` does.

## Context menus

A right-click on a shape (or a Control-click) opens a menu of what can be done to it. It's a
horizontal ([`Sources/ContextMenus`](../Sources/ContextMenus)) like the detail panel: it declares one
extension point, kinds and other plugins fill it, and the core only passes the click along. A
right-click on a subboard:

```
┌─────────────────────────┐
│ Open                    │  a feature's (Boards, through opensBoard): first, as Finder's is
├─────────────────────────┤
│ Create Frame            │  the canvas's (Frames): a frame around what the menu is for
├─────────────────────────┤
│ Cut                     │  the canvas's (Clipboard): Paste once there's something to paste
│ Copy                    │
│ Paste                   │
├─────────────────────────┤
│ Arrange               ▸ │  a scope's (Reordering, the kinds painted in document order):
├─────────────────────────┤    Bring to Front, Bring Forward, Send Backward, Send to Back
│ Lock                    │  the canvas's, in Locking's scope: Unlock once every shape it's for is locked
├─────────────────────────┤
│ Delete                  │  the canvas's (ContextMenus' own): Selection's `.delete`, last
└─────────────────────────┘
```

A sticky note's is the same without Open. Every shape has Delete, ContextMenus' own item for the
canvas (in `SelectionMenuGroup`, `.last`, after Lock, as Keynote has it), which runs
Selection's `.delete` on the menu's shapes, as the Delete key does: a locked one shakes. As shipped,
every shape has Lock (or Unlock) too, and every copyable shape Cut and Copy, items for the canvas,
which are in every menu with shapes; an arrow's menu is those alone, since Arrange leaves it out. A
shape something mentions has Show What Mentions too, after its own items (Mentions', for the
canvas, in `MentionsMenuGroup`, `.after(ShapeMenuGroup.self)`), which goes to what mentions it
([What mentions a shape](#what-mentions-a-shape)). A shape that can be turned into another kind has Turn
into … after it (Transform's, in `TransformMenuGroup`, `.after(ActionsMenuGroup.self)`: a frame's is Turn into Subboard,
[Transform](#transform)), and any shapes a frame can hold have Create Frame after that (Frames', for
the canvas, in `FramesMenuGroup`, `.after(TransformMenuGroup.self)`: a frame put down around them, [Frames](#frames); an
arrow alone has none). On empty canvas the menu is the canvas's items
that apply there alone: Paste, once there's something to paste, which lands centered where the
menu was asked for (⌘V keeps its own rule), and Select All (ContextMenus' own, Selection's
`.selectAll`) while the board has shapes. An empty board with nothing to paste has no menu: the
right-click does nothing.

### Contributing

| Sugar | For |
|---|---|
| `x.contextMenu { items }` | This kind's items, inside `registrar.shape { x in ... }`. A horizontal's opt-in sugar calls it too. |
| `registrar.contextMenu(P.self) { items }` | Another plugin's kind, typed as its own. |
| `x.contextMenu(of: P.self) { items }`, `registrar.contextMenu(of: P.self) { items }` | An [added property](#added-properties), over its value: on this kind's shapes that have one, or on the shapes of every kind that holds it (its scope, "every shape holding <key>"). |
| `registrar.forShapes(holding: P.self) { $0.contextMenu { items } }`, `forShapes(adopting:)`, `forEveryShape` | The kinds a [scope](#scopes) reaches, over `AnyShapeRecord`: those that hold a property, or have a capability (Reordering's `.restackable`, the kinds painted in document order); `when:` picks shapes (`{ $0.box != nil }` for those with a frame). An item for every kind with no scope is refused. |
| `registrar.contextMenuForCanvas { items }` | Items that aren't one shape's (Cut, Copy, Paste; Show What Mentions, since whether a shape is mentioned is what a service knows; Turn into …, since what a shape can turn into is what the registry knows; Create Frame, since it's for the menu's shapes together, whatever their kinds; Delete and Select All), over the menu's `MenuSubject`: its shapes (none on empty canvas), where it was asked for (`point`, world units; nil in [the selection's menu](#the-selections-menu)) and the editor. In every menu, after the shapes' own in their groups' order, and alone on empty canvas. Each is asked once per menu, not per shape. A scope's (`registrar.forShapes(holding: P.self) { $0.contextMenuForCanvas { items } }`) is only in a menu whose every shape it reaches, so never on empty canvas, in its place in plugin order: Locking's Lock and Unlock, Types' Is a ▸, Colors' Color ▸. |

Boards' Open, which a board-owning kind's opt-in brings it ([OpensBoard.swift](../Sources/Boards/OpensBoard.swift)):

```swift
contextMenu { MenuItem(command: .openSelection, title: "Open", in: BoardsMenuGroup.self) }
```

- **`MenuItem(title, in:, id:, when:, isEnabled:, isChecked:) { edit }`** edits each shape it's for
  on the live value, all of them in one transaction, as the panel's `update` does. For what editing
  props can't do (reordering, deleting, selecting), the other form, `{ ids, editor in ... }`, gets
  the shapes, in selection order, and the editor, and changes the document with `editor.transact`.
  Whatever an item does, over however many shapes and transactions, is one undo step, named by its
  title ("Undo Bring to Front").
- **`MenuItem(command: .x, title:, in:, id:, when:, dims:)`** runs a [command](#commands), so the item
  has the command's one rule, title and key. It shows while the command can act on the menu's shapes
  and click (its rule, asked of the subject: `editor.canPerform(_:on:at:)`, never the command's
  moment, since the menu ends editing as it opens), `when` leaving it out besides (Select All, on
  empty canvas only); with `dims: true` it shows wherever `when` says, dimmed while the command can't
  act (Go to Original, for a reference whose original is gone; Make Public on a locked shape).
  Chosen, it runs the command on the menu's shapes and click (`editor.perform(_:on:at:)`), whatever
  the selection is by then. It's titled as the command is (`registry.title(of:)`) unless `title:`
  gives its own, shows the key a menu shows for the command (`registry.menuKey(of:)`, which Keyboard
  fills, so ContextMenus imports no Keyboard), and shows only while a plugin claims the command. A
  command that goes by where the menu was asked for reads the subject's `point`: Clipboard's Paste
  lands centered on the click. Delete, Select All, Open (Boards'), Cut, Copy, Paste, Duplicate, Group,
  Ungroup, Lock, Unlock, Make Public, Make Private, Go to Original, Create Frame, Connect and Arrange ▸
  are such items.
- **`when` leaves an item out; `isEnabled` dims it.** A context menu shows only what applies, so
  reach for `when`. `isChecked` checks it (✓ for every shape, – for some). An item for the canvas
  asks these of its `MenuSubject`, so it can depend on more than a shape (Mentions' Show What Mentions
  is `when: { subject in subject.shapes.contains(where: mentions.isMentioned) }`), and takes the `perform` form, which
  gets the subject's shapes, or the `edit` form, which is handed the subject itself, for an item
  that needs where the menu was asked for (a command reads it as `subject.point`, as Clipboard's
  Paste does). Ask whether an item shows of the subject, not of `editor.canPerform`: the selection
  is the menu's shapes only once the menu is made.
- **`Submenu(title) { items }`** shows when any of its items does.
- **`MenuItems(in:, id:) { subject in … }`** is an item for the canvas that is made when the menu
  opens, for what the registry can't know because it's in the file. It's registered like an item, by
  its group and `id` (two plugins claiming one are a `conflict`), and asked once per menu, with the
  `MenuSubject`; what it returns, written as the other items are (`MenuItem`, `Submenu`, a `for`
  loop), takes its place in the menu, in its entries' own groups. An id met twice at a level shows
  once, the first staying, and a kind's own item with an entry's group and id takes its place as it
  does a registered one's. Returning nothing shows nothing, and a menu with nothing else has no menu.
  It is for the canvas only: the "every shape shows it" rule is never asked of what it makes.
  `MenuItem`'s `perform` form takes `stepName:` for an item whose title only makes sense in its
  submenu (the undo step is named by it: "Set Level ▸ High" is the step "Set Level High").

  ```swift
  registrar.contextMenuForCanvas {
      MenuItems(in: FlagMenuGroup.self, id: "recent-flags") { subject in
          for flag in recentFlags(in: subject.editor) {
              MenuItem("Flag as \(flag.name)", in: FlagMenuGroup.self, id: flag.id) { ids, editor in … }
          }
      }
  }
  ```

  ContextMenusTests' `DynamicItemsTests` hold it: asked once per menu with the subject, in place after
  the shapes' own, made again each menu, an empty result showing nothing (and no menu on empty canvas),
  duplicates deduplicated at each level, `when` and `isEnabled`, a kind's own item taking its place, one
  undo group named for the item or by its `stepName:`, the registration key's conflict and
  `ownerNotInstalled`.
- **Groups are types**, like tabs: a separator falls between groups, each where its `order` puts it,
  as a tab's does ([Order](#order-where-things-go-among-each-other)). An item names its group with
  `in:`; the default is `ShapeMenuGroup`. As shipped:

  | Group | Its order |
  |---|---|
  | What opens a shape (Boards' Open, `BoardsMenuGroup`; References' Go to Original, `ReferencesMenuGroup`) | `.before(ShapeMenuGroup.self)`, as Finder's Open is first |
  | A kind's own items (`ShapeMenuGroup`) | `.first` |
  | A horizontal's feature, on the kinds that opt in (a flag's `FlagMenuGroup`, [below](#something-the-user-turns-on)), or on the shapes it knows something of (`MentionsMenuGroup`) | `.after(ShapeMenuGroup.self)`, in plugin order among themselves |
  | ContextMenus' `ActionsMenuGroup`, which no item is in: where what acts on the shapes begins, after every group right after a kind's own (having no turn of its own) | `.after(ShapeMenuGroup.self)` |
  | What a feature brings to the shapes it can act on (Transform's Turn into …, `TransformMenuGroup`) | `.after(ActionsMenuGroup.self)` |
  | What a vertical makes of the shapes it's for (Frames' Create Frame, `FramesMenuGroup`) | `.after(TransformMenuGroup.self)` |
  | Cut, Copy, Duplicate and Paste (`ClipboardMenuGroup`) | none: in the middle, where it first appears |
  | Arrange ▸ (`ReorderMenuGroup`) | `.before(StateMenuGroup.self)` |
  | What the shape is made from (`StateMenuGroup`, ContextMenus' own, which Grouping's Group and Ungroup, Locking's Lock and Unlock, Types' Is a ▸ and Colors' Color ▸ share with no line between) | `.before(SelectionMenuGroup.self)` |
  | Make Public and Make Private (`PublishMenuGroup`) | `.after(StateMenuGroup.self)` |
  | Delete and Select All (`SelectionMenuGroup`, ContextMenus' own) | `.last` |

  A submenu's groups say nothing, and go in the order it lists them (Is a ▸: `Type`, a line, the
  file's types; Color ▸: the built-in colors, the file's, `None`).

- **Keyed.** Each item claims its target, group and `id` (the title by default), and an item in a
  submenu its path, so two plugins adding one item to a kind are a `conflict`
  ("subboard Open"), and so are two in one scope, or in two scopes that reach one kind. A kind's own
  item replaces a scope's with the same group and id.

### A feature that comes with menu items: Boards

The pattern of a horizontal's opt-in, again. Boards' opt-in sugar contributes to its own
point, Selection's, and this one, so `sub.opensBoard(…)` brings opening and Open, the item
above ([A horizontal's opt-in](#a-horizontals-opt-in-boards)). Its group,
`BoardsMenuGroup`, is placed `.before(ShapeMenuGroup.self)`, so Open comes first, as Finder's does; a
feature's group is usually placed `.after(ShapeMenuGroup.self)`. Items over an added property's value go in `contextMenu(of: P.self) { … }`, as its
sections go in `details(of:)`: a flag's Flagged is over the flag
([Something the user turns on](#something-the-user-turns-on)).

A future horizontal does the same inside its own sugar: its point, its tab, its menu items (over
its property's value, if it adds one), one line on the kind. The edge comes with it: Boards imports
ContextMenus, so a list with a kind that opens boards needs `ContextMenusPlugin` too. A feature
whose menu items should be optional puts them in a plugin value of its own, as Validation puts its
Issues tab in `ValidationDetailsPlugin`.

### Many kinds: Reordering

[`Examples/Reordering`](../Examples/Reordering/Reordering.swift) gives the shapes of many kinds an Arrange
submenu, as in Keynote and tldraw, in a group of its own after the rest. It's a thing you do: no kind opts into
it and nothing imports it. It picks kinds by
capability, a [scope](#scopes) it states once (`.restackable`, "painted in document order"): one painted
by anchor (an arrow, drawn just above the shapes it joins) is left out, since document order doesn't
decide where it's drawn. A line, which has no frame, is in.

```swift
extension CanvasCommand { public static let bringToFront: CanvasCommand = "bringToFront" }   // and the other three

registrar.command(.bringToFront, title: "Bring to Front", menu: "Arrange", order: 100, shortcut: KeyChord("]"), runs: .whenIdle,
                  isEnabled: { $0.restackable }) { subject in
    subject.editor.transact("Bring to Front") { $0.bringToFront(subject.shapes) }
}                                                              // and Bring Forward ⌥], Send Backward ⌥[, Send to Back [
registrar.forShapes(adopting: .restackable) { restackable in
    restackable.contextMenu {
        Submenu("Arrange", in: ReorderMenuGroup.self) {
            MenuItem(command: .bringToFront)                   // titled, keyed and run by the command
            MenuItem(command: .bringForward)
            MenuItem(command: .sendBackward)
            MenuItem(command: .sendToBack)
        }
    }
}

extension ShapeCapability {                                    // the kinds restacking means something for
    static let restackable = ShapeCapability("painted in document order") { !$0.adopts((any PaintOrderAnchored).self) }
}
```

Each of the four is a [command](#commands) of its own, declared once with its title, its key and
its item in the menu bar's Arrange, after Group and Ungroup: `]` brings the selection to the front,
⌥] forward, ⌥[ backward and `[` to the back. They act on shapes all of kinds the scope reaches,
with nothing under way or being edited (`.whenIdle`); they type, so in a note or a field they're the
text's ([keyboard](#keyboard-shortcuts)). The Arrange submenu stays in the context menu, its items
running the same commands on the menu's shapes, and the selection's menu leaves it out, since Arrange
has them. A list without Reordering (and Grouping) has no Arrange menu at all.

The restacking is the core's: `bringToFront`, `sendToBack`, `bringForward` and `sendBackward` each
take a list of shapes, which keep their order among themselves, and refuse read-only ones, as
`move(_:above:)` does. Bring Forward and Send Backward are tldraw's: each shape moves just past the
nearest shape that overlaps it, in that direction, since moving past one it doesn't overlap would
change nothing to see; never one a container holds, which goes with it (a frame steps past its
neighbor, not its own first note), nor one painted by anchor. One with nothing to pass stays.

### What a right-click does

The menu is for the selection, as in Keynote and tldraw.

| Right-click | Does |
|---|---|
| On a shape that isn't selected | The menu is for that shape, which becomes the selection. |
| On a selected shape, or on empty space inside a multi-selection's box | The menu is for the whole selection, which stays. |
| On the rest of the canvas | The canvas's items alone (Paste, landing centered on the click; Select All while the board has shapes); the selection stays. |
| Where nothing applies | Nothing: no menu, and the selection and any editing stay. With Selection installed every shape has Delete, so that's empty canvas on an empty board, or wherever every item that applies is left out by `when`. |
| During a press | Nothing. |

The select tool's hit rule finds the shape, so unselectable shapes are seen through. Opening a menu
ends editing. A right-click opens the menu in any tool; a Control-click only in the select tool,
since other tools may read ⌃ as a modifier.

With several shapes, an item shows when every one of them shows it: the same group and id, whichever
plugin contributed it for each kind, so two flaggable kinds ([below](#something-the-user-turns-on)),
selected together, share Flagged. It's enabled when it is for any of them, and runs on those: each
kind's own `edit`, all in one transaction, then each contribution's `perform` once, with its shapes.
It's checked (✓) when every shape checks it and mixed (–) when some do; a kind whose item has no
`isChecked` counts as unchecked. A submenu holds what its items resolve to. In a group, a kind's own
items come first, then the scopes', each in plugin and builder order, then the canvas's. A shape's
own item with a canvas item's group and id takes its place, shown or not, as a kind's own item takes
a scope's.

### The selection's menu

The same items, over the selection and with no click, are the menu bar's Shape menu (between Edit and
Arrange; [Keyboard shortcuts](#keyboard-shortcuts)). `registrar.menuForSelection` is the core's point for
it, told the commands to leave out: the window passes every one a menu bar item runs
(`BoardMenus.commands(in:)`, found as the bar is made), and the plugin drops each item that runs one of them,
a submenu left with nothing, and a group's line when it has no items. What's left is made as a
right-click on the selection would make it, with `MenuSubject.point` nil, so an item that goes by where
the click was (Types' `Relate to <Type>`) leaves itself out, and an omitted command's rule isn't asked;
an item that runs a command is dimmed as the command is (its rule over the selection, which is the menu's,
and its moment: a shape being edited dims what runs `.whenIdle`), and a pick ends editing first. With
nothing selected there is no menu, not even the canvas's items. Lock or Unlock, Create Frame, Turn into
…, Is a ▸ and Color ▸ are in it for a note, and Turn into Subboard for a frame, beside the keys the menu
shows (⇧L on Lock or Unlock, ⇧⌘F). ContextMenusTests' `selectionMenuForBarTests` hold the plugin's side,
CompositionTests' `shapeMenuShippedTests` the shipped menu.

### The core's part

The core has never heard of context menus. It has one generic hook, like commands: at most one
plugin claims the secondary click (`registrar.menuForSecondaryClick { editor, pointer in ... }`,
returning an `NSMenu` or nil), and ContextMenus does. Beside it is the selection's menu, with no click
(`registrar.menuForSelection { editor, commands in ... }`, `editor.menuForSelection(omitting:)`, host API),
which ContextMenus claims too. `CanvasView.menu(for:)`, which AppKit asks on a
right-click and on a Control-click, passes the click to the editor (`editor.menu(for:)`, host API),
which asks that plugin unless a press is under way. AppKit shows what comes back. A Control-click
with no menu then reaches `mouseDown`, a press with `pointer.isControlClick` set, for the tool to
take or ignore. ContextMenus keeps each kind's items, gathered once, in a service,
`ContextMenuState`.

## The table of contents

The table of contents is an outline of the board, one row per shape, in the right-hand panel, as
data-canvas has it: with nothing selected the detail panel shows it for the whole board; with
several, just them, under their header; with one, that shape's details instead. It's a horizontal
([`Sources/TableOfContents`](../Sources/TableOfContents)) with data-canvas's contract (its TOC
card providers): each kind says how its shapes appear, and which shapes are listed and under what.
It doesn't look like data-canvas's, though: it's a Mac source list, a SwiftUI `List` with the
system's rows, selection, disclosure triangles and keyboard. Its rows run front to back, as a layers
list's do, and dragging them restacks shapes, or moves them into a frame or onto a subboard's board
([Dragging rows](#dragging-rows)).

```
┌─ the panel, with nothing selected ──┐  front to back: the top row is the shape in front
│ Board                               │ header: "Selection", with Show All, when filtered
│ ▾ ▤ Double-click empty space to a…  │ a note: its text, on one line
│     ↗ Arrow                         │   an arrow, under the shape it starts from
│   ▤ Groceries                       │ a titled note: its title (Titles), not its text
│   ▤ Customer                      ● │ a type: its title; the dot, red: its error (Validation's)
│   ▭ Patch                           │ a kind with no row: its label and symbol, dimmed while untitled
│   ▭ Server room                     │   or its title, from Titles
│ ▾ ▤ Payments                        │ a subboard: what's on its board, under it
│     ▤ Refunds                       │   a note on that board
│ ▾ ▭ Sprint 3                        │ a frame: what it holds, under it, open from the start
│     ▤ Ship it                       │   a note in it
│   ▸ ▭ Later                         │   a frame in it, its rows under it, closed by the person
│   ↗ Arrow                           │ an arrow that starts on nothing, at the top
└─────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### A kind's row

StickyNotes' row, in full ([NoteRow.swift](../Sources/StickyNotes/NoteRow.swift)):

```swift
note.contentsRow(affected: MentionRows.affected) { note, context in
    ContentsLabel(context.plainText(note.props.text), placeholder: "Empty Note", color: .yellow)
}
```

- **The row is a view the kind builds**, usually a `ContentsLabel`: a title on one line (each run of
  whitespace folds into a space), a placeholder shown dimmed when the title is blank, an SF Symbol
  (the kind's, unless the row gives one) with an optional color, and a badge of a few
  characters at the trailing end ("12"). A row that stands in for another shape, wearing that
  shape's name and symbol (a reference's), passes `standsIn: true`: an arrow cut into the symbol's
  corner, as a Finder alias's icon has, so it reads as a pointer to the shape and not the shape.
  A row that names a shape somewhere else says where with `path:`, the names of the shapes that one
  is inside, outermost first (a reference's: the frames and boards its original is in): shown before
  the title, dimmed, with "›" between, "Alpha › Beta › Checkout". Each is a `ContentsPathName` (a
  string literal is one), and one that is only what its kind is called (`isPlaceholder`: an untitled
  frame's "Frame") is fainter than a title, as in Jump To's rows. The path gives way before the
  title does: a row without the room for all of it folds the names between the first and the last
  into "…" (`ContentsLabel.folded(_:)`, the first and the nearest always said, as the path over
  the canvas folds its middle), a row narrower than that cuts each name short on its own, the
  longest first and none to less than a few letters (`ContentsStyle.pathNameFloor`, so every name
  still starts and every "›" shows: `ContentsPathLine`, a `Layout`, since a stack would let the title
  push the names down to nothing), and only then is the title cut. VoiceOver says "Checkout, in
  Alpha › Beta".
  Its text is its tooltip, after its path if it has one (`label.help`, none for a
  placeholder with no path; past 200 characters, cut between words with "…"), for a row the list cuts short, in
  the list and in a crumb's menu. The list owns everything around it: row
  height, indentation, disclosure triangles, selection, the header. Any view works, but
  `ContentsLabel` is what keeps rows from different plugins alike; use it unless a row really needs
  something else.
- **A row reads only its shape**, as `when`, `nestedUnder` and `contentsTitle` do, unless it names,
  with `affected`, the shapes whose rows a commit may change ([below](#rows-read-from-more-than-their-shape)). The table of
  contents keeps each shape's row, and where it's listed, from one commit to the next, and redoes
  only those of the shapes the commit's change set names (and the rows nested under a shape that
  came or went), a commit costing what it changed, however big the board: well under a
  millisecond at 10,000 shapes, every one listed.
- **A row says what its shape is, never where it is**, and so do `when`, `nestedUnder` and a name
  from `contentsTitle`: a commit that only moves a shape (`ChangeSet.moved`: a drag's every
  event, `translate`, a frame carrying all it holds) keeps its row, the same object, so the list
  redraws nothing, and reads only its marks again (a mark from a service may follow where a shape
  is: a validation rule that doesn't ignore moves; [marks](#marks-validations-dots)), on the next
  read: the commit only notes which shapes moved, so a drag's every event costs the table of
  contents one set's upkeep, whatever it carries. So a drag makes no row, nor does dragging a frame
  of 10,000 shapes; a shape changed any other way gets its row made again.
- **`when`** lists only some of a kind's shapes: `contentsRow(when: { $0.props.isBound }) { ... }`.
- **`nestedUnder`** names the shape a row goes under; a shape its kind names none for, as every
  shape of a kind without it, goes under the [container](#containers) it's in, a frame
  (`registry.container(of:in:)`, as the core goes by it, read from the shape's own record: joining
  or leaving a container changes it, so its row is made again and placed under the new one). It
  holds only while that shape is listed too, so a selection of just the child still shows it, at
  the top. Rows nest as deep as their shapes do (a frame in a frame, what that holds under it); a
  loop keeps the later shape at the top. Arrows nest under the shape they start from, as
  data-canvas's edges do under their start node, whatever frame that's in.
- **Each level opens and closes on its own**, its own disclosure triangle (`ContentsTree`: a
  `DisclosureGroup` a row, whose rows are trees of their own). A container's row starts expanded
  (`entry.startsExpanded`): what it holds is on the board shown, inside it on the canvas, as a
  folder's contents show in a sidebar. Every other row starts collapsed: the arrows under a note,
  a subboard's board (read only once it's opened, below). A row keeps what the person turns it to
  (`ContentsState.isExpanded(_:)` and `setExpanded(_:_:)`, by shape, for the editor's life): Show
  All, the rows replaced, another board shown and back leave it as it was. Each row observes only
  its own disclosure, so turning one redraws that row and its rows alone.
- **A board under its owner.** A shape that owns a board (a `BoardOwning` kind's, a subboard)
  opens onto that board's rows: the rows its [outline](#another-boards-outline) lists, each as its
  kind draws it and nested alike, then the rows nested under the shape on its own board. Nothing
  opts in: owning a board is what a kind declares to the core, and its board is what it holds. A
  board with no shapes has nothing to open, so its owner's row has no disclosure triangle (one
  whose shapes are all unlisted, kept aside, has one that opens onto nothing). The rows are read
  only once the row is expanded: SwiftUI's outline asks every row on every update for the
  collection of its nested rows, but for what's in it only once it's expanded, so the list hands
  it a lazy one (`BoardRows`), and a collapsed subboard costs its own row, however much its board
  holds; once open, they follow its board as it changes, though it isn't shown (what a type's
  sync writes there). They're of shapes on another board, so they have
  no marks (Validation checks the board shown), selecting one goes there (below), and the pointer
  on one hovers nothing: the canvas doesn't show it. Headless, `entry.nestedBoard` is the board,
  whether or not it has shapes, and `outline(of:)` its rows.
- **Without a row**, a kind is listed by its label and symbol (`registry.label(of:)`: "Arrow",
  which `ArrowsPlugin` declares, "Patch", its tool's), the fallback the detail panel's header uses. Where another
  plugin names the kind's rows (`contentsTitle`, below) that label is a placeholder, dimmed until a
  shape is named, as an untitled note's is, so unnamed patches don't read as named "Patch";
  a kind nobody names (an arrow) shows it at full strength. A kind can keep that
  row and still say where it's listed and what it nests under, as `ArrowsPlugin` does:

  ```swift
  arrow.contentsRow(nestedUnder: { $0.props.start.binding?.shapeID })
  ```

  `registrar.contentsRow(OtherKind.self) { ... }` gives another plugin's kind a row. A
  kind has at most one row: two are a `conflict`.
- **Nesting through a service.** `nestedUnder` has a second form whose closure also gets the
  `ContentsContext` (`ContentsContext.service(_:)`), so a row can nest under what a service says:
  `x.contentsRow(nestedUnder: { shape, context in context.service(Stands.self)?.target(of: shape.id) }) { ... }`
  (the name is required there, and `affected:` can follow it for a row read from more than its shape).
  A service's state changes outside commits, so the service tells the list:
  `editor.contentsDidChange(for: ids)`, as `editor.adornmentsDidChange(for:)` does for adornments. The
  rows named are made again (nesting and all) on the next read, the list reads again (an observer of
  `entries` is told), and no other row is made.
- **A name from another plugin.** `x.contentsTitle { ... }` (the `ContentsTitles` point, or
  `registrar.contentsTitle(OtherKind.self)`) names a kind's rows without replacing them: a name
  that isn't blank takes the place of a `ContentsLabel`'s title, which keeps its symbol, color and
  badge, and nil leaves the row alone. The row a kind without one gets is a `ContentsLabel` too, so
  it takes the name; a row of some other view stays as the kind drew it. Titles names rows this
  way: a note's row is its text until the note has a title. At most one name per kind: two are a
  `conflict`.

| data-canvas's `TocCardProvider` | Here |
|---|---|
| `component` | The view `contentsRow` builds, usually a `ContentsLabel` |
| `filter` | `when:` |
| `getParentShapeId` | `nestedUnder:`, else the shape's container |
| `getZoomConfig` | The shape's geometry bounds, with 100 points of margin, for every kind |
| `onClick` | Return on a picked row opens its shape, as Return on the canvas does (Selection's `editor.open`); a double-click too, where the list stays on screen ([Opening a row](#whats-listed-and-selecting)) |
| `getGroupChildren` | The board a shape owns: its rows, under the shape's ([A board under its owner](#a-kinds-row)); and what a container holds, under it, open from the start |
| The "other" row (type and id) | The kind's label and symbol (`registry.label(of:)`) |

### Rows read from more than their shape

A row may show what other shapes say: a note's row shows its text with the names of the shapes it
mentions, as they're named now, so renaming a shape changes the rows of the notes that mention it
([Mentions](#the-service-mentionstate): `note.contentsRow(affected: MentionRows.affected) { note,
context in ContentsLabel(context.plainText(note.props.text), placeholder: "Empty Note", …) }`). Such a row is built from the shape and a `ContentsContext` (the editor's services, as
a mark's is), returns a `ContentsLabel`, and names, with `affected`, the shapes each commit may
change the rows of without changing them. A ref that shows the name of the shape it refers to,
with a service of its plugin's own that keeps which refs refer to each shape
([AffectedRowTests](../Tests/TableOfContentsTests/AffectedRowTests.swift)):

```swift
ref.contentsRow(affected: { changes, context in
    context.service(RefIndex.self)?.refs(to: changes.shapeIDs.union(changes.elsewhere)) ?? []
}) { ref, context in
    ContentsLabel("→ " + (context.service(RefIndex.self)?.name(of: ref.props.target) ?? "?"))
}
```

- **The rows `affected` names are made again** on the next read, and replaced (so redrawn) only if
  their labels changed: the same title, placeholder, symbol, color, badge, `standsIn` and path keep the
  row, as a mark's `affected` keeps it unless its marks changed. So dragging a shape the refs refer
  to makes their rows again and redraws none of them; renaming it redraws theirs. The shapes a commit
  changes get new rows as always, and a row `affected` names that hasn't been made yet is made
  when it's first listed.
- **`affected` runs on every commit**, whether the list shows or not, so it must cost what the
  commit changed, never the board: a service that keeps who reads what (an index kept up to date
  commit by commit, per shape) answers it.
- **What a commit affects** is asked of the rows and marks once every service has the commit
  (`documentDidSettle`: [services hear a change](#services-hear-a-change)), so an `affected` may read
  any service as the commit left it; a read of the list before then asks them first.
- **Other boards.** A row may read a shape on any board of the file (a mention of a shape inside a
  subboard: `editor.file.record(id)` finds it). What a commit did beyond its board is in
  `changes.elsewhere` (the shapes of the boards a deletion took or a paste brought, and those a
  `transact(on:)` changed), so `affected` looks there too, as `RefIndex` does above: deleting a
  subboard remakes the rows of the refs to what was inside it. The table of contents keeps each
  board's rows for going back to it; on going back to a board as it was left, it hands `affected`
  what changed on the other boards meanwhile, as `elsewhere` (on the next read, once every service
  has followed the switch), so a row that reads a shape renamed, deleted or brought back by undo
  there is made again, and the rest are taken back as they were. It keeps what was touched since
  the board kept longest ago was left, a revision per shape, only while boards are kept and some
  row or mark reads other shapes: a commit costs one more write per shape it touched.
- **`when` and `nestedUnder` still read only the shape**, and `contentsTitle` still names the row:
  a name that isn't blank takes the place of the label's title (a titled note shows its title).
- **What other shapes are, never where they are.** Such a row reads other shapes' names and state,
  not their positions: on a board that isn't shown, where `affected` can't say which rows a commit
  changes, [another board's outline](#another-boards-outline) makes these rows again after a commit
  that did more than move shapes, and not after a move (a drag's every event).
- `registrar.contentsRow(OtherKind.self, affected:) { shape, context in ... }` is the same for
  another plugin's kind. The row that reads only its shape keeps its forms,
  `x.contentsRow { ... }` and `x.contentsRow(when:nestedUnder:)`.

### Marks: Validation's dots

A mark is a small dot, or an SF Symbol (`ContentsMark(symbol:color:help:)`), at the trailing end
of a shape's row, from any plugin: a state worth seeing at a glance down the list. [`ValidationContentsPlugin`](../Sources/Validation/IssueMarks.swift),
a plugin value of Validation's own, which imports TableOfContents for it, marks each shape with issues in the color
the canvas outlines it in, red with an error and orange with warnings alone, and the dot's tooltip
lists them, worst first. So the table of contents is where a board's issues are found: look down
the list for dots, and click a row to select its shape and bring it into view, where the panel
shows its Issues tab.

```swift
registrar.forEveryShape { every in   // every shape is checked (its schema, at least), so any may have issues
    every.contentsMark(affected: { changes, context in
        context.service(ValidationEngine.self)?.affected(by: changes) ?? []
    }) { shape, context in
        guard let result = context.service(ValidationEngine.self)?.result(for: shape.id), let worst = result.worst else { return nil }
        return ContentsMark(color: Color(nsColor: worst.color), help: result.worstFirst.map(\.message).joined(separator: "\n"))
    }
}
```

- **A mark is part of its row**, made with it, and made again with it when a commit changes the
  shape. So a commit still costs the rows it changed, and SwiftUI redraws only those. Reading
  marks in the row's view instead would cost the whole board: the list makes every row's view
  whenever it redraws, and a row view that read the document would be asked for again after
  every commit.
- **`affected`** is for a mark read from more than its shape. Given each commit's change set, it
  names the shapes the commit doesn't change whose marks it may. Their marks are read again on
  the next read, and a row is replaced (and redrawn) only if its marks changed, so a shape many
  rules look at costs its dependents' marks when it's dragged, not their rows. Validation's rules
  may look at other shapes (`context.shape(_:)`), and the engine knows whose did
  (`dependents(of:)`): flattening the box a rule checks marks the shape the rule is for. A rule
  that reads a service names what a commit changes the issues of (`affected`), and the engine
  hands both over (`affected(by:)`), with what was named on a board while it wasn't shown when
  it's given that board's `elsewhere` on going back: a rename on the root that gives a title in a
  subboard a second holder marks its row there. A mark
  read from its shape alone leaves `affected` out.

  A rule's state can also change with no commit at all (a caret leaving a row, a relationship's
  verdict moving far from its arrow). `editor.validation?.recheck(ids)` checks those shapes
  again: on the board shown at the next read, with the ring redrawn, on a board the engine keeps
  when it is taken back. It tells the table of contents to make their rows again itself, since no
  commit may come to ask.
- **Several marks** on one row stand side by side: the kind's, then those whose scope reaches it,
  each in plugin order (`ContentsMarkContribution`, contributed for a kind, is a kind's own).
- **A scope** says which kinds a mark is for, so it goes only on those that opted into what it marks,
  as an adornment's does: `ContentsMarks` takes [scopes](#scopes), so a mark for every kind with no
  scope is refused, and `forEveryShape` is for what every shape has, as the dots above. Locking
  marks a locked shape's row with a lock, on the kinds that can be locked, reading only the record:

  ```swift
  registrar.forShapes(holding: LockedProperty.self) { lock in
      lock.contentsMark { shape, _ in
          shape.isLocked ? ContentsMark(symbol: "lock.fill", color: .secondary, help: "Locked") : nil
      }
  }
  ```
- **Headless**, `entry.marks` is a row's marks.

### What's listed, and selecting

- **Rows run front to back**, at every level: the shape painted over the rest first, as a layers list
  has them (Keynote's, Figma's), so a row dragged up comes forward ([Dragging rows](#dragging-rows)).
  data-canvas's z-ordered outline went back to front, and so did this one until its rows could be
  dragged; the owner chose front to back then. `entries` keeps document order, as the core keeps
  shapes (back to front), and the list shows each level the other way round (`ListedRows`, a
  board's rows open under its owner's in `BoardRows`, a crumb's menu in `OutlineRows.lines`), so
  what's listed is still made and kept by what changed. Selecting a shape doesn't restack it, so
  rows move only when shapes are restacked (Bring to Front, or a row dragged).
- **A shape the board keeps aside has no row**, whatever its kind (one that isn't installed isn't
  listed by its kind's name), since nothing on the canvas sees it
  ([Boards on disk](#boards-on-disk)). A row that names it to nest under stays at the top.
- **Selecting filters the list**, like data-canvas's multi-select summary: select several shapes
  on the canvas and only they are listed, under their header ("2 Shapes") and "Selection"; select
  nothing and the whole board is, under "Board"; select one and the panel shows its details. Show
  All lists the board again without deselecting.
- **A change of what's listed replaces the rows**, so the new scope's come in as one run under the
  header, not around the rows both scopes list (each open or closed as it was). Rows coming
  in at several places at once, the last row among them, make AppKit measure the last row from
  inside measuring the others (a table whose rows size themselves, as a SwiftUI `List`'s do,
  measures new rows a run at a time and resizes itself after each) and log "a reentrant operation
  in its NSTableView delegate", which it says will become an assert. So a commit that brings rows
  in at more than one place replaces the rows too (a `canvas draw` that adds a shape and connects
  two shapes far apart in the list; deleting a note that two arrows start from, as their rows come
  out from under it), while one that brings them in at one place (an arrow drawn, a paste) keeps
  the rows it has. It does so in a list of any length: a list of 250 rows logs it too, rows brought
  in around those kept, and not when they're replaced. AppKit still logs it when a list first
  shows 200 rows or more (it measures 200 at a time). Replaced rows come in open or closed as they
  were, a container's open (as one run all the same), and a row that goes lets go only of a hover
  the pointer on it set (`ContentsState.endHover`), never one the canvas set, so the shape under the
  pointer stays outlined.
- **Selecting rows** (a click, ⌘- and ⇧-clicks, the arrow keys) selects their shapes and brings
  them into view: centered, zoomed to fit with 100 points of margin but no closer than 120%, over
  200 ms (data-canvas's click-to-zoom, and tldraw's zoomToBounds): Selection's `editor.reveal`,
  the one way any plugin brings shapes into view ([Selection](#selection)). A click on one row selects one
  shape, so its details replace the list, as in data-canvas. ⌘- and ⇧-clicks leave several
  selected, and the list keeps listing what it listed, so rows can be added and taken out without
  the rest going away. That holds until the selection next changes some other way, which
  `editor.selectionRevision` tells apart from the same shapes selected again.
- **A row of a board under its owner's** is of a shape that isn't on the board shown, so selecting
  it goes to it, as following a link does (Selection's `editor.goTo`): its board shown, the shape
  selected there and brought into view, one step back, leaving whatever else was selected behind.
  Several such rows go to the board of the one listed first (front to back), selecting those on it in
  document order. That's only when such rows are all a
  selection adds: a ⇧-click whose range passes over an open board's rows selects the rows of the
  board shown in it. Its primary action (a double-click,
  Return) goes into it (`editor.goInto`: there, then opened, as one step back).
- **Hovering links the two.** There's one hovered shape, Selection's `editor.hovered`, and both
  sides set it and show it. The pointer on a row hovers its shape, as the pointer on the shape
  would, and the canvas outlines it faintly. The pointer on a shape on the canvas tints its row:
  a faint accent where the selection's highlight goes, in its shape. A selected shape shows neither,
  only its selection. data-canvas marks a row when its shape is hovered on the canvas (a faint ring);
  its rows don't hover the canvas. A row's tint observes only its own shape's hover
  (`editor.isHovered`) and, while that shape is hovered, the selection, so the pointer moving down
  the list, or across the canvas, redraws the row the hover leaves and the row it reaches. A row
  that read `editor.hovered` instead would be asked for its view again on every hover change, as
  every other row would. A row of a board under its owner's (above) is of a shape the canvas
  doesn't show, so the pointer on it hovers nothing and leaves a hover as it is; Selection's
  `editor.hoveredElsewhere`, observed, says which shape the pointer is on instead
  ([Selection](#selection): the canvas outlines the card that holds it faintly, and
  [Neighbors](#neighbors) lights what it's connected to). The pointer leaving the row, the row going
  away (`endHover`) or another board shown lets go of it: of what the row's pointer set, never of a
  hover another plugin set.
- **The board shown.** It lists `editor.document`, so the board shown and nothing under it. Each
  board's rows, and its listing of every row, are kept for the boards shown last (a `BoardStash`),
  and taken back on the way back to one that hasn't changed since, so going back makes no row. A
  scope pinned by selecting rows or Show All was the board left's, and goes. Another board's rows
  replace this one's in one run, whatever's listed on either (the list's id is the board, the scope
  and how many times a commit has brought rows in at several places, `ContentsListID`).
- **The heading.** The header says "Board" over the whole board. A plugin that knows what a board
  is called can name it instead (the `ContentsHeadings` point, at most one: a second is a
  conflict): `registrar.contentsHeading { editor in … }` returns a `ContentsHeading`, or nil for
  the list's own: a title, a symbol before it, and `up`, a command
  the header offers as a button while it can run (`editor.canPerform`): an arrow turning up, not a
  chevron, which in a list's disclosure column reads as collapsing, named to VoiceOver as the command
  is (`registry.title(of:)`), and `upHelp` is its tooltip, the title and its key, if the command has
  one, as a tool's is. It's read in
  the header's body (`ContentsState.heading`), so it reads observable state and the header alone
  redraws as that changes. The table of contents doesn't know what a board is called; the
  heading's maker does (Boards' `BoardContentsPlugin`: [Boards](#boards)). Filtered, the header is
  "Selection" with Show All, whatever the heading.
- **Opening a row.** A double-click or Return on a row opens its shape, as Return on the canvas
  does: `ContentsState.open(_:)`, the list's primary action, selects it and runs Selection's
  `editor.open` (entering the board it owns, editing it, whatever its kind opens to; one row, that
  `editor.canOpen`; several open nothing). A single click still selects and zooms. That's the list
  on its own; in the app's panel, picking one row selects its shape, so the panel shows that
  shape's panel in the list's place (the list is gone before a double-click's second click) and
  hands the keyboard to the canvas, where Return opens it.
- **Going back.** A row's click is a step in Selection's history like any other change of the
  selection, so the back button in the shape's header (or Go › Back, ⌘[) brings the list back,
  with the view as it was before the zoom, as data-canvas's back button does.
- **The keyboard.** A click gives the list the keyboard, as a source list does: the arrow keys move
  through the rows, Delete runs the `.delete` command (deleting the selected shapes, as Delete on
  the canvas does), and Escape gives the keyboard back to the canvas (`onExit`). So does hiding the panel while the list has the keyboard.
- **Headless**, `ContentsState` (`editor.tableOfContents`) is all of it: `entries` (the rows, a tree),
  `scope`, `select(_:)`, `showAll()`, the rows' hover: `hover(_:)` and `endHover(_:)` as the
  pointer moves onto a row and off it (for a row of another board, read back with
  `editor.hoveredElsewhere`) and `isHovered(_:)` for whether a row shows as hovered; and
  their disclosure, `isExpanded(_:)` and `setExpanded(_:_:)`. Tests read a row's text, symbol and
  badge through `entry.label`, its marks through `entry.marks`, the board its shape owns through
  `entry.nestedBoard` (its rows, `outline(of:)`, are under it in the list), and whether it starts
  expanded through `entry.startsExpanded`; `open(_:)` is a row's primary action. In debug builds,
  `rowsRedrawn` counts how often the list has asked a row for its view, and `rowsMade` how many rows
  it has made. Dragging rows has its own (below).

### Dragging rows

Rows drag, as a layers list's do: dropped above or below a row, what's dragged is restacked beside
its shape, in front of it or behind it; dropped on a frame's row it goes into the frame, and on a
subboard's onto its board; dropped among the rows a frame holds, or a subboard's board's, it goes
there and takes that place in the stack; dropped among the rows of a frame it's in, or of the board,
it comes out of the frames it was in. Rows of a board open under its owner's drag and take drops
like any other, so a shape moves off a subboard's board, onto it, and across.

```
┌─ dragging Eggs ─────────────────────┐
│ Board                               │
│   ▤ Bread                           │
│ ○──────────────────────────────     │ the line: behind Bread, in front of Groceries and all it holds
│ ▾ ▭ Groceries                       │
│     ▤ Milk                          │
│ ╭─────────────────────────────────╮ │ the ring: on Plans' row, onto its board
│ │ ▸ ▤ Plans                       │ │
│ ╰─────────────────────────────────╯ │
│   ▤ Eggs                            │ dragged (and, when it's selected, every selected row)
└─────────────────────────────────────┘
```

- **What drags.** A row's drag is its shape's (`dragged(from:)`), or, when its row is selected,
  every selected shape that can move and whose row shows, in document order, as the table drags every
  selected row that shows then.
  A shape that can't move doesn't: one with no box (an arrow, whose place in the stack doesn't say
  where it's drawn), one read-only (locked, or in a locked frame), one kept aside. Pressing a row and
  dragging doesn't select it (the table selects on the release of a click), so the panel doesn't turn
  to the shape's details under a drag. Each row is a drag source of its own (`.itemProvider`, which
  the list's table asks for what each dragged row carries: `dragItem`, which begins the drag,
  `beginDrag(from:)`) carrying a private type (`com.example.InfiniteCanvas.contents-rows`, conforming
  to `public.data`, which the app declares, `.ownProcess`), so a drop in another app does nothing, and
  a list takes a drop only of a drag it began (`dragShapes`): the drag under way is kept by the editor
  whose list it began in, as AppKit doesn't tell the list how a drag ended.
- **Where it points.** Each row is a drop target of its own (`.onDrop(of:delegate:)`, SwiftUI's
  per-row target, to which AppKit hands a drag over the row), told where on the row's height the drag
  is (`target(onRow:at:)`): on a frame's or a subboard's row its top and bottom quarters are above and
  below it, its middle on it; on any other row, halves. Below an open frame's or subboard's row is
  above the first row it opens onto, so on it (in front of what it holds); below the open row of a
  shape that takes nothing (a note open onto its arrows), nowhere. A drag that can drop there shows a
  line above or below the row, from a ring at its start, or a ring around the row, in the accent
  color, and nothing where it can't (`dragMoved(over:at:)`, `dragLeft(_:)`, observed per row:
  `dropZone(for:)`). Resting on a closed row that opens onto rows (a subboard's) opens it after 700 ms,
  as Finder's folders spring open. Not SwiftUI's own reordering, `onMove` and `onInsert`: an outline
  of them turns every drop on a row into an insertion after it, so a frame's row could never take
  one.
- **A drop's place** (`ContentsPlace`): on a frame's row, in the frame, in front of what it holds; on
  a subboard's, on its board, in front of what it holds; above or below a row, beside its shape where
  it is, in its container or on its board directly, in front of it (and of what it holds) or behind
  it. Not beside a row nested under something other than its container (a pin under what it's pinned
  to), a shape with no box, or one of what's dragged; and the mover refuses what goes with what's
  dragged (a frame into itself or what it holds, a subboard onto its own board).
- **A drop that leaves shapes in their container restacks them** there (`ContentsPlace.restack`),
  keeping their order among themselves: one step, Reorder. Their container takes what it holds along,
  a frame in front of a shape goes in front of it with all it holds, and on another board the core
  restacks there (`move(_:above:on:)`).
- **A drop that takes them elsewhere is `ContentsMoves`'**, a point the list declares and one plugin
  fills (Moving): where they land on the canvas is the contributor's, as placing a shape is
  [`canvas draw`](#draw)'s, and it restacks them where the drop says in the same step
  (`place.restack(_:in:containingKinds:)`). It's asked whether it takes them as a drag moves over the
  rows, so it lays nothing out then (and the list keeps its answer for the drag, the target and the
  editor's revision), and refuses a place that goes with them, where the core's move traps. Without
  one, a drop only restacks:

  ```swift
  registrar.contentsMoves(admits: { shapes, place, editor in Drop(shapes, to: place, in: editor) != nil },
                          move: { shapes, place, editor in Drop(shapes, to: place, in: editor)?.commit() })
  ```
- **Headless**, `dragged(from:)`, `beginDrag(from:)` and `dragShapes` are the drag;
  `target(onRow:at:)`, `admits(_:)`, `drop(on:)` (and `dragMoved(over:at:)`, `dragLeft(_:)`,
  `drop(onRow:at:)`, as the rows' targets call them) the drop; `dropZone(for:)` what a row shows. In
  a window the list's table hands out each dragged row's writer
  (`outlineView(_:pasteboardWriterForItem:)`), and a row's own drop target, the view in its cell
  registered for every type, takes a drag as AppKit hands it one (TableOfContentsTests'
  `DragWindowTests`).

### Another board's outline

The list is the board shown's, as the selection filters it. A view of any board of the file lists
that board's rows through `ContentsState.outline(of: board)`: the rows `entries` would list there
with nothing selected, nested alike, whichever board is shown. What the path's crumb menus show
(Boards: a crumb's menu is its own board, [A crumb's menu](#a-crumbs-menu)).

```swift
ContentsOutline(editor: editor, board: board, highlighted: next, maxHeight: 348) { id in
    editor.goTo([id])
}
```

- **The rows are the list's**, each as its kind draws it (`contentsRow`, named by `contentsTitle`),
  less their marks, which are the board shown's: validation checks only it. A board under its
  owner's row in the list is this outline too.
- **Made once, kept while the board is as it was.** The first read makes every row of the board;
  another is taken back while the board's revision is unchanged and it's on the path to the board
  shown (showing a board forgets the outlines of boards off its path). A read after a commit that
  did more than move shapes makes again the rows that read more than their shapes (a note's, with
  the live names of what it mentions: its kind's `affected` answers only for the board shown, so
  every such row is made again, whatever else the commit touched), and keeps each whose label is
  the same; a move (a drag's every event) names nothing anew, and makes none. Reading it ties the
  reader to every commit, as `entries` does. `./build.sh bench` holds the reads after a move and a
  rename on a subboard under a root of 10,000 to 1 ms and a frame; the first read there is some
  23 ms.
- **`ContentsOutline(editor:board:highlighted:maxHeight:onPick:)`** shows it, for a small panel:
  one line a row, 24 points each, as tall as its rows up to `maxHeight`, past which it scrolls
  (only the rows in view are made into views); nested rows behind a disclosure triangle, as in the
  list: a container's open, the rest collapsed until it's opened, a board under its owner's row
  too, read once it's opened, each time the panel shows (the panel keeps what's turned while it
  shows); `highlighted`'s row tinted as a hovered row is in the list, and the row under the pointer
  lit. A click on a row picks its shape (`onPick`), and what that
  does is the host's. It opens at the top, as data-canvas's menus do (scrolling a lazy stack to a
  row far down lays out the rows before it: some 70 ms to the last of 10,000). Nothing without the
  plugin, or for a board with no rows.

### Hosting

(The app's window wraps the canvas in CanvasUI's `BoardChrome(editor:showsInspector:onExit:)`, a
view modifier that places what the plugins gave [the host's slots](#host-slots): the path, Jump To's
palette (`JumpToPalette`, over the canvas, given `onExit` to give the keyboard back),
the inspector with this panel and its toolbar button, and the rule that shows the inspector while
it's wanted (a takeover is active: Find, open, with the inspector hidden; and hides it again
as Find closes, if that's what showed it); CompositionTests'
`InspectorHost` applies the same modifier. The toolbar and the frame stay the app's.)

The detail panel has [an overview](#the-overview-and-takeovers), a view it shows where it has no
one shape to show, and the table of contents gives its list as that, from a plugin value of its
own, so TableOfContents imports DetailPanel (one horizontal on another) and the list of what ships names
the plugin, after both:

```swift
public struct ContentsOverviewPlugin: ListedPlugin {
    public var id: PluginID { .contentsOverview }      // "contents-overview"
    public func register(into registrar: inout PluginRegistrar) {
        registrar.detailOverview { editor, onExit in TableOfContentsView(editor: editor, onExit: onExit) }
    }
}
```

A list without the panel leaves it out and keeps the list's state, which the path's crumbs' menus
read too; a list with it and no panel is refused (`ownerNotInstalled`).

Bringing shapes into view is Selection's `editor.reveal`, which the table of contents calls. It
takes two generic things from the core: `editor.viewportSize`, which
`CanvasView` reports as it's resized, and `editor.animateCamera(to:duration:)`, eased like
tldraw's camera moves and stopped by any other camera change, as the hand tool's slide is.
`Camera(fitting:in:inset:minZoom:maxZoom:)` (Geometry) does the fit.

## Adornments

An adornment is something small shown on a shape, just outside it or on its corner: a title's
pill, a lock. It's a horizontal ([`Sources/Adornments`](../Sources/Adornments))
through which any plugin puts one on any kind, its own, another plugin's, or every shape. Adornments
lays out each shape's, so none overlaps another, draws them, and makes each its shape's for the
pointer. The core has never heard of one.

```
╭─────────────────────────╮ ╭────╮
│ Groceries for the week… │ │lock│    the row, 9 points above the top edge, 18 tall: a title's
╰─────────────────────────╯ ╰────╯      pill at its left end, a lock at its right end, 4 apart
                           ╭───────╮
┌──────────────────────────│ ☑ 1/3 │  the corner, 16 tall, centered on the top edge: a
│ Buy milk                 ╰───────╯    tally, reaching 6 points past the right edge
│                                │
└────────────────────────────────┘
```

An adornment is never a shape or a record. What it shows is made from its shape's data (its
props, an added property, what the registry says of its kind), so it moves, copies, deletes and
saves with the shape, and there's nothing to attach, keep in step or clean up. Neither of the two
shipped is placed by the plugin that defines the note: Titles places the pill and Locking the
lock, on every shape of the kinds that take part.

### An adornment is a type

An adornment is a type, as a tab or a menu group is: every contribution that names it puts the
same thing in the same place, and a typo doesn't compile. The type says where it goes on its shape
(`placement`) and where among the others there (`order`); what it shows on each shape is a label
the plugin that places it makes from the shape. Locking's chip, whole
([Locking.swift](../Sources/Locking/Locking.swift)):

```swift
public enum LockChip {}

extension LockChip: Adornment {
    public static var placement: AdornmentPlacement { .aboveTopRight }   // the right end of the row above the shape
    public static var order: Order<Self> { .last }                       // a state that comes and goes: farthest out
}

extension LockChip: ClickableAdornment {
    /// A locked shape's chip unlocks it; a just-unlocked one's locks it again.
    public static func click(_ click: AdornmentClick, in editor: CanvasEditor) { editor.service(LockState.self)?.click(click.shape) }
}

// In LockingPlugin.register: on the kinds that can be locked, a lock while a shape is locked, and
// for a moment after, the lock open, fading; on the rest, nothing.
registrar.forShapes(holding: LockedProperty.self) { lock in
    lock.adornment(LockChip.self) { shape, context in
        if shape.isLocked { return AdornmentLabel(systemImage: "lock.fill") }
        return context.service(LockState.self)?.openLockOpacity(of: shape.id).map { AdornmentLabel(systemImage: "lock.open.fill").opacity($0) }
    }
}
```

- **Conform in an extension**, as for a tab: `order` has a default (0), and only there does the
  compiler flag a near miss.
- **The label says what's shown on one shape**, or nil for nothing there, so a lock shows only on
  a locked shape. Locking a shape shows its chip because the label now says so; nothing is added.
- **A `ClickableAdornment`** is one a click does something with: a [canvas button](#canvas-buttons)
  whose `click(_:in:)` gets an `AdornmentClick`: the shape it's on, the label's tag and where the
  chip is ([pointing](#pointing)).

### Placing one

| Sugar | For |
|---|---|
| `x.adornment(A.self) { shape in ... }` | This kind's shapes, inside `registrar.shape { x in ... }`, typed as its own (`ShapeRecord<Props>`). A horizontal's opt-in sugar may call it, so opting in brings its adornment. |
| `registrar.adornment(A.self, on: Kind.self) { shape in ... }` | Another plugin's kind, typed as its own. |
| `scope.adornment(A.self) { shape, context in ... }`, in `registrar.forShapes(holding: P.self)` or `forShapes(adopting:)` | The shapes of the kinds the scope reaches, over `AnyShapeRecord`: what a horizontal places on shapes it doesn't define, only where its feature is. |
| `x.adornments(A.self) { shape in [...] }`, `registrar.adornments(A.self, on: Kind.self) { ... }`, `scope.adornments(A.self) { shape, context in [...] }` | The same three, for several labels in order: a [group](#several-labels-a-group), at `aboveTopLeft` only. |

A scope picks the kinds ([Scopes](#scopes)), so an adornment that shows a fact goes where the fact is:
Locking's lock is `forShapes(holding: LockedProperty.self)`, the kinds that can be locked, and a
capability picks by what a kind is (`forShapes(adopting: (any Editable).self)`, or a fact a module
states). Titles places its pill this way, on the kinds that opted into its own point with a title
that shows one (`forShapes(adopting: .titlePill)`, [Titles](#a-horizontal-plugin)). So
`note.title()` brings the pill, a kind that draws its own says `pill: false`, and the report says
Titles, which defines no kind, places the pill
(`adornment TitlePill → every shape with a title pill`). `ShapeAdornments` takes scopes, so an
adornment for every kind with no scope is refused. A plugin puts one on a kind it doesn't define,
typed:

```swift
public enum SizeBadge {}
extension SizeBadge: Adornment {
    public static var placement: AdornmentPlacement { .onTopRightCorner }
}

registrar.adornment(SizeBadge.self, on: Patch.self) { patch in AdornmentLabel("\(Int(patch.frame.width)) pt") }
```

### Places

Three places, along the top edge, each from the shape's bounds (its geometry's, axis-aligned, so
a kind without a frame has them too), in view points:

| `AdornmentPlacement` | Where | Shipped |
|---|---|---|
| `.aboveTopLeft` | The row just above the top edge, 18 points tall and 9 above it, from its left end rightward, in the room its right end leaves. Text gives way, ending in "…", and needs 30 points, and a symbol's place and gap before it more (`Item.lead`), so it's never a symbol alone: with less, it's left out, and so is what comes after it. The only place that takes [several labels](#several-labels-a-group) from one adornment. | A title's pill |
| `.aboveTopRight` | The same row, from its right end (the shape's right edge) leftward, whole: on a shape too narrow for it, past the shape's left edge. | A lock |
| `.onTopRightCorner` | The top-right corner: 16 points tall, centered on the top edge, from 6 points past the right edge leftward. | None (a tally, as above) |

These are from a closed shape's bounds. An open shape (an arrow) has no top edge to sit on, so
they go from its [anchor](#an-open-shapes-anchor) instead.

A fourth place, `.inLabelLead`, is not one of these: it is the pill at the start of an open shape's
label (an arrow's, where Types puts a relationship's), in the line's cut, with the label's words after
it. The shape's geometry keeps room for it (`ShapeGeometry.labelLead`, a rect in world units within
`label`), and asks how wide the pill is through the layout input Adornments provides
(`AdornmentLead.faces`: the size of each face the pill may take, widest first, so a short line can take a
narrower one, `AdornmentLabel.narrowing(to:)`); Adornments draws the face that fits the rect, in world
units, so it follows the zoom as the words do, and a click on it is a click on a clickable adornment. A
shape whose geometry keeps no room shows none.

In a place, adornments sit 4 points apart. They keep their size on screen down to 25% zoom, and
shrink with the shapes below it (0.4× at 10%); below 35% a shape drawn as a skeleton shows none, but
the shape being edited, drawn in full, keeps its own ([the label](#the-label)). A shape without an
outline (nothing drawn) shows none, and neither does one its
board keeps aside. On a 200-point note, in points from its top-left
corner, y down:

| The note | Laid out |
|---|---|
| Unlocked, with a long title | pill (0, −27, 200, 18) |
| Locked, with a long title | lock (182, −27, 18, 18); pill (0, −27, 178, 18) |
| With a tally on its corner | tally (206 − w, −8, w, 16), `w` its text's width and 10 |
| 40 wide, locked and titled | lock (22, −27, 18, 18); 18 points left in the row, so no pill |

So locking a note with a long title shortens its pill by 22 points, the lock's 18 and the 4
between, and unlocking it gives them back once the open lock has faded.

### What's guaranteed

On one shape, by construction (`AdornmentLayout`, pure geometry, which drawing and hit testing both
go by):

- **Nothing in a place overlaps anything else there**: each place is a run, packed 4 points apart.
- **The row's two ends never meet**: its left end runs in the shape's width, less what its right
  end holds and 4 points.
- **The row never meets the corner**: the row ends 9 points above the top edge and the corner
  starts 8 above it (the row's gap is half the corner's height, and a point), so no two plugins
  have to agree on a number.
- **Text at the row's left end is never wider than its room**: it gives way, ending in "…", or,
  with under 30 points, isn't shown.
- **A group's chips are whole, but the last** (see above), and a fold is the last thing of its group.
- **Nothing reaches far**: the row's right end and the corner go no more than 200 points from
  where they start (what would is left out, with what comes after it), and the row's left end stays
  within the shape's width, so every adornment is within x `min(0, width − 200)` … `width + 6` and
  y −27 … 8 of the shape's top-left corner (its anchor's, for an open shape), which culling and hit
  testing go by.

Not guaranteed: two shapes' adornments may overlap, and stack as their shapes do; an adornment and
another shape may overlap too, and the adornment is drawn over it (and takes presses there). On a
shape narrower than them, the row's right end and the corner run past its
left edge, whole: a lock on a vertical line spans −18 … 0.

### An open shape's anchor

A closed shape's adornments are placed from its bounds. A line has none worth the name, and its
corner is far from anything it says, so an open shape (`geometry.isClosed == false`) uses an
anchor, a rect the places measure from, in the same way:

- its **label** (`geometry.label`, which an arrow's words give), so the chips sit above the
  words; else
- a point, **the middle of its outline** (`outline[count / 2]`: an arrow's arc middle).

Either is widened about its center to at least `AdornmentLayout.minAnchorWidth`, 120 view points
(240 world units at 50%), so a row of chips has room beside a short label or none. The row is 27
points above the anchor's top, the right end is at its right edge, the left end at its left. Where the
anchor is the point (an open shape with no label, an arrow with no words) the row is centred on the
point as one run (the middle of its extent, the left end and the right end together, is the anchor's
middle; the corner rides along), so a chip, a `from` or a `to` sits above the shape's middle; a labelled
shape keeps its row from the label's left edge, and a closed shape reads nothing of this.
Nothing about this is the arrow's: Adornments reads the geometry any shape has, so a plugin with a
label on an open shape gets it as Arrows' arrows do. A locked, labelled arrow's lock is above
its label, and not at the corner of its bounds. Culling grows by the widening (the anchor reaches
60 points past the label's center, and the corner 6 more), so a line just outside the view whose
chips reach in is drawn and hit.

### Slanted shapes

On an open shape that is not level, the shape's own body runs through the middle of its anchor, so the row above the anchor
slides along the anchor (from where centring put it, on a point anchor), toward the side the body leaves clear, only as far as it must: no slot, grown by `AdornmentLayout.margin` (4 points), is crossed
by the body's centre line. The row moves whole (its right end and the corner with its left end), so each keeps its own packing; a falling chord
(`Slant.slope` > 0, y down) keeps the row's leftmost point no farther left than `-(h + rowGap - margin) / slope + margin` from the anchor's middle (`h` half the anchor's
height), a rising one its rightmost no farther right than `(h + rowGap - margin) / |slope| - margin`, at most `maxSlide` (200 world units), at every angle. A level shape is laid out as centring puts it, and every closed one as it was. The
layout slides the slots against the anchor and `editor.adornmentAnchor(of:)` is that anchor moved along with the row, so what hangs from it (a card, a menu) hangs
from where the row is. The slide reasons from the chord, so a straight shape is never crossed; a bent arrow's arc leaves the chord's direction away from the anchor
(more as it bends), and its chip may still be crossed (measured against the arc itself, with a chip centred: touched in one cell of the 150-long grid at +34, nearer than the margin in a few more, clear in the rest). A plugin does nothing for this.

### Plain text and a number

`AdornmentLabel.line(_:ink:)` is plain text with no capsule, in the row as a chip of its width is: a word
