that says what something is where its name would be (Types' `from` and `to` above an end's arrow). Its ink is
`.primary` (the canvas's label color) or `.secondary` (the softer one), each following the appearance, set once
for both as a Core Text line, in the 11-point system font.

`label.counted(n)` puts a number after a chip's text, 4 points past it, in the text's ink at 60%: how many of
something the chip stands for (Types' relationship chip on an arrow says how many fields its type gives the
arrow, and the values are shown nowhere on the board). The chip is wider by the gap and the number, and where
the row's left end gives way the text is cut and the number stays whole at the capsule's right end. It is part of
what makes two labels equal; a symbol alone has none.

### Several labels: a group

An adornment may show several labels, in order, each its own chip: a type chip per type of a
shape. The sugar takes a list, `x.adornments(TypeChip.self) { shape in names.map { AdornmentLabel($0.title).tagged($0.tag) } }`.
Types' `TypeChips` is the shipped one, on every kind that holds `is`
(`registrar.forShapes(holding: IsAProperty.self) { $0.adornments(TypeChips.self) { … } }`), with a
click (`ClickableAdornment`) that pops a menu up below the chip with `editor.popUpMenu`.

- **Left end only.** A group is for `aboveTopLeft`: at the right end a run is cut where it reaches
  200 points and everything after it with it (the lock), and the corner is a tally's. The registry
  refuses a group anywhere else, `RegistryError.invalid` naming the adornment and its plugin.
- **A tag** tells a group's labels apart: `AdornmentLabel(...).tagged(AdornmentTag(id))`, the
  plugin's own name for the label (a type chip's is its type's id). A hover, a press and a click
  go by it, so a chip keeps its look and its click through a rename and a change in the others'
  places. `AdornmentTag` takes a string or a `ShapeID`.
- **Whole or "+N".** A chip is shown whole or not at all, but for the group's last, which may be
  cut short like any text (30 points at least). The first that doesn't fit whole, and those after
  it, fold into one chip, "+N" (N the number it stands for), which always shows: if it wouldn't fit
  whole after the chips before it, those fold into it too, the later first, until it does; with no
  room even for the "+N" of the group's first chip, none of the group is shown. A last chip with
  under 30 points folds into "+1".
- **A title doesn't hide the chips.** Text at the row's left end before a group (a title's pill)
  leaves the group's "+N" its width, 4 points and the chip, so a long title is cut short and every
  type is still reachable. The title keeps the 30 points it needs to be shown at all; below that
  the chips go, as the title always has first claim on 30. The layout is pure
  (`AdornmentLayout.Item.group`, `overflowWidth`), and a group's chips are not "title text": they
  don't make the right end take its compact faces.
- **Missing.** `AdornmentLabel.missing()` draws the chip as a mention's pill does for what is gone:
  no fill, a dashed stroke and italic text in the canvas's own label colors (a symbol before its
  text is left off, being white). Hovered or pressed, a faint fill of the same color.
- **The "+N" is a button of its own**: `AdornmentButton.overflow(of: A.self, on: id)`, a click on it
  with `tag` nil and `isOverflow` true, the plugin shows a menu of every label.

A group reads, as any label does, only its shape and services that call `adornmentsDidChange`; it
is made, kept and dropped as one shape's labels are, and zoomed out below 35% it is not made.

### Order

In a place, each adornment goes where its type's `order` puts it, as tabs and menu groups do
([Order](#order-where-things-go-among-each-other)): one that says nothing where it first appears,
the kind's own, then those whose scope reaches it, each in plugin order. The first is nearest where
the place starts: the row's left end, its right end, the corner's outer end. As shipped:

| Adornment | Its order |
|---|---|
| A kind's own; one a horizontal's feature brings to the kinds that opt in (`TitlePill`) | none |
| Types' chips (`TypeChips`): what a shape is, after what it's called | `.after(TitlePill.self)` |
| A state of the shape that comes and goes (`LockChip`; Publishing's `PublicChip`, after it in plugin order) | `.last`: farthest out, so the others keep their places |

So a flag a kind shows of its own keeps its place at the row's right end whether a lock is beside it
or not, and plugins that don't know each other never need to agree on anything.

### The label

`AdornmentLabel` is what an adornment shows on one shape. Adornments draws every one, so every
plugin's look alike, as `ContentsLabel` keeps rows alike:

- **Text**, `AdornmentLabel("Groceries")`: one line (each run of whitespace, newlines included,
  folds into a space; blank shows nothing), white, in a capsule. In the row it's 11-point medium,
  7 points in from the capsule's ends; on the corner, 10-point semibold figures that line up, 5 in.
  With `systemImage:`, `AdornmentLabel("Order", systemImage: "curlybraces")`, a small SF Symbol
  goes before it (a kind's mark: Titles' pill on a kind that asks, `symbolInPill`), two points
  smaller than the text, semibold, white at 75%, centered in a place as wide as the text is tall
  (11 points in the row, 10 on the corner), 3 points before the text.
- **A placeholder**, `AdornmentLabel(placeholder: "Frame")`: text standing in for what isn't there
  (Titles' pill on an untitled shape whose kind asks for one), laid out as the same text is, a
  symbol before it too, its text dimmed: white at 55%, as secondary text is on a dark surface
  (`isPlaceholder`).
- **A symbol**, `AdornmentLabel(systemImage: "lock.fill")`: an SF Symbol, bold and white, in a
  disc as tall as its place, half as tall as the disc.
- **`tone`**: `.neutral` (the default), a title pill's dark gray; or `.success`, green, for
  something done (a tally with every item done).
- **`opacity(_:)`**: the same label drawn lighter, 0 to 1 (Locking's open lock, fading); a compact
  face (below) goes with it.
- **`brightSymbol()`**: the symbol before the text drawn in full white, as the text is, where it
  is otherwise a little softer (a mark, not news): Publishing's globe; a compact face's too.
- **`compact(_:)`**: `AdornmentLabel("Public · 3", systemImage: "globe").compact(AdornmentLabel(systemImage: "globe"))`,
  a narrower face the label may take at the row's right end (`aboveTopRight`). The row's left end
  (a title's pill) gives way to what's at the right, ending in "…" and needing 30 points, so a
  text chip there can cut a title short or push it out. Whenever the title wouldn't show whole,
  `AdornmentLayout` (pure: it knows every item's width, `Item.compact`) gives the chips that have a
  compact face theirs, nearest the edge first: the fewest that give the title as much width as all
  of them do (one already whole goes no farther), and every one when even that shows no title. A
  title the full chips show whole, or none at all, leaves them in full. So as the shape widens,
  however narrow it starts, the face changes once: compact (no title, then the title cut short,
  ending in "…", then whole) until the full chip and the whole title fit together, then full. A
  public note's title zoomed out to 50% has the compact chip from the narrowest shape, no title
  below 92 points, "Payments ro…" beside the globe and the count from there, the whole title from
  179, and the full "Public · 3" from 221. Nothing of the
  kind is drawn otherwise, and a chip with no compact face costs nothing. The compact face is laid
  out and drawn in the same place, in its own look (a symbol alone, where the label is text with
  a figure), is made with the label (its face is counted in `adornmentFacesMade`), and is the
  label `adornmentFrames(of:)` reports where it's taken. Publishing's chip has one.

- **`tagged(_:)`** and **`missing()`**: which of a group's labels it is, and the look of a name
  that is gone ([above](#several-labels-a-group)).
- **`line(_:ink:)`**, plain text with no capsule, and **`counted(_:)`**, a number after a chip's text
  ([above](#plain-text-and-a-number)).
- **`wrong()`**: the look of something wrong, a chip in red: the fill is red at 14% (22% hovered, 30%
  pressed) with no line inside the edge, its text and symbol red (the system red, which follows the
  appearance), and a wavy line under the text, a point wide, a corner every 2 points, drawn with the
  chip in the overlay. It wins over a tint, whether set before or after; a missing label stays missing;
  a symbol alone is a red disc with no wave. It is the look only: what
  is wrong is for the plugin that says so.
- **`tinted(_:)`**: `AdornmentLabel("Person").tinted(AdornmentTint(color, ink: ink, style: .light))`,
  a color in place of the tone's (a type's, in Types). `color` is fixed, the same in both
  appearances, so Adornments makes a tint's fills once; `ink` (the color by default) may follow the
  appearance. Solid: the capsule is the color, lighter hovered (15% white) and darker pressed (20%
  black), its text and symbol white. Light: the capsule is the color at 14% (22% hovered, 30%
  pressed) with a 1-point line of it at 35% inside the edge, its text and symbol the ink (a
  placeholder's at 60%); a light label's symbol is made again for the appearance drawn, since an
  image made with a dynamic color is fixed when it is made. A tint wins over the tone; a missing
  label ignores it; `opacity(_:)` and `tagged(_:)` keep it; a compact face is tinted only if its
  maker tinted it; the tint is part of the label's equality, so a changed tint lays the row out
  again; the group's "+N" is never tinted.

A clickable one draws lighter hovered and darker pressed (a missing one, a faint fill). A label can't draw itself (a sparkline):
that's [not built yet](#not-built-yet).

**Zoomed out**, below 35%, each shape follows its own level (`editor.drawsSkeleton(of:)`). A shape
drawn as a [skeleton](#skeletons) shows no adornments: none is drawn, laid out
(`editor.adornmentFrames(of:)` is empty), pointed at (a lock can't be clicked, and a point where a
pill would be is empty canvas, or whatever's there), made or kept. A skeleton is what a shape is
and where, so what's said just outside it is left off as its text is greeked, and what a title
says is said on the shape itself: Titles' [cover](#a-cover-zoomed-out). The shape being edited is
drawn in full, so its adornments are too, drawn and pointed at in full, while its neighbors' aren't
shown.

### One of each on a shape

`ShapeAdornments` is keyed: a contribution claims its target and its type, and on each kind its scope
reaches what it would claim for that kind alone, so an adornment is placed on a kind at most once.
Two plugins putting one adornment on a kind (a kind's own and another plugin's), or on one kind
through two scopes, are a `conflict`, and a contribution without Adornments is `ownerNotInstalled`:

```
titles and captions both claim sticky-note Titles.TitlePill in ShapeAdornments
titles contributes to ShapeAdornments, but adornments, which owns it, isn't installed
ShapeAdornments: Tags.Flags (from tags) shows several labels, which only aboveTopLeft allows, not aboveTopRight
```

A kind's own takes the place of a scoped one of the same type, as a kind's own menu item
does. So a shape shows each adornment once at most, by construction: a contribution names a type,
never an instance, and there's no second one to attach. Its one `check` refuses a group anywhere but `aboveTopLeft`: places are a closed
set, and orders needn't be unique. Adornments builds on Selection (a clickable adornment is its
canvas button), so a list with `AdornmentsPlugin` needs `SelectionPlugin` and `KeyboardPlugin` too.
The report shows each on its placer's line, with its order if it says one: `adornment TitlePill →
every shape with a title pill`, `adornment LockChip last → every shape holding locked`, or
`adornment Flag → box` for one kind.

### What a label reads

A kind's own label, and another plugin's for the kind, reads only its shape. One for the kinds a scope reaches also gets an
`AdornmentContext`, with what else it may read: the registry (`context.registry`), which never
changes, and a service's state (`context.service(S.self)`), but only a service that tells
Adornments when what it keeps changes: `editor.adornmentsDidChange(for: ids)`. `ChipFade` (below)
keeps how far each chip that shows a moment has faded, and says so each frame of the fade.

### A chip that fades: ChipFade

A state that comes and goes and then fades away (Locking's open lock after an unlock) is the same
machine whoever shows it, so Adornments has it, `ChipFade`, a service every list with
`AdornmentsPlugin` has (`editor.service(ChipFade.self)`, public). A plugin shows a chip
(`fade.show(MyChip.self, on: id)`), reads its opacity from the chip's label
(`context.service(ChipFade.self)?.opacity(of: MyChip.self, on: shape.id)`: nil when it isn't
showing, 1 while it is in full, less each frame of the fade), asks whether it's showing
(`isShowing`, for a click that takes it back) and takes it away at once when something else says
so (`hide`, whether it was showing). It's kept by the chip and the shape, so two chips on one shape
fade apart, and `show` on a chip that's showing, in its fade too, starts its linger over. The chip
shows in full for 1500 ms, longer while the pointer's on it (looked at again every 500 ms: it
may be about to be clicked), then fades over 300 ms in 16 ms frames on `editor.scheduler`, each
frame telling Adornments (`adornmentsDidChange`) for the shapes fading, and is gone. A plugin tells
Adornments for what it does itself (`show` and `hide`), once for all the chips it changes. A deleted
shape's chips go with it (told once), and what was under way on a board stops with the board.
`AdornmentStyle` holds the constants.

Adornments makes a shape's labels once, when it first draws or points at the shape in full, and
keeps them until a commit names the shape (its `ChangeSet`) or `adornmentsDidChange` does, with
their faces ([Drawing and cost](#drawing-and-cost)); a shape drawn as a skeleton has none made. So a label read from anything else (another
shape, the clock, a service that doesn't say) goes stale. `adornmentsDidChange` also redraws the
canvas, and has the select tool look again for a button under a still pointer
(`canvasButtonsDidChange`), so a lock that comes or goes under it is hovered, or no longer is. A
shape's labels read as services take a commit in are read after Adornments has, since looking it up
has it take the commit in first ([services hear a change](#services-hear-a-change)); what
`adornmentsDidChange` is told then has its leads looked at once services have settled, and the select
tool looks for a button under a still pointer then too.

### Drawing and cost

- **One overlay**, `AdornmentOverlay`, draws every shape's adornments, at Adornments' place in the
  plugin list: the shipped app puts `AdornmentsPlugin` after Validation, so they're over its
  outline, and under the marquee and Selection's handles. It goes back to front, a shape at a time,
  so a front shape's adornments are over a back shape's, and all of them are above every shape: a
  back shape's pill shows over a shape in front of it (and takes presses there).
- **Where the shape is drawn.** Adornments follow a [drawing offset](#the-cores-part-drawing-offsets)
  (a locked shape's shake moves its lock and its pill), keep drawing while a session runs (a drag),
  and stay out of the minimap and damage.
- **Only what's in view.** The overlay goes through `editor.paintOrder(in:)` with the visible rect
  grown by as far as adornments reach from their shapes (`AdornmentLayout.area(showing:scale:)`):
  a shape just below the view has its row in it, and a shape up to 200 points to its right can
  have a run reaching back into it. It's grown first by the farthest any shape is drawn from where
  it is (`context.worldDrawingReach`, zero unless one is), so a shape just outside the view that a
  shake draws toward it shows what of its adornments reaches in.
- **Kept, not remade.** `AdornmentState`, a service, finds each kind's adornments once (the
  registry is frozen), and keeps each shape's labels with their faces (the text set and measured,
  the symbol's image), made when the shape is drawn or pointed at in full, dropping them for the
  shapes each commit's change set names. As the canvas starts drawing skeletons
  (`drawsSkeletonsDidChange`) it lets everything go (the shape being edited makes its own again as
  it's drawn); zoomed back in, it makes those of what a frame draws. It doesn't look under the
  pointer itself: Selection hears the level change too and looks again, buttons first, and the
  layouts answer at the new level whichever hears first. So zooming out over a thousand adorned
  shapes makes and measures nothing (a frame zoomed out has no adornment to look at: the overlay
  returns at once, but for the shape being edited), and zooming in again makes what's in view.
  Where they go is worked out when it's asked, from what's kept, since it follows the zoom
  and geometry that follows other shapes: a few additions per adorned shape in view. So a frame
  costs a lookup and the drawing per adorned shape in view, and a drag the labels of what moves.
  Once labels are kept, a frame allocates nothing per adorned shape: one buffer of slots a frame
  (`AdornmentLayout.slots(of:width:into:)`), and the hovered and pressed buttons read once and
  compared field by field, never boxed (at 10% on the 10,000-shape bench board, 558 adorned shapes
  and 155 locks in view, the overlay took about a millisecond, as measured, with no array a shape
  or box a lock). `./build.sh bench` holds a hover and a drag at 10,000 shapes, with pills and locks
  in view, and a hover onto a pill, to a frame (16 ms).

### Pointing

| Adornment | What the pointer does |
|---|---|
| A `ClickableAdornment` (the lock) | It's a [canvas button](#canvas-buttons), through Adornments' own source: in the select tool, a press and a release on it click it (its type's `click(_:in:)`), before handles and shapes; dragged off, nothing, and Escape lets go. The pointing hand shows over it, and it draws lighter hovered and darker pressed. In other tools it's only drawn. |
| Any other adornment (a pill) | It's its shape's ([DecorationHits](#drawn-for-a-shape-decorationhits)): hover hovers the shape, a press selects it and a drag moves it, a double-click edits it, and a right-click opens its menu. A clickable one (the lock) is its shape's only for the right-click, which offers Unlock; everything else on it is the button's (a double-click is two clicks). |

- **A hit** is within 3 points of the adornment's capsule, so a disc's is a circle, 12 points from
  its middle, and not its box's corner. Of one shape's adornments the nearest takes it; of several
  shapes', the front-most shape's, as they're drawn, so a front shape's pill over a back shape's
  lock takes the press. Hits go by where a shape is, not where a shake draws it, as it's drawn:
  a shape drawn as a skeleton (`editor.drawsSkeleton(of:)`) shows no adornments, so none is hit
  there (a lock can't be clicked); the shape being edited's are hit in full. An
  unselectable shape's adornments are seen through, as it is, but a button isn't: a lock is clicked
  whatever its shape.
- **`editor.hoveredButton`** and `editor.pressedButton` hold an `AdornmentButton` on a clickable
  one: `AdornmentButton(LockChip.self, on: id)`, the type and the shape, and for a group's chip its
  `tag: AdornmentTag(...)`; the "+N" chip is `AdornmentButton.overflow(of: A.self, on: id)`.
- **A click** is an `AdornmentClick`: `shape`, the chip's `tag` (nil for an untagged label and for the
  "+N", which `isOverflow` says) and `rect`, where the chip is in world units now, the place to put a
  menu below.
- **`editor.adornmentFrames(of: id)`** is where each of a shape's adornments is now: an
  `AdornmentFrame` each (`adornment`, as `.of(TitlePill.self)`; its `label`, with its `tag`; its
  `isOverflow`, a group's "+N", its label the "+N" itself; and its `rect`, in
  world units at the current zoom, where the shape is), in the order they're
  claimed, leaving out those without room. It's empty for a shape with none, and for one drawn as
  a skeleton.
- **`editor.adornmentAnchor(of: id)`** is the rect that row is laid out against, in world units at
  the zoom now: a closed shape's bounds (a note's top-left is the row's), an open shape's label
  (above an arrow's words) or a point at the middle of its outline, widened about its center to what
  a row needs. What something that hangs from the same place goes by (a menu under an arrow, a
  card at a shape's pill) so it hangs where the row does. Nil for a shape that isn't there or has
  nothing drawn.
- **`editor.adornmentExtent(of: record)`** is how far above its top edge a shape reaches with the
  adornments it would show at 100% zoom (`AdornmentLayout.extent(of:in:)`: the row above reaches 27, a
  chip on the corner 8, none 0), in world units, for a record that need not be on any board (nothing is
  kept for it): what a tool that lays shapes out clear of each other's titles needs (`canvas measure`).

### Something the user turns on

data-canvas's sticker put a record beside a shape to say it was public. Here, what the user turns
on is something the shape knows, an [added property](#added-properties), and the adornment only
shows it. A flag, as a horizontal any kind opts into:

```swift
/// Whether a shape is flagged.
public enum FlagProperty {}
extension FlagProperty: ShapeProperty {
    public static let key: PropertyKey = "flagged"
    public static var defaultValue: Bool? { false }       // every flaggable shape has one, for the menu's item to be over
}

/// A flag at the right end of the row above a flagged shape.
public enum FlagChip {}
extension FlagChip: Adornment {
    public static var placement: AdornmentPlacement { .aboveTopRight }   // no order: nearer the row's end than a lock, which is last
}

public enum FlagMenuGroup {}
extension FlagMenuGroup: MenuGroup {
    public static var order: Order<Self> { .after(ShapeMenuGroup.self) }   // a feature's items, after a kind's own
}

extension ShapeRegistrar {
    /// Lets this kind's shapes be flagged: Flagged in their context menu, and a flag above each that is.
    public mutating func flaggable() {
        optIn(to: FlagProperty.self)
        contextMenu(of: FlagProperty.self) {
            MenuItem("Flagged", in: FlagMenuGroup.self, isChecked: { $0 }) { $0.toggle() }
        }
        adornment(FlagChip.self) { $0[FlagProperty.self] == true ? AdornmentLabel(systemImage: "flag.fill") : nil }
    }
}
```

The plugin declares the property (`registrar.declare(FlagProperty.self)`), and a kind opts in with
one line, `note.flaggable()`, as `note.title()` does. What that gives:

- **The fact is the shape's.** It's in the kind's schema, saved with the shape, copied with it (a
  flagged note's copy is flagged) and gone with it; the flag has nothing of its own to keep in
  step, and a board opened without the plugin keeps the value aside and saves it back.
- **One flag per shape**, by construction: the label says whether there is one.
- **The default is `false`, not nil**, so every flaggable shape has a value, which the menu's item
  is over. With a nil default only flagged shapes would carry it, as locked ones carry `locked`,
  but an item over the value shows only once it's set ([not built yet](#not-built-yet)), so the
  item would be one for the canvas, as Locking's Lock and Unlock are.

## The clipboard

Cut, copy and paste are a horizontal ([`Sources/Clipboard`](../Sources/Clipboard)) built on three
others: Selection (what's copied, and what's selected after a paste), Keyboard (⌘X, ⌘C and ⌘V) and
ContextMenus (Cut, Copy and Paste in every context menu). The core has never heard of a clipboard. It
lends four generic things: [commands](#commands), which may answer AppKit's Edit › Cut, Copy and Paste
(`answering:`; the commands themselves, `.cut`, `.copy`, `.paste` and the rest, are Clipboard's), shape [metadata](#metadata), the `ShapeReferencing` [capability](#capabilities), and
`CanvasFile.isUnused(_:)`, whether anything in the file goes by an id, which a paste asks before
giving a shape back the id it had.

| | Does |
|---|---|
| ⌘C, Edit › Copy, Copy | Puts copies of the selection's copyable shapes on the pasteboard, back to front, with what the boards they own hold, and what the containers among them hold. The board doesn't change. |
| ⌘X, Edit › Cut, Cut | Copies, marked as a cut's, then deletes what it copied whole, in one transaction. What can't be copied stays, and so does a shape whose board holds one, and a [locked](#locking) shape, or one on a locked subboard's board, copied all the same (it shakes, as with Delete). |
| ⌘D, Edit › Duplicate | Puts copies of the selection's copyable shapes beside it (`ClipboardStyle.duplicateOffset`, 16 view points down and right), selected, in one step, "Duplicate", without touching the pasteboard: a paste's own machinery, new ids all the way down, each copy naming its original, settled in place first (a container's copy lies over its original, and the copies go in the containers their originals are in) and then moved. Off mid-gesture, on a board that takes no shapes, and with nothing copyable. A drag of the selection with ⌥ held does the same in place at the press and drags the copies (Selection's `registrar.copiesOnDrag`, claimed by Clipboard), in the press's step; Escape takes them away again; read-only shapes are not copied (the drag refuses them, as ever). |
| ⌘V, Edit › Paste, Paste | Puts what's on the pasteboard on top of the board, settled where it lands by the in-or-out rule, and selects it: what a copy put there as copies, with new ids all the way down; what a cut put there moved, under the ids it had. Off on a board that takes no shapes (a locked subboard's, `editor.isBoardReadOnly`). |
| ⇧⌘V, Edit › Paste at Pointer | ⌘V, but what's put down lands centered on the pointer (`editor.pointerWorldLocation`) while it's over the canvas (`editor.isPointerOverCanvas`, which the host sets as the pointer moves over the canvas or presses there, and clears as it leaves it for the minimap, a view over the canvas or the window's edge, whatever the tool); otherwise, or with the pointer outside the view, as ⌘V pastes. The `.pasteAtPointer` command is claimed like `.paste`, so it's off where Paste is. |
| ⇧⌘C, Edit › Copy as Image | Not a command: the window's item draws what Clipboard gives its [host slot](#host-slots) (`registrar.imageSource`): the shapes a copy of the selection would take (`editor.imageShapes()`: the copyable shapes, with what the containers among them hold), or, with nothing selected, every copyable shape of the board shown, drawn from the board's own file. Dimmed with none (`editor.canCopyAsImage`). |

- **Copies that shared a group are a group of their own** ([Grouping](#grouping)): the copies on a
  board that were in one group are in a new one, under a new id, and a group only one of them was in
  is none of theirs; a shape a cut moves keeps its groups, as it keeps its id.
- **Copies get new ids, and remember their originals.** Each copy's metadata names the shape it
  was copied from: `record.copiedFrom`, which is `meta[CopiedFrom.self]?.shape`, and its board
  keeps it. That's the shape the copy was made from: a copy, if a copy was copied; in whichever
  board it was copied from, this one or another; and maybe gone since. Pasting a copy twice makes
  two copies of the same shapes. The rest of a shape's metadata comes with it, and so do its
  [added properties](#added-properties)' values: a locked shape's copy is locked, as tldraw's is. A paste moves its copies (`translate`) in the transaction that puts them
  in, which a lock doesn't stop.
- **Cut and paste is a move.** A cut marks what it writes as a cut's: a token beside the shapes,
  under a type of the app's own (`com.example.InfiniteCanvas.cut`), a fresh UUID each cut, in the
  same write. A copy writes none, and any later write clears it, this app's or another's. A paste
  of what a cut put there keeps each id nothing in the file goes by (`CanvasFile.isUnused`, the
  core's: no shape has it, no board is kept under it, and no entry that didn't read as a board is
  kept under the key its board would be written under), so the shapes the cut took come back as
  themselves, on whatever board the paste lands, and whatever names them (a
  [mention](#mentions-across-boards), on any board of the file) names them again. Such a shape gets
  no `CopiedFrom`: it's the same shape, moved, and keeps the metadata it had, an older
  `CopiedFrom` included, so a shape without one may still have been pasted. An id in use (the
  shapes an earlier paste of the same cut put down, or one whose deletion the cut had refused)
  makes that shape a copy, from the same map as the rest, so what's pasted names each of its
  shapes as pasted. There's no ledger of pastes: the first paste's shapes hold the ids, so pasting
  again copies, and undoing the first paste frees them. Pasted into another window, a cut moves
  there too, where the file doesn't use its ids. A binding from outside what was cut lets go of
  what the cut took, as it would of a deleted shape (a binding must be on its board), and the paste
  doesn't bind it again: an arrow to a note that moved stays where it's drawn, free. Only names
  survive a move.
- **Where a paste lands** is tldraw's: where the originals were, if any of them would be in view
  there; otherwise centered in the view, the shapes keeping their places among themselves. A paste
  in place lies exactly over its originals, as in tldraw and Figma. The context menu's Paste lands
  centered on its click instead (`editor.paste(centeredAt:)`, the menu's `point`), wherever what
  it pastes was copied from. Moving them is
  `transaction.translate(ids, by:)`, which moves every kind as dragging would: boxes by their frame,
  others by their `CustomTranslation`.
- **What's pasted is put down there as one**, as a drop is, by the in-or-out rule
  (`transaction.settle`, [Containers](#containers)), in the paste's step: into the container
  holding most of it, nudged fully in across its edge, or out of any it reaches into, gliding there
  (`editor.glide`); a container pasted takes in what it lands on. Over all of a container, what's
  pasted is beside it, not in it: a frame pasted in place, on its original, holds only its own
  copies, and takes none of the original's. What's selected is what isn't in another shape pasted
  with it. A read-only container (a locked frame, or a locked frame's copy just pasted) takes
  nothing: a paste one would take puts nothing down, given up whole (`editor.transactWhole`) so no
  step is left and what there was to redo stays, and services hear the container refused (Selection
  shakes it), as they hear a drop's.
- **Shapes bound to shapes.** A kind whose props are bound to other shapes (an arrow's bound ends)
  adopts the core's `ShapeReferencing`, which deleting a shape asks too. Copying asks it to let go
  of the shapes left out of the copy, and pasting asks it to bind the copies of those copied with it. So
  two notes and the arrow between them paste as two notes and an arrow between the copies, and an
  arrow copied alone pastes free, ending where it was drawn, as it would if its notes were deleted.
  tldraw's copy does the same. A shape that can't let go of one it can't find (an arrow bound to a
  shape its board keeps aside, or one a paste can't read) is left out, rather than copied wrong.
- **Shapes that only name shapes** ([`ShapeNaming`](#values-that-name-shapes), a mention) go through
  the same call, `record.remappingReferences`, which renames their names too: a copy names the
  copies of the shapes copied with it, and goes on naming the rest. Across a tree of boards a paste
  passes names through the whole tree's map (`remappingReferences(_:naming:in:)`): a note at the top
  pasted with a subboard mentions the copy of a shape two boards down, and a note inside mentions the
  copy of the subboard it's in, while bindings stay on their own board.
- **Shapes that own boards** (`BoardOwning`) are copied with what they hold, all the way down:
  the board a copied shape owns, the boards its shapes own, and so on, read with
  `editor.contents(of:)`. On each board, the shapes that can be copied go, letting go of those left
  out on that board, and a shape left out takes the boards under it. A shape of a kind that owns no
  board is copied without whatever board a file keeps under its id. A paste renames every shape on
  every board from one map (a copy's to new ids, a move's to its own), so shapes inside stay bound
  to each other and name each other (an arrow on a subboard stays bound), and each copy, nested
  ones included, names its original. Each owner goes in with its boards, keyed by its id as pasted
  (`transaction.insert(_:contents:)`, one commit); only the top-level shapes are moved into place
  and selected. A copy's new ids make a new tree, so a subboard pasted onto its own board is a copy
  inside itself, never a loop. Cut deletes only the shapes copied whole: one whose boards held
  something that couldn't be copied stays, as an uncopyable shape does, with everything under it,
  and its id being in use, it pastes as a copy.
- **Containers** ([`ShapeContaining`](#containers): a frame) are copied with what they hold, at any
  depth, as an owner is with its board: each shape in a copied container that can be copied goes
  too, its copy in the container's copy (`AnyShapeRecord.copy(as:container:)`, the container renamed
  through the paste's one map, as every id is), and a shape copied without its container is in none,
  and written so: the pasteboard is format 5 only when a container goes with something it holds, on
  any board copied. Cut takes a container with what it copied of it, a container being whole without
  what it holds (deleting it lets go of what stays): what it holds that couldn't be copied, or is
  read-only (a locked note in an unlocked frame, copied all the same, so it pastes back as a copy, in
  the frame), stays where it is, let go of. A cut and its paste move a container with what it holds,
  every id kept, each shape in its container again.
- **The pasteboard** holds a small board: `BoardCodec`'s JSON, each kind and added property at its version, under the
  app's own type. So one window can paste what another copied, a paste into a newer app migrates as
  opening a board does, and a kind the board doesn't install is left out of a paste, on any board,
  and with it the boards under it. With boards under the copied shapes it's a whole file,
  `CanvasFile`, at format 4, the boards under their owners' original ids; without, it's written
  as it always was, so an app that doesn't know boards pastes it, and one that doesn't know format
  4 pastes nothing. A pasted shape whose kind owns no board in this app gets none. Anything else
  on the pasteboard (text, an image from another app) is left alone for now. ⌘V, Edit › Paste and
  Paste are there only when something would paste, and the board shown takes shapes (`canPaste`),
  so otherwise ⌘V's key goes on, Edit › Paste is dimmed and the context menu has none; on a locked
  subboard's board nothing is pasted, and nothing refused, since there's nothing to try. Copy and
  Cut work there as they do for a locked shape: copies, and a cut deletes nothing and shakes. The pasteboard is
  read again only when it's changed. `ClipboardPlugin(pasteboard:)` takes the pasteboard, the
  system's by default.
- **Where the keys work.** ⌘X, ⌘C, ⌘V and ⌘D are Keyboard's while the canvas has the keyboard.
  Elsewhere the menu has them: the board's window controller answers Edit › Cut, Copy and Paste
  wherever the keyboard is, the table of contents' list included, except in text (a note being
  edited, a panel's field), which takes them first. Cut and Paste don't run mid-gesture; Copy does.
- **Undo.** Cut and Paste are one step each, "Cut" and "Paste" (a duplicate's is "Duplicate", a ⌥-drag's copy and its move together), by key, menu or context menu.
  Undoing a cut brings the shapes back selected; undoing a paste selects what was before it, and
  redoing it brings back the same copies (the same ids, `copiedFrom` and all). Undoing a move's
  paste takes the shapes out and frees their ids (a paste after it moves them again), redoing it
  puts them back under them, and undoing the cut too puts the file back as it was, showing the
  board the cut was made on.
- **In the context menu**, Cut, Copy, Duplicate and Paste are items for the canvas
  (`registrar.contextMenuForCanvas`), in `ClipboardMenuGroup` (no order: after a kind's own items and a feature's, before Arrange), asked
  once per menu. Cut, Copy and Duplicate (⌘D's, beside the shapes) show when some of the menu's shapes can
  be copied, and act on those; Paste shows when something would paste, on shapes and on empty canvas, and lands where the menu
  was asked for.

**Opting out.** Every kind is copyable unless it says otherwise, for all its shapes or for some, as
with selecting:

```swift
registrar.shape(TicketDefinition()) { ticket in ticket.uncopyable() }
registrar.shape(StampDefinition()) { stamp in stamp.copyable { !$0.props.isSealed } }
```

A selection's uncopyable shapes are left out of a copy, and stay when it's cut. With only such
shapes selected, ⌘C and ⌘X pass the key on, and the menu has no Cut or Copy. Everything
else treats them as usual: they're selected, moved, deleted and erased. The rule is
`ShapeCopyability`: at most one per kind, plus one for every kind, which a kind's own overrides.

### Metadata

A shape's metadata (`AnyShapeRecord.meta`) is the core's place for what a plugin keeps about a
shape, such as where it was copied from, as opposed to what the shape knows: its kind's properties,
and those plugins add to it ([Properties](#properties-and-metadata)). A member is typed by a key the
plugin that owns it declares, as an extension point is:

```swift
public enum CopiedFrom {}
extension CopiedFrom: ShapeMetaKey {
    public typealias Value = CopySource        // { shape: ShapeID }
    public static var owner: PluginID { .clipboard }
    public static var name: String { "copiedFrom" }
}
```

Read it with `record.meta[CopiedFrom.self]`, and change it in a transaction:
`tx.update(id) { $0.meta[Key.self] = value }`. A board keeps it beside the props, under the
owner's id, then the name (`"meta" : { "clipboard" : { "copiedFrom" : { "shape" : "…" } } }`), so
two plugins' members never share a place; members no installed plugin knows are kept, and a copy
(`record.copy(as:)`) takes it along. A board with any metadata is format 2 at least, which an app
from before it won't open rather than save without it; opening one leaves out metadata that isn't an
object for each plugin, and says so (`LoadReport.Repair.droppedMeta`). Unlike props, members
aren't versioned: add only optional fields to a value, since one that no longer decodes reads as
nil.

## Locking

A locked shape can't be changed: not moved, restacked, resized, edited or deleted, whatever tries,
until it's unlocked. A locked frame locks what it holds, and a locked subboard what's on its board,
and on every board under it. Each try shakes it a little, and a lock chip sits just above its
top-right corner, and a lock at the end of its row in the table of contents. Shapes are locked from the
context menu, with ⇧L, or by `/lock` typed on a line of their text, and unlocked from the menu, with ⇧L or with a
click on the chip, which shows the lock open for a moment, where a click locks the shape again.
It's a horizontal
([`Sources/Locking`](../Sources/Locking)) that every kind is in, built on Adornments, ContextMenus, Keyboard,
Selection, SlashCommands and TableOfContents; the core has never heard of a lock. It lends two generic things, read-only shapes
and drawing offsets, [Adornments](#adornments) lays out, draws and points the chip (a clickable
adornment, so a [canvas button](#canvas-buttons)), and Locking does the rest
([Locking.swift](../Sources/Locking/Locking.swift)):

```swift
registrar.declare(LockedProperty.self)                  // `locked: true` on a locked shape; nothing on the rest
registrar.optInEveryShape(to: LockedProperty.self)
registrar.readOnlyShapes { $0.isLocked }                // the core refuses changes to them
registrar.service { LockState(editor: $0) }             // which just-unlocked shapes show their lock open (a ChipFade); what is locked is the records'
registrar.command(.lock, title: "Lock", runs: .whenIdle, isEnabled: { !$0.locks.allLocked }) { subject in
    subject.editor.lock(subject.locks.tried)            // the shapes whose own lock can change
}
registrar.command(.unlock, title: "Unlock", runs: .whenIdle, isEnabled: { $0.locks.canUnlock }) { subject in
    subject.editor.unlock(subject.locks.tried)
}
registrar.shortcut(KeyChord("l", .shift), "Lock or Unlock", forCommands: [.lock, .unlock])   // ⇧L: whichever can run
registrar.forShapes(holding: LockedProperty.self) { lock in  // everything Locking puts on shapes goes on the kinds that can be locked, and no other
    lock.adornment(LockChip.self) { shape, context in  // the chip: closed while locked, open a moment after
        if shape.isLocked { return AdornmentLabel(systemImage: "lock.fill") }
        return context.service(LockState.self)?.openLockOpacity(of: shape.id).map { AdornmentLabel(systemImage: "lock.open.fill").opacity($0) }  // from Adornments' ChipFade
    }
    lock.contentsMark { shape, _ in  // a lock at the end of its row
        shape.isLocked ? ContentsMark(symbol: "lock.fill", color: .secondary, help: "Locked") : nil
    }
    lock.contextMenuForCanvas {                         // shown by the commands' rules: one of the two
        MenuItem(command: .lock, in: StateMenuGroup.self)
        MenuItem(command: .unlock, in: StateMenuGroup.self)
    }
    lock.slashCommands {                                // `/lock`, while the shape isn't locked
        SlashCommand("lock", command: .lock)
    }
}

extension LockChip: ClickableAdornment {                // a click on the chip: a try of Unlock or Lock
    public static func click(_ click: AdornmentClick, in editor: CanvasEditor) { editor.service(LockState.self)?.click(click.shape) }
}
```

- **A lock is something the shape knows**, as tldraw's `isLocked` is: an [added
  property](#added-properties), `locked`, that every kind opts into, so it's in every kind's schema
  and saved with the shape (`"added" : { "locked" : true }`). Its default is nil, so only locked
  shapes carry it, and unlocking takes it away. Read it with `record.isLocked`, and change it with
  `editor.lock(ids)` and `editor.unlock(ids)`, each one transaction.
- **The menu** has one of two items, in `StateMenuGroup` (ContextMenus', right before Delete's; Types' Is a ▸ is in it too, right after), as
  tldraw's toggle: Unlock when every shape the menu is for is locked, and otherwise Lock, which locks
  the rest. They're items for the canvas in Locking's scope (a menu whose every shape holds `locked`,
  as every kind does), so a mix of locked and unlocked shapes gets one; on empty canvas, neither. They run Locking's two [commands](#commands), `.lock` and `.unlock`, whose rules
  are the items' (Lock while some shape whose lock can change isn't locked, Unlock while all are);
  ⇧L runs whichever can, and both items show it ([context menus](#context-menus)); `/lock` is the
  other way in, and the chip's click is a try of one (`editor.attempt`), so a shape whose lock can't
  change shakes. Both go by the shapes' own locks, of those whose lock can change: a shape in a locked frame, or on a locked subboard's
  board (below), can't change, its own lock included, so neither item is for it
  (`isLockedByContainer`, O(its depth)): a menu for only such shapes has neither, and one for some
  of them and others locks or unlocks the others, trying none of them (so none shakes).
- **`/lock` is a [slash command](#slash-commands)**: typed on a line of its own in a shape's text (a
  note's), it locks the shape, as the menu's Lock does. It's offered
  on every kind that holds `LockedProperty` (`lock.slashCommands` in its scope, so by what a
  kind opted into), `when` the shape isn't locked, and takes no arguments (`/lock now` stays
  text). Return takes the line out of the text first, then locks, which ends the editing a
  read-only shape can't be in: the text keeps its other lines, the lock is a step named "Lock", and
  the typing before it, with the line's removal in it, is the step before
  ([Undoing a command](#undoing-a-command)). There is no `/unlock`: a locked shape's text can't be
  edited, so nothing could be typed there. A plugin list with Locking needs `SlashCommandsPlugin()`
  (`ownerNotInstalled` otherwise), which the shipped list has; the text it's typed in is Mentions'.
- **A locked frame locks what it holds**, at any depth: the core makes a shape in a read-only
  [container](#containers) read-only too, so it refuses every change as a locked shape does, and
  each try shakes the shape tried (a drag of a note in the frame, Delete on it); nothing joins or
  leaves the frame. (A frame that isn't locked carries a shape locked on its own as it moves: a
  lock stops changes to a shape, not its frame carrying it.) Only the frame shows the lock: the
  chip and the lock on a row are a shape's own lock (`isLocked`), so what it holds shows neither,
  and a shape locked on its own inside shows its own. Unlocking the frame frees what it holds, at
  once.
- **A locked subboard locks its board**, and every board under it, at any depth: it's entered like
  any board (entering isn't a change to it), but the core makes the board read-only
  (`editor.isBoardReadOnly`, [below](#the-cores-part-read-only-shapes)), so every shape on it
  refuses every change as one in a locked frame does, its own lock included, each try shaking the
  shape tried, and nothing goes on it. The toolbar dims the tools that place shapes there and their
  keys pass ([the keyboard](#keyboard-shortcuts)), Paste is off ([the
  clipboard](#the-clipboard)), no port dots show ([Ports](#ports)), `canvas draw` refuses a shape or
  an edge for it (`read_only`, [draw](#draw)), and neither Lock nor Unlock is offered for what's on
  it. A shape locked on its own there keeps its chip, and a click on it is refused: it shakes, and
  stays locked. A subboard on that board opens, and its board is read-only too, though that
  subboard isn't locked: the lock above reaches it. [The path](#the-path) marks where the
  read-only part starts, one lock after that crumb's name. Unlocking the subboard frees its board
  and every board under it, at once.
- **The chip is a button** (`LockChip`, a [clickable adornment](#pointing), so a canvas button): in
  the select tool, a click on a locked shape's chip unlocks it. Then the chip shows the lock open
  for 1.5 s, however the shape was unlocked (the menu too), so a click by mistake can be taken back:
  a click on the open lock locks the shape again. It stays while the pointer's on it (looking again
  every 0.5 s), then fades over 0.3 s and is gone, since an unlocked shape has no chip. The pointing
  hand shows over a chip, which draws lighter hovered and darker pressed, and a click on one selects
  nothing. A right-click on it is on its shape, as on any adornment: the menu offers Unlock.
- **Everything refuses a locked shape**, since everything changes shapes through a transaction.
  A drag leaves it where it is and moves the rest of the selection (a click, even one that jitters
  under the drag threshold, doesn't count as a try); Delete and Cut leave it and take
  the rest; Return and a double-click don't edit it (a kind that opens some other way, into its
  board, still opens); it shows no handles; Arrange doesn't restack it;
  a menu item that edits it changes nothing. Each of those shakes it.
- **What isn't a change still works.** It's selected, hovered, outlined, copied, listed and bound
  to (an arrow may start or end on it) as any other shape. An arrow bound to a shape that moves
  follows it, locked or not, since its props don't change; and a locked arrow still lets go of a
  shape that's deleted (`ShapeReferencing`), which keeps it where it's drawn. The detail panel shows
  a locked shape's details, disabled.
- **Undo.** Each lock and unlock is a step of its own, "Lock" or "Unlock" (from the menu, the
  chip or `/lock`). Undo is below the read-only rule, so undoing Lock unlocks the shape without a shake (its
  chip shows open, as for any unlock), redoing it locks it again, and undoing a chip's Unlock locks
  it. A try a lock refuses (a drag, Delete) changes nothing, so it records nothing: the next ⌘Z
  undoes the step before it.
- **The shake** is Selection's, not Locking's: `RefusalShake`, a service of `SelectionPlugin`
  ([Refusing a change: the shake](#refusing-a-change-the-shake)), plays on every refusal the core
  reports, whichever plugin's rule made the shape read-only, so a locked shape shakes through it
  with Locking doing nothing: side to side, 5 points at most, 3 times over 360 ms, dying away. Every
  refused shape shakes, locked or not: a shape whose board holds a locked shape isn't deleted
  either, so it's the one that shakes. A container shakes with what it holds, at any depth, as it
  moves with it (a locked frame tried shakes with its notes, not under them).
- **Another board shown** costs Locking nothing: `LockState` keeps no copy of which shapes are
  locked (a commit's unlocked shapes are those locked before it, `ChangeSet.before`, and not now),
  and what was under way on the board left, its shakes (`RefusalShake`) and the locks showing open
  (`ChipFade`), stops there. A locked shape that owns a board is entered like any other:
  entering isn't a change to it, and what's on its board is read-only (above).
- **The chip** is an 18-point disc with a lock, the dark of a title's pill, at the right end of the
  row just above the shape, ending at its right edge. Its order is 300, a state that comes and
  goes, so it's farthest out of what's at that end, and a title's pill at the other end stops 4
  points short of it. Adornments lays it out with the rest, keeps its size on screen down to 25%,
  shows none below 35% on a shape drawn as a [skeleton](#skeletons), as a locked shape always
  is, since it can't be edited (so it can't be clicked there either: [the label](#the-label)), and draws it
  where its shape is drawn, so it shakes with it. A click within 3 points of its edge
  still clicks it. The open lock, fading, is a label from Adornments' [`ChipFade`](#a-chip-that-fades-chipfade)
  (`LockState.openLockOpacity(of:)` reads it: nil but for a shape just unlocked): `LockState` shows
  it when a commit unlocks a shape and takes it away when one locks the shape again, telling
  Adornments once for all it changes, and `ChipFade` tells Adornments each frame of the fade and
  its going (`editor.adornmentsDidChange(for:)`), so the chip's label is made again only then, or
  when a commit changes the shape.

### The core's part: read-only shapes

`registrar.readOnlyShapes { record in ... }` says which shapes can't change; a shape is read-only
when any plugin's rule says so, or one says so of a container it's in, or of the shape that owns its
board (or of one above that), and the core asks it every way a shape is read: `editor.isReadOnly(id)`
on the board shown, `editor.isReadOnly(inFile: id)` on any board (`editor.isReadOnly(record, in: holding)`, its
shape part alone, for a caller that asks of many shapes of one board), `transaction.isReadOnly(record)`
inside a transaction, and `reading.isReadOnly(record)` of a board read in place
(`editor.reading(of:)`); `registry.isReadOnly(record)` is the rules alone, reading nothing but the
record. The core holds them where every change goes through it:

- **Transactions.** A read-only shape that was in the document before the transaction isn't
  changed (`update`), restacked (`bringToFront`, `sendToBack`, `bringForward`, `sendBackward`,
  `move(_:above:)`, ...), moved (`translate`) or deleted by it; nor is a shape
  whose board, or a board under it, holds a read-only shape (as the Finder won't trash a folder
  holding a locked file), since deleting it would take that shape too.
  The change is dropped, the rest of the transaction stands, and once it's done
  services hear every shape it refused: `EditorService.didRefuseChanges(to:in:)`. A change that
  leaves the shape no longer read-only goes through, whatever else it changes (unlocking, tldraw's
  rule too), and so does one that makes it read-only. A shape the transaction put in isn't held
  (a paste moves its locked copies into place). Nor is what a deletion does to keep the board
  whole: its `willDelete` handlers' changes (a read-only dependent goes with the shape it depends
  on, as a locked shape in tldraw goes with its deleted parent), and shapes letting go of what's
  deleted (`ShapeReferencing`).
- **Drags.** A `TranslatingSession` leaves read-only shapes out of what it moves (so a
  `CustomTranslation` knows what moves with it), and tells services once the pointer passes the drag
  threshold, once.
- **Editing.** `beginEditing` refuses a read-only shape, and services hear it; a shape that becomes
  read-only while it's edited stops being edited.
- **Containers.** A shape in a read-only container, at any depth, is read-only too
  ([Containers](#containers)): `editor.isReadOnly(_:)` says so; a transaction changes it not at
  all, its own lock included, and nothing joins or leaves the container; editing it ends. A
  container that moves carries what it holds, locked or not.
- **Boards.** A board whose owner is read-only (a locked subboard, one in a locked frame) is
  read-only, and so is every board under it, at any depth: `editor.isReadOnly(board:)`, and
  `editor.isBoardReadOnly` for the board shown, with `editor.readOnlyStart`, where its path turns
  read-only (one climb tells every board on the path), kept from the editor's start (one opened on
  such a board is read-only at once) as each switch and commit leaves the file (a lock above it may
  come in a commit on another board, `transact(on:)`, or a file put in place) and observed apart
  from `document`, each set only when it changes, so a view that dims what can't be done there
  redraws then and never on every commit. It's entered like any board, and its shapes are
  selected, copied and opened, but each is read-only, as in a read-only container, its own lock
  included; and nothing goes on it: a transaction there (`transaction.isBoardReadOnly`) drops an
  insert, a move onto it (`move(_:to:)`) is refused, and services hear the board's owner refused,
  as a read-only container is when a shape would join it; `place` puts nothing down and says the
  same (`place(_:around:)`, all or nothing, says the shapes it would hold were refused, and they
  shake there); a tool that places shapes isn't enabled there (`editor.isToolEnabled(_:)`: `setTool` doesn't
  take it, and one in use goes back to the default tool as the board becomes read-only); and a
  shape edited there as it becomes read-only stops being edited.
- **Changing everything or nothing.** `transaction.refusedShapes` is the read-only shapes the
  transaction was asked to change, restack, move or delete so far and didn't (and the read-only
  containers that wouldn't take a shape, a settle's included, and the owners of read-only boards that
  wouldn't). A change that makes no sense in part (a shape turned into another kind that must take
  what it held with it, a group, a move, a paste) goes through `editor.transactWhole(name) { … }`:
  one transaction that commits only when its body returns with nothing refused, and otherwise commits
  nothing, opens no step (what there was to redo stays) and shakes the refused shapes
  (`editor.refuseChanges(to:)`), answering the body's value or nil. A body gives up for a reason of
  its own by throwing `Transaction.Refused(shapes)` (they shake too); one that throws anything else
  gives up with nothing shaking, as a body that throws out of `transact` is heard refusing nothing.
  `shaking:` says exactly what shakes instead, whatever stopped it (the note whose row asked, or
  none). Grouping, Colors'
  file-wide rewrites, Moving, Transform, Clipboard's paste, Types' relationship writes, Connect and
  the core's own placements go through it; no plugin keeps a refusal error of its own.

Selection shows no handles on a read-only shape, and the detail panel disables its controls; both
ask the core (`editor.isReadOnly`, the panel of the shape it shows on every commit), not Locking.
`registry.isReadOnly(_:in:)`, a shape's rules and containers on its board alone, is the core's own:
it doesn't see a read-only board, so nothing outside the core asks it. A rule reads only the record
it's given, since a transaction asks it of a shape before and after a change, of each container a
shape is in, and of each owner up a board's path. It's asked about every shape a transaction
changes, so keep it cheap: Locking's reads one added value.

### The core's part: drawing offsets

`editor.setDrawingOffset(offset, for: id)` draws a shape `offset` view points from where it is, until
it's set back to zero: an animation that moves how a shape looks without changing it. The core
draws the shape and its outlines there; an overlay that decorates a shape moves its decoration by
`context.worldDrawingOffset(of:)` (the same offset, in world units), as Adornments does for every
[adornment](#adornments) (a title's pill, the lock chip) and Validation for its
outline. One that culls by the view can grow the rect by `context.worldDrawingReach`, the farthest
any shape is drawn from where it is (world units, zero unless one is), so a shape drawn into view
from just outside it is decorated there, as Adornments does. Everything else goes by where the
shape is: hit testing, handles, arrows bound to it, and pictures of the board (the minimap).
Deleting a shape drops its offset. The core's glide (`editor.glide(_:)`, a shape nudged into or out
of a [container](#containers) easing there) is drawing offsets too.

## Grouping

Shapes grouped together are selected as one from then on, as in tldraw and Keynote, until they're
ungrouped. A group is something its shapes have, as a lock is, not a shape: nothing new is on the
board or in the table of contents, and a drag, Delete, Copy, Lock or a color acts on the whole
group because a click selected all of it. Group (⌥⌘G) and Ungroup (⌥⇧⌘G) are in the context menu
beside Lock and in Arrange in the menu bar. It's a horizontal
([`Sources/Grouping`](../Sources/Grouping)) on Selection, ContextMenus, Keyboard and Queries,
that every kind is in; what a click, the marquee, the hover and Escape do with groups is
[Selection's](#groups-selected-as-one) ([Grouping.swift](../Sources/Grouping/Grouping.swift)):

```swift
registrar.declare(GroupsProperty.self)                  // the groups a shape is in, outermost first, by id
registrar.optInEveryShape(to: GroupsProperty.self)
registrar.service { GroupIndex(editor: $0) }            // the board shown's groups, kept as commits write paths
registrar.selectionGroups { $0.service(GroupIndex.self) }
registrar.command(.group, title: "Group", menu: "Arrange", order: 0, shortcut: KeyChord("g", [.command, .option]), runs: .whenIdle,
                  isEnabled: { $0.editor.canGroup($0.shapes) }) { $0.editor.group($0.shapes) }
registrar.command(.ungroup, title: "Ungroup", menu: "Arrange", order: 10, shortcut: KeyChord("g", [.command, .option, .shift]),
                  runs: .whenIdle, isEnabled: { $0.editor.canUngroup($0.shapes) }) { $0.editor.ungroup($0.shapes) }
registrar.contextMenuForCanvas {                        // shown by the commands' rules, over the menu's shapes
    MenuItem(command: .group, in: StateMenuGroup.self)
    MenuItem(command: .ungroup, in: StateMenuGroup.self)
}
```

- **A shape's groups are an [added property](#added-properties)**, `groups`: the ids of the groups
  it's in, outermost first, a UUID's string each, nothing on a shape in none. It's `unlisted()`
  (`x-canvas-unlisted`): neither `canvas draw` nor `canvas query` lists, reads or writes it, since a
  group has no name an agent could know it by; they get words of their own (below).
- **What counts is the board's** (`BoardGroups`, pure, made from the shapes' paths alone, so the
  board shown, a transaction, a query and a copy read groups alike): a group is its shapes on one
  board, and counts while it holds two parts or more there, a part being a shape or a group in it
  that counts. A group a delete, a move to another board or a regrouping leaves with one part is no
  group, and a shape may still hold its id, harmlessly, until something writes its path again.
- **Group** puts the shapes in a new group inside the groups they're all in (as the selection is
  inside them), a group they hold whole staying a group in the new one, a group they hold part of
  left; it needs two parts or more. **Ungroup** takes apart the outermost groups they hold whole,
  a level, as tldraw's does. Each is one step, "Group" or "Ungroup", all or nothing: a locked shape
  among them leaves them as they were, and shakes. Nothing is restacked.
- **Copies** that shared a group are a group of their own ([the clipboard](#the-clipboard): a
  paste, ⌘D, a drag with ⌥), and a group only one copy was in is none of theirs; a cut and its paste
  move the shapes, which keep their groups.
- **Agents** group shapes with `canvas draw`'s `group "A" and "B"` and take one out with `ungroup
  "A"` ([the command line](#the-command-line)), and find a shape's group with `canvas query`'s
  `:grouped-with("A")` (`GroupQueriesPlugin`, a plugin value of its own, so a list without Queries
  leaves it out), a relation read from the file's paths off the main actor, the outermost group.

## Ports

Ports are data-canvas's: dots just outside the sides of the shape the pointer is over, from which
a drag draws an arrow to another shape. Not to any shape: each port is on a channel, a kind of
connection, and the arrow may end only on a shape that takes its channel, so a note links to a note,
while a subboard takes every
channel, so anything with ports links to one, and one to anything with ports. They belong to
Connections ([`Sources/Connections`](../Sources/Connections)), a horizontal any kind opts into,
built on Selection, whose [canvas buttons](#canvas-buttons) the dots are, and on Draw, whose edges its
connections are (what tells two of one pair apart, an arrow's `is`, Types says to Draw itself). It holds ports,
channels and the connector's interface, in three plugin values, `PortsPlugin`, `PortEdgesPlugin` and
`ConnectMenuPlugin` (Connect in a right-click, after `ContextMenusPlugin`), and names no arrow. The connector is [Arrows](#the-connector-arrows) ([`Sources/Arrows`](../Sources/Arrows)),
a product of its own on Connections (and on TableOfContents and TextEditing, for the arrow's row and
its label's spelling, and on [Mentions](#mentions), which draws, edits and finds an arrow's label,
mention text), in plugin values of its own, `ArrowsPlugin` and `ArrowPortsPlugin`, so a list can
have arrows without ports, or ports with a connector of its own. The core has never heard of a port, the ports code has never heard of an
arrow, nor the arrow code of a channel: `ArrowPortsPlugin` ([below](#the-connector-arrows)) makes
arrows what a drag from a port draws. The same rules hold for a connection made by name, with no
drag ([Connecting without a drag](#connecting-without-a-drag)), as `canvas draw`'s edges are.
Connections builds on [Topology](#topology) too: a connection bound at both ends is an edge of the
file's graph, of its channel's type. `PortsPlugin` itself
([Ports.swift](../Sources/Connections/Ports.swift)):

```swift
registrar.declare(ChannelProperty.self)                 // `channel` on a connection drawn from a port
registrar.service { PortState(editor: $0) }             // every kind's ports, and whose dots show
registrar.overlay(PortOverlay())                        // the dots; while a connection is drawn, what it could end on
registrar.canvasButtons(at: { editor, point in editor.service(PortState.self)?.dot(atViewPoint: point) },
                        drag: { dot, origin, editor in editor.service(PortState.self)?.connect(from: dot, at: origin) })
```

and what a sticky note adds, its channel and its ports
([NoteLinks.swift](../Sources/StickyNotes/NoteLinks.swift), [StickyNotes.swift](../Sources/StickyNotes/StickyNotes.swift)):

```swift
public enum NoteLink {}

extension NoteLink: Channel {
    public static let id: ChannelID = "note-link"
    /// A brown amber, darker than the note, so a dot reads beside one.
    public static var color: NSColor { NSColor(srgbRed: 0.70, green: 0.45, blue: 0.05, alpha: 1) }
    public static let summary: String? = "an arrow drawn on the note-link channel"
}

extension ShapeRegistrar where Definition == StickyNoteDefinition {
    /// Ports on all four sides, the top too. A titled note's pill is in the row above its top edge, so
    /// a long title runs under the top dot, which draws above it and is pressed before it, as it is
    /// before a lock chip.
    mutating func noteLinks() {
        ports(NoteLink.self)
    }
}

// In StickyNotesPlugin.register:
registrar.shape(StickyNoteDefinition()) { note in
    ...
    note.noteLinks()                                   // and ports: arrows from a note to a note
}
registrar.channel(NoteLink.self)                       // which this plugin declares
```

[Subboards](#subboards)
have a channel of their own, `SubboardLink` (`subboard-link`, the card's indigo), and ports on it
and then on every other, so a note links to a subboard on its own channel, a
subboard to a note on its, and two subboards on `subboard-link`
([SubboardLinks.swift](../Sources/Subboards/SubboardLinks.swift)):

```swift
extension ShapeRegistrar where Definition == SubboardDefinition {
    /// Ports on all four sides, the top too, as a note's: a long title's pill runs under the
    /// top dot. Its own channel is first, so its dots are indigo (a dot is its first channel's
    /// color) and a drag to another subboard is on it (a drag is drawn on the first of the dot's
    /// channels the shape it ends on takes); every channel there is comes after, so what has ports
    /// on any of them links to a subboard, and a subboard to it.
    mutating func subboardLinks() {
        ports(SubboardLink.self)
        portsOnEveryChannel()
    }
}
```

What links to what is then all the ports say: a note to a note or a subboard, and a subboard to anything with ports. The channels say nothing more yet: a
channel is where a connection's meaning would go (one schema referring to another, say), and it's
already what a connection is in Topology's graph: its edge type.

### Channels

- **A channel is a type** (`Channel`), as a tab or an added property is: its `id` (`ChannelID`),
  the color of its dots (`static var color`, computed, since colors aren't `Sendable`; gray by
  default), and what a connection drawn on it is, in a line (`static var summary`, nil by default:
  its edge type's [summary](#types)). The plugin that owns what a connection on it means declares it,
  `registrar.channel(C.self)` (the `Channels` point: a channel declared twice is a `conflict`), and
  kinds have ports on it by its type, so a plugin that gives a kind ports on another's channel
  imports that plugin's module. StickyNotes declares `NoteLink` for its notes and Subboards
  `SubboardLink` for its subboards; a channel that joins kinds of several plugins would be declared by the
  horizontal whose meaning it is (data-canvas's `registerHostChannel` calls come from such a
  feature), and given to their kinds by a plugin that imports both.
- **A channel is an edge type too.** `registrar.channel(C.self)` also declares Topology's edge type
  of the same name (`note-link`), under the family of edges the connector draws (`arrow`,
  [below](#the-connector-arrows)), a root without a connector: so a query for every arrow
  (`.within("arrow")`) finds those on every channel, and one for a channel finds its own. A
  channel's id that's another edge type's is a `conflict`, as two channels of one id are.
- **The id never changes once shipped**, since connections keep it. The id audit holds a
  `ChannelID` literal to the module that declares it, as it does a kind
  ([The module graph](#the-module-graph)).
- **What a connection knows is its channel**: `ChannelProperty` (key `channel`), an [added
  property](#added-properties) `PortsPlugin` declares and the connector's kind opts into. It has no
  default, so only a connection drawn on a channel has one, from a port or by name
  (`"added" : { "channel" : "note-link" }`), and an arrow drawn by `canvas draw` with `channel:
  none` has none. In the arrow's schema it's a string of at least
  one character, since the channels are whatever plugins declare; its fixture is
  `Fixtures/added/channel.v0.json`.

### A kind's ports

`x.ports(C.self, sides:role:)` gives a kind ports on a channel (`registrar.ports(K.self, on:
C.self, sides:role:)` for another plugin's kind). It's the `ShapePorts` point, one
contribution per kind and channel, and a kind may have ports on several:

- **`sides`** (`PortSide`: `.top`, `.right`, `.bottom`, `.left`; all four by default) are where
  its dots are, one just outside the middle of each. A side with ports on several channels has one
  dot, in its first channel's color, and a connection from it is drawn on the first of its channels
  the shape it ends on takes (a subboard's: indigo, and `subboard-link` to another subboard, but
  `note-link` to a note).
- **`role`** (`PortRole`, a data-canvas port's end) is what the ports let the kind be: `.both`
  (the default), `.source` (its dots start connections, and none ends on it) or `.target`
  (connections end on it, and it has no dots).

The registry refuses ports on a channel no installed plugin declares, and ports on the connector's
own kind, since a connection neither starts nor ends on another (`ShapePorts.check`):

```
ShapePorts: ratings gives box ports on channel wire, which no installed plugin declares
ShapePorts: ratings gives arrow ports, but it's what connections are
```

Its report shows `ports note-link → sticky-note` on the line of the plugin that gives the kind its
ports, and `channel note-link` on the declarer's.

**One port table.** Everything that asks about ports reads one table of each kind's ports
([PortTable.swift](../Sources/Connections/PortTable.swift): `KindPorts`, built on demand from the frozen
registry, and kept whole by each editor's `PortState`): the dots and a drag from one,
`editor.channel(of:endingAt:)`, `accepts`, and the lookups below. So a kind's channels are in one
order everywhere, plugin order: the order of the `ShapePorts` contributions in the plugin list,
whether one is for the kind or for every kind, and a kind's first contribution on a channel is its
only one there, its role and its sides. A drag and a connection asked for by name
([without a drag](#connecting-without-a-drag)) can't pick different channels. The lookups, on
`Registry`:

| Lookup | Is |
|---|---|
| `connectorKind`, `makesConnections` | The kind connections are (nil without a connector), and whether the connector makes them without a drag (it has `make` and `ends`). |
| `hasPorts(kind)`, `portChannels(of: kind)` | Whether a kind has ports on any channel, and on which, in the table's order. |
| `dotChannels(of: kind, side:)` | The channels a drag from its dot on that side starts connections on, as `Connection.channels` has them; with no side, all its dots' channels, each once. A `.target` port has no dot. |
| `takes(kind, channel, as: role, side:)`, `portSides(of: kind, on: channel, as: role)`, `portSides(of: kind)` | Whether its ports on a channel let it be a `.source` or a `.target` (on a side, if named), and on which sides; and, with no channel, on which sides it takes connections at all, each once. |
| `connectionChannel(from: kind, fromSide:, to: target, toSide:)` | The channel a connection from a shape of `kind` to one of `target` is on when none is named, as a drag picks one (`editor.channel(of:endingAt:)`): the first of `kind`'s dot channels (on `fromSide`, if named) that `target` takes as a target (on `toSide`, if named); nil if they share none. An edge `canvas draw` draws with no channel written is on it ([`PortEdgesPlugin`](#edges-and-their-channels-portedgesplugin)). |
| `accepts(shape, on: channel, as: role)`, `declares(channel)` | `takes` for a shape (none for one kept aside), and whether some installed plugin declares the channel: what rules about connections already drawn go by. |
| `canConnect(id, in: shapes)` | The connector's `canConnect`, for a shape in any `ShapeContext`: the editor's, or a transaction's, which has the shapes it inserted. |
| `connection(_:existing:in:)`, `connectionEnds(of:)` | A connection made, or changed, without a drag, and the shapes one joins ([below](#connecting-without-a-drag)). |

Each of those that asks about a kind takes `standingFor:` too (`hasPorts(kind, standingFor:)`,
`dotChannels(of:standingFor:side:)`, `takes(kind, standingFor:, channel, as:, side:)`,
`portSides(of:standingFor:on:as:)`, `connectionChannel(from:fromSide:fromStandingFor:to:toSide:toStandingFor:)`):
the kinds of the shapes a stand-in of that kind stands for, none by default, which answers for the
stand-in as [Ports at a stand-in](#ports-at-a-stand-in) has it, for a connection made by name.

`editor.channel(of: connection, endingAt: record)` is the channel a drag's connection would be
drawn on if it ended at a shape: the first of its channels the shape takes as a target (for a
shape that stands for others, [what it stands for](#ports-at-a-stand-in)), and nil for the shape it
starts from, a shape kept aside, or one that takes none.

### Ports at a stand-in

A [stand-in](#stand-ins-forwarding) (a [reference](#references): a pill that stands for another
shape, so an arrow into it counts as an arrow into the shape) can't have ports on one channel, for
what it takes is what it stands for. So a kind has them on **every channel**:
`x.portsOnEveryChannel(sides: [.left, .right], role: .both)` (`registrar.portsOnEveryChannel(K.self,
…)` for another plugin's kind) contributes a `ShapePorts` entry the port table expands, when it is
built, to each channel the registry declares, in plugin order, where the entry stands in the list (a
channel the kind was given ports on earlier keeps those). The kind names none, so it needs none of
the plugins that own the channels; and because `registry.accepts` is then true of it on every
channel, an arrow [translated](#the-connector-arrows) onto one keeps its binding, and a script's
edge picks a channel by its kind alone, as `connectionChannel` has it. A kind that isn't a stand-in
uses it too, after a channel of its own, to take every channel there is: a subboard's ports are
`ports(SubboardLink.self)` and then `portsOnEveryChannel()`, so its own channel is first in its
table, its dots are that channel's color, and anything with ports links to it.

What a person sees and drags is **per shape**, though, a deliberate departure from ports being per
kind: `PortState.ports(of: record)` replaces the kind's table in every question about one shape (its
dots, a drag from one, `editor.channel(of:endingAt:)`, the faint outlines while a connection is
drawn). For a shape whose kind stands in (Topology's `standInKinds`) it answers from
`topology.forwards(of:)`:

- **One kind stood for:** that kind's channels and roles, in its order, on the stand-in's own
  sides. The order is the shape's, not the stand-in's (which, for ports on every channel, is the
  order the channels are declared in), so a pill for a subboard draws what a subboard draws: its
  indigo dots, and a `subboard-link` to a subboard, where the pill's own order would give it
  `note-link`'s color and channel first.
- **Several kinds** (a reference for every match of a query): the channels all of them take, in the
  order of the first shape stood for, each with the roles all of them allow (a kind whose
  connections only start and one whose connections only end share none).
- **Nothing** (empty, pending, missing, private, unavailable): none. No dots show, and no drag ends
  on it. An arrow on no channel (`channel: none`'s) still binds there, as it binds anywhere.

It is kept for each stand-in until `topology.revision(of:)` changes (re-pointed, what it stands for
made private or deleted, an answer provided), so a pointer move costs a dictionary hit, and until the
stand-in goes (deleted on the board shown, taken with a board, or the file put in place), so a session
that deletes stand-ins keeps none of their ports. A move costs the upkeep nothing.

An arrow whose end is [re-aimed](#the-connector-arrows) is judged the same way. The binding rule
`ArrowPortsPlugin` contributes is static (per kind), so on its own it would let any channel bind to
a stand-in; Arrows' `ArrowTargeting` also asks Connections (`editor.portsAllow(_:as:at:)`, over
`PortState`) whether the arrow's channel is taken now, in that end's role (the start as a source, the
end as a target), and an end looks through a
stand-in that doesn't take it, as it does through any shape that doesn't. Only the translation of
an arrow keeps the static rule: it keeps a binding that already exists.

**By name.** A connection made by name (`canvas draw`'s edge, [without a drag](#connecting-without-a-drag))
asks the same questions without a `PortState`, from kinds alone, since the stand-in it joins may not
be in any editor yet (a reference it is about to put beside a shape, standing for one on a board that
isn't shown): the `standingFor:` lookups give a stand-in of a kind, standing for shapes of the kinds
given, the ports `PortState.ports(of:)` gives the shape (its kind's, as far as every kind stood for
takes them, on its own sides; none if they have none). So an edge to a reference for a note is on
`note-link`, as a drag from a note's port to the reference would be, and the sides it may name for the
reference are the reference's own, left and right.

An arrow keeps its bindings and its channel when what it is bound to changes (tldraw's never let
go), so re-pointing a stand-in can leave an arrow attached whose channel the new targets don't
take. The resolved edge follows the new targets in the same commit, and `canvas query` still
reports it, typed as the channel. The reference says so, and no more: a warning triangle trails its
pill, and its panel says `“Order” doesn’t take note links.` (`ChannelID.pluralName` is "note
links" for `note-link`). It isn't a [validation](#validation) rule: Connections has no Validation,
and a rule may not read what a dynamic reference is given. References works it out from the pill's
literal edges and `registry.accepts`, once per revision of the reference's edges
(`ReferenceState.channelMismatch(of:)`).

### The dots and the select tool

The dots are canvas buttons, dragged rather than clicked (`PortDot`: a shape and a side, what
`editor.hoveredButton` and `editor.pressedButton` are while the pointer's on one). They show for
one shape at a time, the host, as data-canvas's show on the hovered shape:
