### Completing the JSON

⌃Space (or ⌥⎋, or F5) in a type's JSON lists what can be typed at the caret, a keyword with its
description after it, a type's names, a `required` list's properties, and a pick writes it as it
goes in, opening the list again where it leaves the caret among more. The list and its keys are the
code editor's ([`completions:`](#anatomy-and-conventions)); a pick is typing (one step of the "Change
JSON" run, which the sync hears as a person's edit, and not before the list closes otherwise:
`TypeSync.completing`); while the model writes the schema nothing opens. `JSONCaret.at(_:in:)` reads
the half-typed text leniently and says where the caret is; `JSONCompleter`, generic over any JSON
Schema, walks the schema along that path and offers the keys the object's schemas list or the values
the place's schemas give, each written as it goes in. What it knows of JSON Schema is data:
`MetaSchema`, the 2020-12 meta-schema flattened, with `x-canvas-when`, the app's one annotation.
`TypeCompletions` adds in code only what no schema can say: a `required` list's names; a `$ref`'s
targets, `#` and the root's definitions, then the file's other titled types by name, each written as
its URI (`types`, asked only at a `$ref`'s value: `TypeIndex.referenceTargets(from:)`); that
`$vocabulary` goes only in the root and `$schema` only in the root or a subschema with an `$id`; no
`title` at the root; the root's `$title` directive (in the root's `properties` a `$title` key written with
its `x-canvas-from` member, in it that key alone, and as its value the root's fields that can title, each with
its type); the root's `$color` (a `$color` key written with its `const`, in it that key alone, and as its
value the colors, each with its value: `colors`, the book's names from the Schema tab, the built-in ones
otherwise); and what a caller adds where a value goes (`extra`). The engine's own seam for a key a schema
doesn't list is `JSONCompleter(schema:offers:keys:)`: `keys` answers a `JSONCompletionKeyOffer` (the key, its
detail, the JSON its value starts as and where the caret lands in it, whether the list opens again there) for
a caret, appended after the schema's keys, those the object holds left out.

### Rows on a type's note

A type's note has, under its words, one row for each field its type gives it (a note that is one has its fields
in the same place, with its values). Types lays the rows out and draws them; a kind says only where they go,
as it says where its words are, and Types knows no kind:

```swift
note.typeRows(drawnIn: { shape, context in NoteLayout(shape, in: context).block })   // where the rows are drawn
// and in its render, under the highlights and before the editing guard:
if let block = layout.block { context.drawTypeRows(of: shape, in: block) }
```

- **The room** is `TypeRows.extent` (`LayoutInputKey<RowsExtent>`: the least width and the height), a layout
  input Types provides (`RowBook.provide`) only for the kinds that say where their rows go
  (`TypeRowsPlaces`, one contribution a kind, refused for a kind that holds neither `schema` nor `is`). The
  note is a `LaidOutBox` that reads it: at least 320 wide and as tall as its words and the rows, never
  shorter than a new note, with no record written: the stored box is the note as it is with no rows.
  Nothing is stored of the rows, and no change of them is an undo step. A relationship type has no rows: it is a
  pill. Types provides `TypeRows.pill` (`LayoutInputKey<TypePill>`: its name or none, its field count, and the size
  its text measures) for every shape that holds `schema` and the mark, of a kind that says where its rows go, whatever
  it holds. The note lays the type out at that size, about the middle of the box it stores (a `LaidOutBox` that answers
  an anchor, `laidOutAnchor`, besides its size, so a longer name grows both ways and what is drawn through it stays put),
  paints a capsule in the type's color with its name and `· 2`, and edits its name in place (the title, never the words).
  Nothing is written when it grows or shrinks.
- **The rows** are `RowList`'s: nine fields or fewer all show; ten or more fold the rows a type builds on
  into `from Person` (two or more of them) and show at most eight of the rest and `+N more`, so a note has at
  most ten rows. `RowBook` (`editor.rowBook`) keeps one template for each distinct list of types, dropped
  whole when a type changes, so ten thousand notes of one type share one.
- **A type's note** (what its rows' spot says, `RowBook.spot(of:)`): its rows; else three bars while the
  model writes the schema; else the reason the last read failed (`Retry`, `Settings…`, or nothing to try
  again); else nothing under its words while the first words are typed and nothing has answered; else
  `No fields`. A type with rows keeps them while it is read again. Making a note a type starts the read on the
  scheduler's next turn, with no 3 second wait.
- **A row** is the field's name at the left, the kind at the right (`Text`, `2 fields`, `List of Text`, `Either`)
  or the type's chip (Adornments draws it as the chip above a note: `AdornmentLabel.draw(at:in:)`), a needed
  field's amber dot, and `›` where a read-only card would have something to show. An inherited row is faint and
  ticked in its type's color in the paper's left padding.
- **Relation rows.** A relationship type's ends give the notes of the types at them a row: every note of a type at a
  drawn end, on every board, and both type notes, the moment the end is drawn, whatever any arrow is. The row comes
  after the fields (`RowTemplateItem.relation`, from `relationships.rows(for:isType:)`), under a dashed line that
  takes `TypesStyle.relationRuleHeight` (8) points and shows only between fields and relation rows; relation rows
  never fold. A note's height is so a function of its types and the drawn ends, never of its arrows: a relationship
  drawn or deleted lays out nothing, an end drawn or deleted lays out the end type's instances near and far and the
  type notes (`RelationshipChange.layout`). A row is named as `RelationshipRow.name(in:)` says (the later of two
  relationship types' rows of one name adds ` · Employment`). On a type's note it says the way it runs (`→`, `←`,
  `↔`) and the types at the other end as chips (`any` for an open side), and is no edit. On a note that is one it
  holds a pill for each relationship (`ShownPill`: the note, the pill the arrow ends on, the arrow, what the end
  reads as, sorted by the name each shows, `+N` for those that do not fit) or reads `add layer`; a pill is solid
  for a note and dashed in every other state of the far end. A click on a pill goes to its note, on a dashed one to
  the pill the arrow ends on, on a type's row to the relationship type.
- **Setting a relationship from a row.** Typing, Space or a click on the value of a relation row lists the notes that fit
  (`RelationPicker`: the instances of the row's other types on every board, a note with no title or words named by its
  values, `· will be made public` on a line whose pick does that); Return picks and draws the arrow (`editor.relate`, "Add
  Relationship": the arrow runs by the row's side, nothing is written to either note); for a note on another board the pick
  puts a pill on the board shown where `canvas draw` puts it and makes the note public in the same step, and one Undo returns
  both boards byte for byte. ← → move a focus between pills, Backspace twice removes a relationship (`editor.unrelate`: the
  arrow, its values and the pill it empties, on whichever board, "Remove Relationship"). `FieldValues.name(of:)` is the
  record-only name by values a kind gives its `untitled:`.
- **The release of a port's drag.** Arrows tells Types the arrow it drew is finished
  (`ArrowConnecting.finished`, in the press): `editor.connectionDrawn(arrow)` gives an arrow between two notes
  the one relationship type that fits it, in the press's step (`Add Arrow`); opens a list of the types that
  fit at the arrow (`Add Type`, a step of its own) when several do, and selects the arrow while it is open;
  leaves it plain when none is taken (an open type, one with no end drawn, is offered by `/is-a` and never
  taken alone); counts a drag between a type and a relationship type as an end and nothing more. The arrow a
  drag is still changing is not counted until the release (`Session.touching`, `editor.connectionReleased`): a
  pass over a relationship type makes no end and lays out no instance.
- **A relationship type from a drag.** Released between two types, the arrow is replaced, in one step ("New
  Relationship Type"), by a relationship type placed between them (`Surroundings.between`, drawn as a pill) and an
  arrow to it from each type (`registry.drawConnection`, as `canvas draw` makes an edge); the type is selected
  and not edited, and a card with one field is shown at its pill by the writer itself, inside the step, with
  `CanvasCard.adoptsPress`: the name typed is part of the step, so one Undo, once the card is dismissed, takes
  back the type, both arrows and the name. Types' IsA names nothing above it, so the card is a hook
  (`RelationshipHooks`) that `TypesPlugin` fills with Form's.
  The same writer relates a type to itself (`from == to`): two arrows, never a two-headed one, the second
  asked of the connection maker beside the first (`beside:` names it, so the two are stored bent apart), the new type landing beside the type with
  the room both arrows need.
- **Deleting a relationship type** deletes its end arrows in the same step, but a locked one (Types' `willDelete`
  handler; `RelationshipIndex.endArrows(of:reading:)` lists them: the index's, on whichever boards they are,
  through pills as well, and the arrows bound to it on its own board, read from the transaction, so one drawn in the
  same transaction counts; a step on a board that is not shown leaves the ends on the board shown
  (`Transaction.mayReachBoardShown`), and a delete of shapes that are no relationship type costs one lookup of
  an added value an id). A handler runs where the core's refusal checks are off, so it leaves a locked arrow for
  itself (`RelationshipIndex.isLocked`): that arrow lets go of the type where it was drawn and stays, an orange loose
  end when it has a name or a rule on it and one end at a type's note (`This arrow isn’t attached at both ends.`; with
  neither it is indistinguishable from a plain arrow that lost an end, and says nothing). The delete of the type is
  never refused, and one Undo brings the type and its end arrows back on every board, as bytes. A deviation from
  tldraw, where an arrow outlives the shape it is bound to. A type related to itself is two arrows, never a
  two-headed one, by two port drags, `Relate to Person` or one script; an arrow from a note to itself is never made
  (a port's drag cannot end on its own shape, a row's pick refuses it, and a script's is refused with `no_channel`).
- **Relate to Layer.** A pill in a type's words that names another type the type is not yet related to
  (and does not hold the fields of, a `$ref`) is a face (Selection's `shapeFaces`, Types', asked before
  Mentions' since Types is listed after it): a click pops one menu under it, `Relate to Layer`, whose item
  is `newRelationshipType` between the two types, from the type whose words mention to the type mentioned,
  in one step with the name typed in its pill inside it, and writes neither type's words nor schema (the sync hears no
  change, so no model is asked). A double-click and the hover are Mentions' as before, given by the face
  itself, so only the single click changes. The same item is in the canvas's context menu on the pill. A
  type that mentions itself is made related to itself; a type on another board is related through a pill,
  and the item says when it will be made public. Where a relationship type already joins the two types,
  or the pill names a relationship type, a note that is no type or a dead shape, the pill is Mentions'.
- **A note that is one** has the same rows with its values at the right: `RowBook.rows(of:)` pairs each row with
  the value its field holds (`ShownRow.Content`: `.text`, `.empty("add gift note")`, `.box`, `.choice`, `.summary`
  for a row with more in it, `.gone` for another type's fields whose type is gone), kept for each shape and let
  go of when a commit changes it. A value is drawn as `RowLook.of(content:mark:)` says from the check's mark
  (`FieldChecks`): wrong is red with a wavy line, a needed field with no value is amber.
- **Clicks.** Nothing in a type's rows is edited. Types registers one `shapeFaces` (Selection): a row with `›`
  and a fold ask `editor.rowBook?.openCard` for a read-only card, a `Choice` or `Choices` value lists its
  options (every item disabled), `Retry` reads again (a read-only type shakes instead) and `Settings…` opens
  Settings; anywhere else a press is the note's. Its `doubleClick` does the same for the first two, so the
  second press of a fast pair does not begin an edit. While the words are edited a kind's editing view lays
  Types' `RowsView` over its rows (`context.service(RowBook.self)?.makeRowsView(for:host:)`, as
  `NoteEditor` does) and a press there is the rows': the same clicks, and no caret moved. On a note that is one
  a click on a value acts at once, even on a note that is not selected: a typed value or a row with more in it
  begins the note's editing session in that row (`editor.beginEditing(_:at:)`), a box is ticked, a choice pops
  its menu; a click on a name only selects the note (its double-click edits the words), and on a locked note a
  change shakes it while a card opens to be read.
- **Typing in a row.** A note that is one has two places for the caret in its one editing session, the words
  and a row. `NoteEditor` hosts Types' `RowsView` over the rows (`makeRowsView`) and hands it the press that began
  the session (`rows.begin(at:clickCount:)`: a typed value's field takes the keyboard, the caret where it was
  pressed). A typed value (text, a number, a date, either of two such kinds) is edited by a one-line field,
  each keystroke a commit through `editor.fieldWriter` (one undo step a field, `Change Email`), stored as
  `FieldText` says (`9.50` is 9.5, `02134` is text, `3/3/26` is the day) and shown as typed while the caret is
  there; the field tells `editor.fieldChecks` it is the one typed in, so what is half typed is never red. Tab,
  ⇧Tab, ↑ and ↓ walk the rows, Return and Escape end editing, Space toggles a box and pops a choice's menu, and
  Return on a row with more in it asks for its card; a row that is not typed swallows every other key.
- **⌘F finds a value.** Types' `FieldFindPlugin` (a plugin value of its own, after Find and Types) gives
  [Find](#find) the texts of a note that is one's values as its rows show them, and a hit marks that row's value
  (a match inside a row with more in it marks the row, a folded one the fold). Its `affected` is
  `RowBook.reached(by:)`, asked once every service has the commit, so the type index has told the book which
  instances the commit reached.
- **For [Neighbors](#neighbors)**, `TypeLightsPlugin` (a plugin value of Types' own, after Neighbors, and after
  mentions' lights in the shipped list) gives two lights in one pink (`TypesStyle.instancesLight`), only while the
  hovered shape is a type: Instances (`TypesStyle.instances`), `:is-a(#id[schema]):not([schema])`, what is of it
  however far and never a type (myCar, a Toyota, under Car), and Subtypes (`TypesStyle.subtypes`),
  `[schema]:is-a(#id[schema])`, the types built on it however far (Toyota under Car). So a type's Connections tab
  lists both. They ask Types' own word, `:is-a` (`TypeQueriesPlugin`), so they follow it, through a shape that
  is no type now, where a shape's Types tab and rows follow the chain, which stops there.
- **Zoomed out** a kind's skeleton asks `context.showsTypeRowBars` (14% and up) and calls
  `context.fillTypeRowBars(of:in:)`: a bar for each row's name (as wide as its columns, never laid out), three
  dots for a fold, three bars while the model reads, one for `No fields` and a reason (also under a type's rows,
  below); below 14% no bar is drawn.
- **Announcements.** A type's change, which moves what a list resolves to, has the type, its instances near and
  far, and the instances the same commit added laid out again (`editor.shapesDidChangeLayout`): no commit, no
  step. A rename moves no size and only redraws. The sync's status or wait changing has a type's note laid out
  again: one with no rows shows another spot, and one with rows gains or loses a row at their foot, where a read
  that failed says why (`RowBook.foot(of:)`: the reason and `Retry`, `No API key` and `Settings…`, `Schema too
  long to rewrite`; the rows above it are the last good ones, and while a read is out they stay with no bars). A
  layout asked mid-transaction (a draw, a paste, a type and its instance written
  together) resolves over the shapes as the transaction leaves them.

### References between types

A type refers to another as a JSON Schema refers to another document: with a `$ref` to its URI,
`urn:uuid:` and its id, lowercase (`SchemaReferences.uri(of:)`; `target(of:)` reads one, in any case,
whole or with a fragment), so a rename changes no schema and a type on any board of the file is
found. Its words say so with a mention of the type: a note's text is plain mention text, so the `@`
picker lists every mentionable shape, and a mention of a type is a `$ref` to it while a mention of
anything else stays words.

- **A name, as a mention is.** `SchemaText` is [`ShapeNaming`](#values-that-name-shapes): a copy of a
  type with the types it refers to refers to the copies, in its schema as in its words, and one
  copied alone to the originals; a cut and paste keeps them; deleting a type writes nothing, its
  `$ref`s pointing nowhere until the deletion is undone; `canvas draw` warns of a `$ref` to a shape
  that isn't in the file.
- **What the model sees.** Never an id: each type a type's texts name is `@` and a word of its name
  (`SchemaReferenceNames`: its words run together, each after the first capitalized, then a number
  for a second type of one word), listed first in `<schemas>`; a mention is its word, a `$ref` that
  word as its URI. What it writes is read back: a `$ref` to a word is its type's URI again, and `@`
  and a word in the words a mention of its type. A mention of a shape that isn't a type is read as
  its label, and so is a mention of a relationship type (`TypeIndex.canBeEmbedded`: a type that is no
  relationship type, asked by the sync, the request for highlights and the `$ref` completion): its fields
  belong to its arrows, so another type's words naming it are plain words, and the `$ref` completion
  leaves it out. A `$ref` to one written by hand still reads as its word. What the sync's two prompts say of a title from a field (`toSchemaTitle`,
  `toSchemaNewTitle`, `toPromptTitle`) goes after each on every request; for the words of a
  relationship type (the shape holds the mark) the to-schema prompt gets one more literal after
  those (`toSchemaRelationshipType`: its ends are arrows and never properties, its properties are only
  what the relationship itself holds), and what the prompts say of other schemas
  (`toSchemaReferences`, `toPromptReferences`, `highlightsReferences`) goes after that only in a request
  that names some (`SchemaPrompts.system(_:schemas:relationship:)`).

### The card and the form

A row of a note that is one that holds more than a row can show (a group, a list, pairs, the fold of
inherited fields, a type's own row of a kind with more in it) opens a [card](#cards): `editor.fieldCards`
(`FieldCards.open(_:)`, asked with a `FieldCardRequest`: the row's rect, which fold, a way to find the row
again) shows the core's `CanvasCard` about the note, holding a `FieldFormView`, one AppKit view with one
text editor over the focused cell. The form is values first: `FieldSheets.sheet` is a pure `FieldSheet` of
lines, cells and stops for every kind of field (a draft for the lines a file does not hold), and the view
only draws and keys it (Tab, Return, Esc, the arrows; a row with more opens in the same card, Esc goes
back). Every write is `editor.fieldWriter`'s, in the step named for the top-level field (`.card(key:)`, so a
card's edits are one step until it closes), each keystroke a commit; the cell with the caret tells
`editor.fieldChecks` and is not marked while it does. A type's own note and a locked note open a card to
be read (`mode: .kinds`, `isReadOnly`). The panel holds the same form under a field's name
(`FieldForm`, `presentation: .panel`): closed until opened, open on its own where a value is wrong, and a
box of JSON for a field no control suits (`Other`).

An arrow of a relationship type has a card of its own: `editor.openRelationshipCard(for: arrow)`, which the
chip of a relationship type that has fields opens (a click on any other chip pops its menu), asks for a
`FieldCardRequest` whose target is `.shape` (`FieldFormRoot.shape`): a line for every field of the arrow's
types, under the type's chip, hung 4 points under the arrow's [adornment anchor](#adornments) and following it,
the arrow selected while it is open, each field its own undo step named for it (`Change Role`), read-only on a
locked arrow, refused among skeletons and where the types have no fields.

A relation row that holds a relationship ends in `›` and opens a card of its own (`FieldCardRequest.Target.relations`,
`FieldFormRoot.relations`, `FieldSheets.relationSheet`): the `table(names)` layout with an `owner` on each cell and line, a
line for each relationship (the note at the other end, then a cell for each field of the relationship type, each written to
that line's arrow through the one writer, on whichever board the arrow is) and a blank line that lists the notes the row
may name and draws the arrow. Everything done in it while it stays open, cells on several arrows, a pick, a line taken
out, is one undo step named for the row (`Change Friends`).

A relationship's values are shown nowhere on the board: the chip of a relationship type on an arrow says how
many fields the type gives the arrow (`friendship 2`, Adornments' [`counted(_:)`](#plain-text-and-a-number)), and a
click on it opens the arrow's card, where they are.

An end's arrow (the arrow between a type and a relationship type) says nothing on the line: the two arrows at a
relationship type are the halves of one line through its pill (a layout input, `EndArrow.input`, which Arrows reads:
no head at the pill, no words, and, with one end on each side, each half its part of the circle through the two
types and the pill), and the type's card names the rows.

### The values a type's fields hold, checked

A note that is an instance of types holds values for their fields (`fieldValues`), and
`editor.fieldChecks` says what is wrong with them: `fullCheck(of:)` for a record is a `FieldCheck`, a
list of problems each at a path a row names, of three classes. A **needed** field has no value (`required`,
`dependentRequired`, or "at least one of"; a needed yes or no never counts, an unticked box is a
value), and is an issue of Validation's third level: amber on its row, no ring, and `:incomplete`. A **wrong** value breaks a rule (`type`, `enum`,
`pattern`, a bound, a `format`, a list limit), and is an error from a rule of Types' own, so the note
is ringed, listed in the Issues tab and `:invalid`. A **warning** is orange (a type whose JSON refers to a
type that is gone): a ring and an Issues line, no red, not `:invalid`. A rule across
fields that is broken is a wrong problem at the root, with no row.

It is the core's validator run over the composed schema of the shape's types, made checkable
(`FieldSchemas.checkable`) so it says what people mean: a value no field names is never wrong, an
`if` on a field asks only once the field has a value, "at least one of" names every field it would take,
and a pattern ICU cannot read is not the note's fault. The formats `email`, `date`,
`date-time`, `time`, `uri` and `uuid` are checked, as `SchemaFormats.standard`. One checker is kept for each
distinct list of types and one answer for each shape asked; an answer is trusted while its inputs are
the ones it was made from, so nothing is invalidated when a type changes. A type's edit reaches the
shapes through `TypeIndex.onChange`, and Validation through the rule's `affected`
(`FieldChecks.affected(by:)`), asked once every service has the commit.

The caret is `typing`: the path of the field being typed in is left out of `check(of:)`, so a half-typed
value is never red; it returns when the caret leaves.

### Keeping the words and the schema in step: `TypeSync`

Edit the words and Claude rewrites the schema; edit the schema by hand and Claude rewrites the words
to say what it now holds. `TypeSync<Schema>` does it per shape, generic over the property it writes
and the prompts it sends (`SyncedSchema`: a type's is `TypeSchemaProperty`, with `SchemaSyncPrompts.types`,
"Update Schema", and its name put in), through `editor.languageModel`; `editor.typeSync` is a type's.

- **When.** Only the person's edits to the two sides: never its own write, a board read again (which
  takes every type of the file afresh), a change to anything else (a move, a lock, a rename), or an
  agent's write (`ChangeSet.byAgent`), whose sides are taken as in step. A shape the person makes a
  type waits as an edit does and is committed on the scheduler's next turn: the read starts at once,
  with no 3 s wait. A commit (editing its words ended, however it ended,
  `EditorService.editingDidEnd`, the next turn; ⌘↩ in the JSON, or the keyboard leaving it) syncs at
  once; otherwise `TypeSync.idleDelay` (3 s) after the last keystroke, on `editor.scheduler`, not
  while the JSON's completion list is open.
- **Which way.** The words changed (and aren't empty): the schema is written from them, the model told
  the words at the last sync. Else the schema changed in meaning (a reformat, a reorder or a root
  `"title"` doesn't count): the words are written from it. A schema past 34 KB is never sent: "Schema
  too long to rewrite", and the person edits it by hand.
- **The name.** The type's title goes in as the root `"title"` of each schema sent (unless the person
  typed one there), so the prompts, and the evals that read them, are unchanged; the model's root
  `"title"` comes out of what it writes back, and names an untitled shape in the same step.
- **The color.** A type's `$color` and `$autofill` are never sent (the highlights' request leaves them
  out too), a change to them alone is no change of meaning (the pair in step takes the new text, and
  nothing waits), and a schema the model writes, or words that are JSON taken as the schema, keep them
  (`HeldDirectives`).
- **Never** while the schema isn't a JSON object, for a read-only shape (on whichever board it is,
  asked as the sync starts and as an answer lands), or for a shape with no fields and no words; with
  no model at all, a side to write fails saying "No language model". A shape seen for the first time is in step, but words over a schema with no fields,
  never answered, are ahead.
- **While a call is out** the side it writes is read-only (the JSON, `detailUpdating`; a note's editor,
  read-only and faint, showing what lands), and its answer is dropped if that side changed; edits to
  the other side wait for it. A failure says why, with Retry, Open Settings… alone (saving a key
  retries) or nothing (`editByHand`); `NO_CHANGE` writes nothing. The file closing (the editor
  going, and the sync with it: the `isolated deinit` of its `SyncShapes`, a class apart and not
  generic, since Swift's optimizer crashes on one in a generic class built for macOS 14) cancels
  every call out and every edit's wait,
  so none runs on spending the person's tokens on an answer nothing lands.
- **The words' answer** comes inside `<answer>` and `</answer>` (`SchemaPrompts.answerTag`), and
  only what is inside them is the words (`SchemaPrompts.parse`): the model sometimes opens with a
  remark, and asking it not to made that worse. The last complete pair is read; an opening tag
  never closed takes what follows it; an answer with no tags is read whole; `NO_CHANGE` is judged
  outside the tags and inside them; tags with nothing in them are an unusable answer. The schema is
  answered bare.
- **Undo.** Its write is a step of its own ("Update Schema", "Update Text", the words through the
  kind's `TypeWords.write`), on the shape's board shown or not (`transact(on:)`); undo and redo start
  no sync (`ChangeSet.restoredStep`), and the pair last synced goes back and forth with the steps
  (`UndoParticipant`).
- **What it asks** is `SchemaPrompts`: the two system prompts (raw string literals, byte for byte,
  which [`scripts/schema-prompts/evals.py`](../scripts/schema-prompts) reads out of the Swift; they
  still say "prompt" for the words), the user message (`<schemas>`, `<previous_prompt>`, `<prompt>`,
  `<schema>`; or `<schemas>`, `<prompt>`, `<previous_schema>`, `<schema>`), Haiku 5.5 at `medium`, and
  `parse`. `editor.typeSync?.status(of: id)` is observed a shape at a
  time, so a panel redraws for its own sync only.

### Filling a note's fields from its words: `FieldFill`

Write "purpose is to sort the mail, already started" on a Feature and Claude fills its `purpose` and its
`status`. `FieldFill` (`editor.fieldFill`) does it, one way: the words are the person's, the values
follow them, and a value typed by hand never rewrites the words.

- **When.** Only the person's edit of the note itself: its words (once editing them ends, else 3 s after
  the last keystroke), a type given to it, its own say turned on, or editing it ending over words never
  read (a note written before its type had fields). Never an agent's write, undo or redo, a board
  opened, a type's change (that would ask once for every note of it), a type's own note, a read-only
  note, empty words, or types that give no fields.
- **What's asked.** `FillPrompts`: the fields as a JSON Schema (another type's fields written out in place
  of its reference), what they hold, today, and the words, with the words they were last filled from,
  so the model changes what the edit changed and a value typed by hand that the edit didn't touch
  stays. The answer is the changes, a JSON object (`null` takes a value away), written to the note's
  fields alone, never over a value the person changed while it was out, through the one writer
  (`FieldWriter.fill`): one undo step, "Fill Fields". Haiku 5.5 at `medium`; `fill_evals.py` is its lite
  eval.
- **Whether.** `autofill` on the note (its own say), else what its types say (a type's `"$autofill":
  {"const": false}`, kept in step with the type's own `autofill` as `$color` is with its color, and
  passed down to the types built on it), else on: `TypeIndex.autofills`. The box at the foot of the
  Types tab (`Fill fields from words`), and of a type's Schema tab (`Notes fill fields from words`),
  says it; a note holds its own say only where it differs from its types'.
- **On the board.** While a call is out the note's empty fields show a bar where `add …` was; the panel
  says `Filling fields…`, or why it failed, with Retry or Open Settings….

## Colors

Colors ([`Sources/Colors`](../Sources/Colors)) is a horizontal: a shape of a kind that opted in has a
color, and its kind draws it. It is loosely tldraw's color system: a set of named colors, each drawn
in roles that suit a line, a surface, text and a sheet of paper on the light canvas and the dark, and
colors of a document's own. What a color looks like is [Palette](#palette)'s `Swatch`; which names
there are, and what each shape's color is, is Colors'; what a kind does with its color is the kind's.

A color is a named color or a hex value (`ShapeColor`: `.named("blue")`, `.value(RGB(hex: 0x4465E9))`),
one string on a board. Ten names are built in (gray, red, orange, yellow, green, teal, blue, indigo,
purple, pink), and a file adds its own (a name and a value, kept on the file as a
[file value](#file-values)). Every list of colors offers the named ones only; a hex comes from the
system color panel, or is typed.

A kind opts in where it's registered, and reads its colors where it draws:

```swift
registrar.shape(StickyNoteDefinition()) { note in
    note.colorable(default: .yellow)        // a note has a color: its paper, yellow without one
}

func render(_ shape: ShapeRecord<StickyNote>, in context: RenderContext) {
    let colors = context.colors(of: shape)  // the roles, in the appearance being drawn
    context.cg.setFillColor(colors?.paper ?? NoteStyle.color.cgColor)
    …
}
```

- **`colorable(default:)`** opts the kind into `ColorProperty` (key `color`, nil on a shape with no
  color of its own) and says what such a shape is drawn in: a built-in name or a value, or nothing,
  for a kind whose shapes then look as the kind does on its own (`frame.colorable()`). The registry
  refuses a default that names a color no file is sure to have. In the kind's schema the property is
  a string with `contentMediaType` `text/x-canvas-color`.
- **`context.colors(of: shape)`** is the seven roles as `CGColor`s (`SwatchColors`), or nil for a
  shape drawn as its kind looks on its own. One lookup a shape, so a skeleton reads it too. A shape
  whose color is a name the file lacks is drawn as though it held none, and warned of.
- **A color given.** A shape with no color of its own takes the one another plugin gives it, before
  its kind's default: `InheritedColors`, a face on the kinds a scope reaches, answered from what a
  service keeps, since it's asked whenever such a shape is drawn or listed. Types gives the shapes of
  a type the color its type's shape holds:

  ```swift
  registrar.forShapes(holding: IsAProperty.self) { typeable in
      typeable.inheritedColor { id, editor in editor.types?.color(inheritedBy: id) }
  }
  ```

  The first answer the file has wins, in plugin order; nothing is written to the shape. When what a
  plugin gives changes with no commit naming the shapes (a type given another color), it calls
  `editor.colors?.inheritedColorsDidChange()`, and the canvas, the lists' tints and the panel's row
  follow.
- **`editor.colors`** (`ColorBook`) is what another plugin asks: `names` (the built-in ones, then
  the file's), `color(of: record)` (the color a shape is drawn in: its own, else the one it's
  given, else its kind's default), `swatch(of: record)`, `swatch(for: color)`,
  `color(\.solid, of: record)` (one role as a color that follows the appearance, for a view; a
  kind's own typed shape too, for its title's cover) and `onChange`, called when the file's colors
  change. `editor.setColor(_:of:)` gives shapes a color, or takes theirs away, in one step.
- **Where a color is picked.** The panel's Color row, one line in the Style tab, on the kinds that
  hold a color (`forShapes(holding: ColorProperty.self)`, over the record): a dot and the
  color's name, which opens a grid of the named colors, None and Other… (the system color panel); a
  value picked there can be named, which adds it to the file, and a color of the file's is renamed,
  changed and removed from its dot's menu. `/color` in a shape's text lists the named colors, each a
  chip in its color, and takes a typed hex. Color ▸ in a shape's menu colors the whole selection.
- **A file's colors.** `editor.defineColor(named:value:)`, `renameColor(_:to:)` (every shape that
  holds the name, on every board, is renamed in the same step), `setColorValue(of:to:)` (every shape
  that names it is recolored, and none is rewritten) and `removeColor(_:)` (each shape that held it
  takes the value as a hex, so it looks as it did).
- **What agents write.** `canvas draw` takes `color: blue` or `color: "#4465E9"` on a kind that has
  one, and on an edge for its arrow; a name the file lacks is refused with the names it has.
  `canvas query` finds `[color="blue"]`, and `[color]` is a shape with a color of its own.

What the shipped kinds do: a note's paper is its color's `paper` (its type's color without one of
its own, else yellow; a type's note stays white), a frame's surface and border are `surface` and
`solid` (none without one), a subboard's card and border likewise (indigo without one), an arrow's
line is `solid` and its label `ink` (its relationship type's color without one of its own), and a
type's color is the color its note holds, written in its schema as `$color`, else one of eight names
by its id. Only a color a type's note holds passes to the shapes of it (the first its chain holds, a
later type first and a type before what it builds on, as fields resolve); the one its id says is its
pill's and chips' alone. A listed shape's symbol (Find, Jump To, a mention's pill, the table of
contents, the Connections tab) is in its own color where it has one, else the one it's given,
through the core's `registrar.shapeTints`.

## Language models

LanguageModels ([`Sources/LanguageModels`](../Sources/LanguageModels)) is a horizontal that declares
no extension point: it lends every editor one language model, `editor.languageModel`, for any plugin
to ask, and knows nothing of what they ask it for.

```swift
guard let model = editor.languageModel else { return }      // nil without LanguageModelsPlugin
let request = ModelRequest(system: "Answer with JSON only.", messages: [.user(prompt)], maxTokens: 2000)
do throws(LanguageModelError) {
    let response = try await model.respond(to: request)     // response.text, .stopReason
} catch {
    status = error.message                                   // "No API key"
}
```

- **The protocol.** `LanguageModel` is one async call: a `ModelRequest` (a system prompt, the
  conversation as `ModelMessage`s, `maxTokens`, `temperature`, `stopSequences`, and `model` and
  `effort`, below) in, a `ModelResponse` (its text, `stopReason`, token counts) out, or a
  `LanguageModelError` (no key,
  unauthorized, rate limited, overloaded, another status with the service's message, the network, a
  malformed answer, no answer in time, cancelled), each with a short `message` for a person and
  `isTransient` for whether trying again later may work. A message names what went wrong in a
  fragment, never what to do about it, which the button beside it says: "No API key", "API key
  rejected", "Rate limited", "Anthropic overloaded", "Anthropic error 500", "Can’t reach
  Anthropic", "Timed out", "Unusable answer"; a request the service refused (a 4xx) is its message's
  first sentence ("Your credit balance is too low to access the Anthropic API"), with the key taken
  out, were it ever in it. Cancelling the task asking throws `.cancelled`.
- **The app's model.** `AnthropicModel` calls Anthropic's Messages API from the app, with
  URLSession (no SDK, no streaming, no retries), Claude Haiku 4.5 by default, or the model a
  request names (`ModelRequest.model`, by its id: for a plugin whose task another model does
  better). It sends what a request says and leaves out what's nil: `temperature` (Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku
  5.5 refuse any but their default), `effort` (sent as `output_config.effort`; Haiku 4.5 refuses a request
  that says one), and `fallbacks` (`ModelFallbacks.default`: the service answers a decline with the
  model it recommends for the decline's category, sent as `"fallbacks": "default"` with the header
  `anthropic-beta: server-side-fallback-2026-07-01`, neither unless asked; an answer another model
  gave reads as any other, the block that marks the switch not being text). Nothing streams, so the answer comes whole, all at once: it waits a minute, and
  a second more for every 100 tokens
  the request may write (`timeout(for:)`: 16,000 wait 220 s; Haiku writes some 150 a second), and
  throws `.timedOut` past that. It reads the key at every call, so a key saved in Settings works at
  once; Save and Remove in Settings post `Notification.Name.languageModelKeyDidChange`, so a plugin
  whose call failed for want of a key can try again by itself.
- **The key.** `AnthropicKeyStore.standard` is
  `~/Library/Application Support/InfiniteCanvas/anthropic-api-key`: the key and nothing else, mode
  0600, written whole and renamed into place; a missing file is no key. Not the Keychain: the app
  isn't signed, so each build would be a new app to it. Infinite Canvas › Settings… (⌘,) shows
  `AnthropicSettingsView` (a secure field, "Anthropic API key", whose prompt says whether one is
  saved and whose tooltip says where; Save, Remove, and Test, a five-token call; a status only for
  a test and for what failed, a symbol in its tone then the words, as the panel's status lines are,
  a failure in the warning's tone, as the panel shows the same failures; and a link, "Get a key"),
  which the plugin gives as a pane of the Settings window ([the host's slot](#host-slots) for
  panes, `registrar.settingsPane`) when the model it was handed is the Anthropic one, over that
  model's key store, so the pane and the model read one key and a list given another model (a
  test's) has no pane; the app's `SettingsWindow(registry:)` (CanvasUI) hosts the panes: made
  afresh each time the window opens, and sized before it goes in, so the window opens where it was
  left. A test that can't save the key typed stops there, a test's outcome reads again whether a
  key is saved (its file may have gone meanwhile), and Remove waits for a test to finish. A plugin that finds no key offers to
  open it: `AnthropicSettingsView.showSettings()` sends `showSettings:` up the responder chain,
  which the app's delegate answers (the same selector as `BoardMenus.showSettings`).
- **Reading an answer**: `ModelAnswer.unwrapped(_:tag:)` takes off what a model sometimes wraps its
  answer in, though its prompt asks for neither (fence lines, a line of a tag alone, the answer's own
  block tags), from either end until nothing changes; a type's sync and `--ask` both read
  their answers through it (a type's words are first taken from inside the `<answer>` tags their
  prompt asks for, `SchemaPrompts.parse`).
- **`--ask`** ([`canvas query`](#--ask)) asks a model to write a query, through the editor's
  `languageModel`, with the settings `AskStyle` holds: what ships is `AskStyle.shipped`, `.haiku55`,
  Haiku 5.5 named on every request (no temperature, effort `high`, no fallback), chosen by the live
  evaluation's round 4 (99.3% over ten rounds; Haiku 4.5 missed the bar in one category);
  a type's sync asks Haiku 5.5 too (`SchemaPrompts.model`), the editor's own model, Haiku 4.5, answering only a request that names none. Its prompt is
  measured against the live model by CompositionTests' "Query prompt, live" (`QUERY_LIVE=1`;
  `scripts/query-prompts`), which asks every case on the shipped list with `AnthropicModel` and the
  key Settings saves.
- **Tests** pass a `ScriptedLanguageModel` ([Testing plugins](#testing-plugins)), never the network,
  but for the two live evaluations, TypesTests' (`SCHEMA_LIVE=1`) and `--ask`'s (`QUERY_LIVE=1`),
  which `./test.sh` never sets.

## Prose maps

ProseMaps ([`Sources/ProseMaps`](../Sources/ProseMaps)) is an engine that declares no extension
point: for any plugin that keeps a text in plain words beside a text in a lower language (a JSON
Schema, code, a query, data), it says which words say which part, as a source map says which part
of what a compiler wrote came from which part of the source. A type's highlights are one:
its words mapped into its schema. A map is a list of links, each the words as the prose
writes them and an address in the target, and both ends are found by what they are in the texts as
they are now, never by a position: words typed around a link keep it, a target laid out anew keeps
it, and a link whose words or part are gone drops. The model says the links, in a call of its own
once the target exists, whoever wrote it (the person, an agent, the model in another call), so a
map checks what made the target rather than restating it. Nothing is saved: a map is what the model
said of two texts, kept by their text.

```swift
enum Snippet {}                                     // a target: what words are mapped into
extension Snippet: ProseTarget {
    static let name = "code"                        // the model's word for it, its block's tag
    static let guide = "An address is the shortest stretch of the code, copied exactly, …"
}

// Where the words are drawn, on every frame (a render reads `context.proseMaps`):
if let map = context.proseMaps?.map(Snippet.self, of: shape.id, prose: words, target: code,
                                    askingIf: { sync.isInStep(shape.id) }) {
    for link in map.links { fill(link.inProse, link.role) }       // and link.inTarget, link.address
}
```

- **A target** (`ProseTarget`) is a type with no value, declared by the plugin that owns its
  language: its `name` (the model's word for it, "schema", "code", and its block's tag in the
  request) and its `guide` (what the model is told of it beside every target's rules: what it is,
  what an address looks like, what's worth linking, an example). That's all a target needs: its
  `Address` is then a quote of the target's text, found where it's written exactly once, a run of
  whitespace in it matching any run there (`ProseMapText.find`), so a quote of code survives its
  lines being broken anew, and one written twice leads nowhere rather than to a place it may not
  mean. A language with an address of its own, which survives the text being laid out anew, names
  it (`Address`, anything `LosslessStringConvertible`, as the model writes it), finds it
  (`locate`, given every link's address at once, so a parser reads the text once) and says what
  each leads to (`role(of:)`): Types' `SchemaTarget` addresses a JSON Pointer
  ([Types](#types-shapes-that-hold-a-schema)). Conform in an extension.
- **One legend** (`LinkRole`): a link's words say something the target has (`.element`: a field, a
  function, a column) or a rule it keeps (`.rule`: a bound, a condition, a filter), so a color
  means one thing wherever words are mapped (a type's pale blue and pale amber). A quote
  says nothing of what it is: `.element`, unless its target says otherwise.
- **A map** (`ProseMap<Target>`) is links placed on one pair of texts: each one's words found in
  the prose (in order, never overlapping, whole words before parts of words, as written before
  ignoring case: `ProseMapText.anchor`) and its address in the target, in the prose's order, each
  with where its words are (`inProse`), where its part is (`inTarget`) and its `role`; a link found
  on one side only is left out. `link(at:)` is the one whose words are at a place in the prose,
  `links(atTarget:)` those whose parts hold a place in the target, innermost first, and
  `excerpt(of:)` its part as a person reads it, each line after the first less its first line's
  indent (`ProseMapText.excerpt`). It's immutable, and the same object while nothing it's placed
  from changes, so what a reader works out from one (where its words are drawn) is kept by its
  identity. `ProseMap(placing:prose:target:)` places links you have.
- **Reading one** (`ProseMapService`, `editor.proseMaps`, each editor's; nil without
  `ProseMapsPlugin`) is `map(_:of:prose:target:context:askingIf:)`: the shape's pair's answer
  placed on the two texts, else the shape's last answer for that target placed on them (so words
  being typed keep the links still there), else nil. Give the texts as the model reads them (a
  mention as a word it can copy, an id as a name): the links are found in them, and a reader that
  draws other text moves them onto it (a type's pills). `context` is what one pair needs
  said beyond its target's guide (the types its words name), and is part of what an answer is
  kept by. Read it where the words are drawn, on every frame: with the same strings as last time it
  costs a lookup, and a target is searched again only when it, or what the links lead to, changed
  (the same text is equal and as long in UTF-8: an accent written as two scalars is another map,
  whose ranges are of its own text).
- **Asking.** A pair read with no answer is asked about as the frame that read it ends (an overlay
  that draws nothing, `ProseMapFrames`), so only what's drawn in full is asked about, never a shape
  out of view or drawn as a skeleton, which reads nothing: if `askingIf` says it may be (called
  only then: a type says "while its words and schema are in step", so what's linked
  is what both say, and a shape whose readiness changes without a commit asks for a frame,
  `editor.setNeedsDisplay()`), its prose isn't blank, its shape isn't being edited (its words aren't
  done) and is on the board shown, and the editor has a model. A pair is asked about once per
  session, whatever shape reads it (undo, a copy and a file opened twice ask nothing again: answers
  are kept process-wide by their texts, 1,024 of them), at most 4 at a time (`concurrentCalls`), the
  rest waiting their turn, which another board shown drops for shapes not on it. An answer is kept
  for its pair whatever the shape says by the time it lands, and is the shape's last unless one
  asked after it has landed, as is an answer a shape reads for its pair (a copy's, one undo
  brought back); the canvas draws again, and `revision(of:)` (observed per shape) changes. A
  failure keeps nothing, and its pair isn't asked about again until a key is saved in Settings, but one
  that may pass (too many requests, overloaded, the network, a timeout) is asked again 30 s later
  (`retryDelay`), when it's next drawn; a cancelled call is asked again when it's next read. A shape taken out of the file keeps nothing but
  its answers, by their texts; one moved to another board keeps its last. While the editor lives no
  call is cancelled; the file closing (the service going with its editor, an `isolated deinit`)
  cancels every call out, whose answer nothing would land.
- **The request** (`ProseMapPrompt`) is one for every target: the `frame`, every target's task and
  rules (copy the words exactly, typos and all; the fewest words; never overlapping, in the prose's
  order; only what the target says), with the target's name and its guide in it, and the context
  after it, a blank line apart, only for a request that has one, so every other request is sent
  exactly what it always was; one user message of `<prose>` and the target's block
  (`<schema>`), each trimmed. It asks Haiku 5.5 at medium effort, its temperature its own and no
  fallback (`ProseMapPrompt.model`, `effort`, `maxTokens`): every target
  does, until its own evals say otherwise. The answer is a JSON array of `{"text", "address"}`
  (`ProseMapPrompt.links(from:)`: fenced, tagged, taken back and written again, or explained after,
  its last array; an item without words or an address left out).
- **Evals.** A target ships when its evals find what a person would link, with none pointing at
  the wrong part: a type's are `scripts/schema-prompts/highlight_evals.py`, which reads the
  frame and the settings out of `ProseMapPrompt.swift` and the guide out of `SchemaPrompts.swift`,
  and scores each link as the app reads it (right, misattributed, an extra, invalid, and recall).
- **Tests** pass a `ScriptedLanguageModel` and draw frames with `renderBitmap`, whose end hands over
  what was read: ProseMapsTests' fixtures are a quoted target (`Snippet`, code) and one with an
  address of its own (`Steps`, a recipe's line numbers, a check a rule), read on CanvasTesting's
  boxes, pockets and cards (`MapBench`); `ProseMapService.forgetEveryAnswer()` (debug builds)
  forgets the process-wide answers between tests, and `placed` counts the maps placed.

## Snapping

What a drag moves snaps to the shapes around it, as it does in Keynote and Freeform: its edges and
its middle line up with theirs, and it keeps the spaces between them even, centered between two or
as far from one as the space beside it, while guides show what lines up. It's a thing you do
([`Sources/Snapping`](../Sources/Snapping)) with no extension point of its own: every kind with a
frame takes part, and the core lends one hook, the [translation
adjuster](#the-cores-part-the-translation-adjuster), which Snapping claims
([Snapping.swift](../Sources/Snapping/Snapping.swift)):

```swift
registrar.service { _ in SnapState() }                                          // the drag under way, told of others' writes
registrar.translationAdjuster { editor, start in SnapDrag(start, in: editor) }   // nil for a drag that moves no frame
```

- **What snaps** is everything a `TranslatingSession` moves: the selection dragged with the select
  tool, and a shape just placed, which follows the pointer until the release. It snaps as one rect
  (the frames it moves, together, as they were when the drag began) to the frames of the shapes in
  view but its own, along each axis on its own, to the nearest within 8 view points whatever the
  zoom (tldraw's `snapThreshold`) of: one of its edges or its middle onto one of theirs (tldraw's
  snap points, the corners and the center); its middle onto the middle of the space between two
  neighbors, if it fits there; its far edge onto where a space as long as the one between two
  neighbors would begin before them, or its near edge onto where it would end after them. Ties go
  to edges and middles before spaces, and to the near edge first. Along an axis where it snaps it
  lands exactly on the line; along the other it follows the pointer exactly, as without Snapping.
  A frame is the one the shape is laid out in (`context.frame(of:)`), so a note grown by its type
  snaps by its laid-out edges and others snap to them, and a layout change mid-drag
  (`editor.layoutRevision`) is followed at the next event.
- **Guides** show while the drag lasts, in tldraw's snap red (hsl(0, 76%, 60%), light and dark
  alike), a view point wide: for every line it's on exactly, snapped there or not, a line through
  the corners and centers on it, a ✕ at each; for every space it makes as long as one between
  neighbors, the spaces of that length side by side with ticks at their edges and middles, those
  in a row before and after them too (tldraw's). `editor.snapGuides` is what shows (`SnapGuide`:
  `.alignment(axis, at:, points:)`, `.spacing(axis, gaps:)`), none once the drag is over.
- **Always on**, unlike tldraw's (on only while ⌘ is held, or in its snap mode), but only once the
  pointer is past the drag threshold from the press, so a click, whose lone box follows the pointer
  from the press, moves it no more than the pointer does. ⌘ or ⌃ held once the drag is under way
  lets what moves follow the pointer exactly: Keynote's ⌘, and ⌃ too, as either lets an arrow's end
  bind to nothing. (At the press they're the select tool's: ⌘ on a shape starts a marquee, and ⌃ is
  the secondary click.) A key pressed or let go mid-drag takes effect at once, where the pointer is,
  and one let go counts as held for 150 ms (`editor.effectiveModifiers`), so letting go of ⌘ with
  the mouse leaves what moved where the pointer put it. Kept to one axis with ⇧ (the core's),
  it snaps along that axis alone, and shows only its guides.
- **Kinds with a frame** (`BoxShapeProps`: notes, subboards, frames) snap and
  are snapped to, locked shapes too (they stay put, and don't count in what
  moves). Kinds without one neither snap nor are snapped to: arrows, whose geometry follows the
  shapes they join (tldraw's arrows can't be snapped to either, `canSnap`).
- **Only shapes in view**: the view's world rect when the drag first snaps, read again once the
  camera moves or a shape the drag doesn't move changes (a plugin's write, an agent's). With no view
  (`editor.viewportSize` zero, as in a headless editor), nothing is in view, and nothing snaps.
- **Only neighbors' spaces count**: each frame's nearest past its far edge along the axis that
  overlaps it across the axis, and its nearest short of its near edge, so a third frame between two
  keeps their space out, and a frame has at most two where tldraw compares every pair in view. What
  moves must share the stretch across the axis that the two share by more than the threshold
  (tldraw's asks for any of it), so snapping along the other axis never takes it out of that
  stretch, where the space's guide wouldn't show.
- **Cost.** `SnapTargets` (pure: world units in and out) keeps the frames' edges and middles along
  each axis in order, and their neighbors. It's made when a drag first snaps, from what's in view,
  some 6 ms with 10,000 shapes in view (at 10%, where a frame takes over 100 ms to draw them); each
  event after is a binary search for each edge and a pass over the neighbors' spaces, 0.12 ms with
  10,000 in view, and a drag at 100% costs what it did without Snapping. `./build.sh bench` holds
  the first event to a frame and the rest to a drag event's input budget.
- **Undo** is as without it: the drag is one step, Move, and Escape puts everything back.

### The core's part: the translation adjuster

`registrar.translationAdjuster { editor, start in … }` lets one plugin decide where a
`TranslatingSession` puts what it moves. It gets the drag as it begins (`TranslationStart`: what it
moves, read-only shapes left out, and where it was pressed, in world units) and returns a
`TranslationAdjuster`, kept for the drag, or nil to leave it following the pointer. On each drag
event the session asks `adjust(_:along:for:in:)` how far to move the shapes, given how far the pointer has
come from the press, and moves them by that: along an axis it gives back as it came, a box follows
the pointer exactly as with no adjuster (the POC's `pointer.world − grabOffset`, which the
characterization tests pin); along one it changes, each box moves by exactly what it says from where
it began, so an edge snapped to a line lands on it; and a `CustomTranslation` kind's move gets what
it says. While ⇧ keeps the drag to one axis, `along` says which (`TranslationAxis`), the delta is
zero across it, and what the adjuster says across it is ignored: what moves stays there. When held
keys change mid-drag, the session asks again with the same pointer, and moves again. `draw(in:)` draws with the session, above the world overlays, so what it shows goes when the
drag does. At most one plugin may claim it; the report shows it as `translation adjuster`.

## Capabilities

Some behavior belongs to a kind itself rather than to a concern others can join. That's a
**capability**: a protocol refining `ShapeDefinition`, found with `as?` by the module that declares
it, the core or a horizontal.

| Capability | For | Used by |
|---|---|---|
| `Editable` | Edited in place: an editing placement, or opening it (Selection's double-click, Return and ⌘↓), unless its kind has an opener of its own. Supplies an `NSView` laid over the shape's editing frame (`editingFrame(of:in:)`, world units, looked at again as the shape or the camera changes: a box kind's box by default; a kind without one says where); writes go through `EditContext.update`. Only a box kind has an editing placement. | StickyNotes, Arrows (its label, which grows with what's typed) |
| `LabeledShape` (Selection's) | An `Editable` kind with a label, text on part of the shape (`labelFrame(of:in:)`, nil while it has none; an arrow's is its kept geometry's `label`, `ShapeGeometry.label`, tldraw's `isLabel` geometry): a click on the only selected shape edits it only on its label, and a drag from its label, past the threshold, is `labelDragSession`'s (the shape selected alone first, ⇧ adding it), not the selection's; a read-only shape's drag is the selection's, refused as ever. tldraw's arrow labels. | Arrows (a drag slides the label along the arrow) |
| `CustomTranslation` | Moving by its own rules instead of by its frame, when a `TranslatingSession` moves it (dragging the selection, a shape just placed). When a drag starts, `beginTranslation` gets the shape, every shape moving with it and the starting transaction (committed on its own, before the first move), and returns a `ShapeTranslation`: a closure run on every drag event with the drag's delta (the pointer's, or what the [translation adjuster](#the-cores-part-the-translation-adjuster) made of it: Snapping's snap), after the moving boxes have moved. A kind without a frame needs this to be movable at all. | Arrows (alone, bound ends slide on their shapes; with a shape they're bound to, they keep every binding) |
| `HandleProviding` (Selection's) | Draggable handles on the only selected shape. The select tool finds, draws and hit-tests them; `pressHandle` returns `.drag` or `.consumed`, and `dragSession` does the dragging. | Arrows |
| `BrushHitTesting` (Selection's) | Whether the marquee touches it, when the brush overlaps its bounds without containing them. Default: `ShapeGeometry.isHit(byBrush:)`. | Arrows (against the visible arc) |
| `DerivedProps` | Props that hold something following from the rest, which the kind's setters keep in step. A shape made from properties written somewhere else, `registry.shape(_:properties:)`, or given some of its own that way, `registry.shape(_:setting:)` (the command line's `draw`), goes through `derive(_:)` first, so it's as its setters would have left it, and so does one handed to `registry.derived(_:)` (`draw`'s width alone); a board read (a shape is as saved), a paste, and what a person does don't. | StickyNotes (a note's height, from its text) |
| `CustomSkeleton` | Drawn more simply zoomed out. `renderSkeleton` draws in `render`'s place while the canvas draws [skeletons](#skeletons) (the camera's zoom under `editor.skeletonZoom`, 35%), but for the shape being edited: its fills, and bars where its text would be (`context.fillSkeletonText`, each as long as its text's columns, `SkeletonText`), never text, shadows or pictures of its own, cheaply: the shape, its kept geometry and `context.zoom`, and what its plugin already keeps of the shape if it's there, never parsing or laying out text; a picture only through `RenderContext` (a subboard's board preview). Its outline there (selected, hovered, the hint) is its kept geometry's, right for a skeleton that fills its geometry or differs from a rect only by corners rounded a pixel or two, unless it adopts `CustomSkeletonOutline`; a shape a few pixels across is outlined by its bounds. Without it a kind is the default skeleton, its geometry in one gray (`context.drawSkeleton(of:color:)`). | StickyNotes (its yellow, its text greeked), Subboards (fills and its preview), Arrows (its arc and heads) |
| `CustomSkeletonOutline` | A `CustomSkeleton` outlined its own way while skeletons are drawn (selected, hovered, the hint): `skeletonIndicatorPath(of:in:)`, what `renderSkeleton` draws, so the outline and the skeleton agree, made from the shape and its kept geometry, since ⌘A zoomed out asks it of every shape of the kind in view each frame; nil for its kept geometry's. Found once per kind (`registry.skeletonOutlines`), so no other kind's shape is asked; never asked for a shape a few pixels across, outlined by its bounds. | Arrows (the arc and its heads, where its kept geometry is three points) |
| `StrokedShape` | A kind drawn as a line, an open shape, saying how wide its line is, in world units: `lineWidth(of:in:)`. What a tinted outline of it (`Outlines.tinted`, a plugin's own colors: Neighbors' lights) covers, drawn in full: as wide on screen as the line and a point more, round, so the shape's own line and heads don't show along the middle of the outline, a stripe in a thick line at 200% and wider than a thin one at 50%. Zoomed out, where the skeleton is a point-wide line, a tint is its plain width, and the selection's and a hover's outlines stay thin whatever it says. Found once per kind (`registry.strokedShapes`), so no other kind's shape is asked; `registry.lineWidth(of:in:)` reads it, for what decorates along a line. | Arrows (3.5, `ArrowStyle.strokeWidth`); CanvasTesting's `Cable` |
| `PaintOrderAnchored` | Painted just above another shape, whatever its place in the document. The anchor follows from the shape's own props and the document's order, since the paint order is kept until one of those changes. | Arrows (above the shapes they join) |
| `LaidOutBox` | A box kind laid out larger or smaller than the box it stores, by `laidOutSize(of:in:)` over its layout inputs: the laid-out frame has the stored origin and the size the kind answers (the box's own for one that isn't finite and above zero), and everything that asks how much room the shape takes (`context.frame(of:)`) goes by it; its geometry, outline and editing frame default to it. Not a container. | the core's geometry, hit testing, settling and enclosing, snapping, selection |
| `ShapeContaining` | Each shape of the box kind holds shapes on its board, a frame: what names it as its container (`AnyShapeRecord.container`) moves, restacks, locks and is let go with it, and nothing put down sits across its edge (`Transaction.settle`). Nothing to implement. [Containers](#containers). | CanvasTesting's `Corral` |
| `BoardOwning` | Each shape of the kind owns a board, a subboard, which the file keeps under the shape's id, never in its props (`CanvasFile`, `BoardID(owner:)`). Nothing to implement: deleting a shape takes its board and every board under it, a copy takes what it holds, a file saves every board ([format 4](#boards-on-disk)), and `editor.showBoard` shows one; Boards' `x.opensBoard(placeholder:systemImage:)` opens it. Its schema is marked `x-canvas-board`. [Boards in a file](#boards-in-a-file). | [Subboards](#subboards)' `Subboard`; CanvasTesting's `Pocket` |
| `ShapeReferencing` | Props bound to other shapes: every kind whose props are adopts it, or it stays bound to a shape once it's gone. `remappingReferences(of:_:in:)` passes each through a map: bound to the shape it gives, or, for nil, let go of where it's drawn. Deleting a shape asks it of every shape bound to it (after `willDelete` handlers, before anything's removed), and copying asks it of each copy (`record.remappingReferences(_:in:)`). It returns nil when it can't let go of a shape it can't find: a deletion leaves it as it was, and a copy leaves it out. These are bindings, which must be on the board; a name that may outlive its shape (a mention) is a value instead, [`ShapeNaming`](#values-that-name-shapes). | Arrows (an end lets go where it's drawn, keeping the curve; a copy stays bound to the copies of its shapes); CanvasTesting's `Tag` |

The rule of thumb: behavior intrinsic to a kind is a capability; behavior anyone can add, to any
kind, from any plugin, is an extension point. What a kind shows in the detail panel is an extension
point, not a capability: the kind's own plugin, a horizontal it opts into, and any other plugin that imports it can all add
to it. A capability can also pick the kinds a contribution is for: `registrar.forShapes(adopting:
(any BoardOwning).self)`, or a `ShapeCapability` a module states ([Scopes](#scopes)).

An editing view's `EditContext` is its way back into the editor: `update` changes the shape in a
transaction, and `end()` ends editing. `shape` is the shape as it is now, observed as the document
is, for what something other than typing writes while it's edited (a language model's answer: a
type note's words). `service(_:)` lends it the editor's services (a completion list's
candidates, the sync a type note's editor follows), as the detail panel's, the table of contents'
and adornments' contexts do. Services hear editing end, however it ends (Escape, a click elsewhere,
another shape edited, another board shown, an undo), what it wrote committed
(`EditorService.editingDidEnd`), its step closed unless what ended it is an action still under way
(an undo about to apply a step, a command, a draw, a file put in place), so a service that answers
it waits a turn (`editor.scheduler`): a type's sync takes its words as done then.
Two hooks of `Editable` shape what ending a session does. `discardsWhenEditingEnds(_ props:) -> Bool`
(default false) is asked by `endEditing` once the view has saved what it holds and before the step
closes, as the person ends the session (Escape, a click elsewhere, another shape edited); a true
answer deletes the shape inside that still-open step, so a shape placed and left empty nets to
nothing and no step is left (tldraw's empty text). It is not asked when an undo, redo, command, draw
or board switch ends the session (nor for a file put in place, or a shape made read-only): that
action owns the open step, and an undo may be taking the shape away itself (`endEditing(discarding:)`
passes false for those; any action under way is one). `editingStepName: String?` (default nil, so
"Typing") names the step a session opens, as a menu says Undo Edit Reference; a step an action holds
open (a placement's "Add ...") keeps the action's name.
`keepInView(_:)` brings a rect of the view (in its coordinates: world units, the shape's editing
frame at their origin, which `frame` says) into the part of the canvas the host leaves clear, 16 points in from its edges,
panning the camera at once by as little as it takes, with no zoom and no undo step: the canvas
scrolls no text of its own, so a note's editor keeps its caret in view this way as the note grows
past the window's bottom with what's typed, or an arrow key moves the caret out of view.
`startPoint` is where the press that began editing was, in world units, when whatever began it said
so (`editor.beginEditing(id, at: point, clickCount:)`), and `startClickCount` how many clicks it
was, for the view to put its selection there as a text view would (the character pressed, or the
word for a double-click); the editor keeps them as `editingStartPoint` and `editingStartClickCount`
while editing lasts. Selection's double-click passes its press and its count (`open(id, at:clickCount:)`),
and a click on the only selected shape of an `Editable` kind edits it from the release (tldraw's; the
press waits for the drag threshold, as a face's does, so a drag still moves it; not a read-only
one, which the click only selects), each only for a press on the shape itself: on what's drawn for
it outside it (a title's pill, `DecorationHits`), which isn't in its text, a double-click passes no
point and a click doesn't edit. The click that brings the window forward doesn't edit either
(`Pointer.activatesWindow`, from the host's `acceptsFirstMouse`). Return and a placement say
nothing, and the view chooses, as it always has. A note too short for its text as editing begins
(saved before notes grew with it, or drawn with a `size:`) grows to it then, in the editing's step.

## The editor, the document, and drawing

- **The document is a value.** `CanvasDocument` holds every shape, back to front, in the order of
  their stacking keys: each record carries its own (`stackingKey`, a fractional index as in
  tldraw), so moving a shape in the stack changes that shape alone. The only way to change it is
  `editor.transact { tx in ... }`: `insert` (on top), `update` (typed with `as:`; it can't change a
  shape's id, key or container), `bringToFront` and `sendToBack` (of a shape or a list),
  `bringForward` and `sendBackward` (of a list; a list keeps its order), `move(_:above:)`,
  `move(_:below:)`, `delete`, `translate(_:by:)`, which moves shapes as dragging them would,
  `moveBox(_:to:)`, which puts a box where a drag does, `turn(_:into:)`, which makes a shape
  another kind under its id ([Containers](#containers)), `move(_:to:)`, which takes shapes onto
  another board of the file, `move(_:toBoardOwnedBy:)` onto the board a shape on this one owns,
  `move(_:from:to:)` off any board onto any other, `translate(_:by:on:)`, which moves them there,
  and `move(_:above:on:)` and `move(_:below:on:)`, which restack them there, `update(_:on:_:)`, which changes a shape there, and
  `delete(_:on:)` and `delete(inFile:)`, which delete one there, `board(containing:)`, which says where a shape is ([Boards in a file](#the-editor-and-the-file)), and for [containers](#containers),
  `setContainer(_:to:)` and `settle(_:)` (`settle(_:on:)` on another board). A record carries its props, the
  values of its [added properties](#added-properties) and its [metadata](#metadata), and
  `record.copy(as:)` is the same shape under another id.
  A transaction commits once, if anything changed, and bumps `editor.revision`. What it did goes
  with it, record by record: its `ChangeSet` names the shapes it added, changed and removed, and
  of those changed, the ones it only moved (`moveBox`, as a drag and `translate` do, and nothing
  else; `edited` is what it added or changed other than by moving, and `onlyMoves` says it did
  nothing but move shapes on its board), says whether the stack changed, and the boards it took out of the file or brought in
  (`boardsRemoved`, `boardsAdded`: [Boards in a file](#the-editor-and-the-file)), or changed
  (`boardsChanged`: shapes moved onto a board that held some, the root always, or settled there,
  Delete Hidden Shapes, undoing it, and `transact(on:)`; `boardsReached` is all three), with the
  shapes it touched on them (`elsewhere`), and whether an agent made it (`byAgent`, which the
  transaction says: `transaction.byAgent`). Transactions don't nest. A body that throws commits
  nothing, whatever it changed first: services hear of no change and no refusal, the board isn't
  edited, no undo step opens (what there was to redo stays), and the error comes out of `transact`
  (untyped: catch it and cast), as [`canvas draw`](#draw) throws to leave whole; a plugin's work that
  must happen whole or not at all goes through `editor.transactWhole` ([the core's
  part](#the-cores-part-read-only-shapes)), which shakes what was refused. A frame that isn't finite never gets in: such an insert or update is dropped, since a board
  must always save. An added value the shape's kind can't hold is dropped too, and an insert fills
  in the defaults of what its kind opts into. A read-only shape (a locked one,
  `registrar.readOnlyShapes`) keeps whatever a transaction does to it, unless the change leaves it
  no longer read-only, and services hear it was refused ([read-only
  shapes](#the-cores-part-read-only-shapes)). Every commit goes into an [undo step](#undo)
  (`editor.undoHistory`): everything from a press to its release, a key, a command or a group is
  one step, and so is everything while a shape is being edited; `transact("Move")` names it, and
  `editor.undo()` and `editor.redo()` put a step's records back exactly.
- **`willDelete`** handlers run inside the deleting transaction, before anything is removed, and
  see every shape as it was, so a plugin can act on shapes about to disappear (delete what depends
  on them). They may delete more, and change what they must, read-only shapes included, and not
  only on the board of the delete: `tx.update(id, on: board) { … }` changes a shape on any board of
  the file inside the same undo step, so a handler that takes back what a deleted shape gave to
  shapes on other boards is undone, and redone, with the delete in one ⌘Z ([Boards in a
  file](#the-editor-and-the-file)); each shape's handlers run once, and they run for a shape
  deleted on another board too (`tx.delete(ids, on: board)`), with `tx.board` that board. Then every shape bound to one of them, and stays, lets go of it, as
  its kind's `ShapeReferencing` says (arrows bake their curve there). Names of them
  ([`ShapeNaming`](#values-that-name-shapes), a mention) are never looked at, and stay.
- **Lookups.** `editor.shapeContext` looks up the editor's shapes (and keeps their geometry from
  frame to frame), `transaction.shapes` a transaction's as it is so far, and
  `ShapeContext(document:registry:)` a document of your own (what's on the pasteboard).
  `bounds(of:)` is the union of shapes' geometry: what boxes a selection, or brings shapes into
  view. `solidBounds(of:)` is one shape's bounds where it has an inside (closed, finite and not
  flat; none for one kept aside): what shapes placed among others keep clear of, as
  [`canvas draw`](#draw)'s obstacles.
- **The hint** (`hintedShapeID`, a target outlined whatever the tool) always names a shape that
  exists, and so does `editingShapeID`, the shape being edited (and `editingSelectedText` what's
  selected in its editing view, if that's text: the host says, `CanvasEditorDelegate`, so headless
  it's nil; [Find](#find)'s ⌘F types it; an attachment that adopts the core's `ReadsAsText`, a
  mention's pill, reads as its text in it and any other is dropped). After every transaction that
  changed the document, services hear `documentDidChange` with its change set, in the order
  [below](#services-hear-a-change): they drop what's gone (the selection does), and redo what they
  keep per shape for just those shapes (validation does). `replaceDocument` (a board read again: a revert, a reload after the file changed on disk)
  sends one too, marked `replacedDocument`: its shapes are as saved, not as anyone changed them, so
  a service that acts on edits takes them as shapes seen for the first time (a type's sync
  does). Undo and redo send theirs marked `restoredStep`: the shapes are as a step began or ended,
  so such a service follows none of it as an edit, and puts back what it kept as it was then, as an
  [`UndoParticipant`](#undo). What's selected is [Selection's](#selection).
- **What the editor keeps.** Each shape's geometry and extent (its geometry's bounds, with its
  box), and the paint order, from one frame to the next, so a frame costs what's in view and what
  changed rather than what's on the board. A shape's geometry is kept until the shape changes or a
  shape its definition looked up through its `ShapeContext` does. The paint order is kept until
  the stack changes or an anchored shape's anchor does, which is why an anchor follows from the
  shape's own props and the document's order. `editor.shape(at:)` asks a shape's `hitTest` only
  about points within its extent grown by its `hitMargin`, and `editor.paintOrder(in:)` is the
  paint order of just the shapes that may show in a world rect: what drawing goes through, and
  overlays too, with `context.visibleRect`. Code that runs per frame doesn't go through every
  shape; `./build.sh bench` holds a hover and a drag at 10,000 shapes to a frame (16 ms), with the
  minimap drawn too, and a frame zoomed out to fit the board (at 10,000, as far as the 10% zoom
  goes), where they're [skeletons](#skeletons), and the table of contents' rows after a commit to a
  millisecond. The editor also keeps the bounds of every shape, and where each commit moved or
  reshaped shapes (its damage: where the shapes it touched were and are, with every shape whose
  geometry followed them), for a picture of the whole board kept from frame to frame, the
  minimap's, which redraws only that. Damage says where shapes are, not which is on top: a restack names the shapes it
  moved in the stack, not one it carried along above its anchor. It's host API (`shapeBounds`,
  `damageMark`, `damage(since:)`, and `outlines`, what the canvas outlines), as the minimap is
  the host's.
- **Drawing**, back to front: background and the dot grid (`DotGrid`: tiles of dots filled once,
  copied at whole device pixels, kept while the camera stays); shapes in paint order (culled by extent: those
  more than 40 world units out of view don't draw, so a shadow just out of view shows at its edge,
  a pad grown by the farthest any shape is drawn from where it is, so one shaken into view shows,
  and a shape with no outline always does), each where it's drawn
